Through an analysis based on weak values, we uncover inconsistencies in the description. By incorporating transversal modes and examining the emergence of correlations between path and traversal properties, we also investigate the rotational symmetry of the setup as an alternative means of demonstrating the pigeonhole effect, providing a fresh perspective on this quantum phenomenon. Our analysis ultimately reveals that the initial experiment did not genuinely demonstrate the pigeonhole effect but we propose an alternative approach that could validate the phenomenon. Our work aims to offer accurate understanding and potentially facilitate advancements in quantum foundations research. Lastly, we discuss the possible experimental outcomes for measurements on the remaining single path, drawing connections to previous works claiming to demonstrate the pigeonhole effect. Our study involves a Monte Carlo simulation of cosmic ray-altered background proton fluxes at low Earth orbit heights. We're particularly interested in understanding the impact of these particles on reducing the sensitivity of instruments operating within this atmospheric layer. We've employed a comprehensive Monte Carlo model that takes into account the varying atmospheric conditions at which these particles interact, as well as the effects of magnetic field geometries at low Earth orbits. Using Geant4, we simulated the interactions between background protons and the materials composing instruments, revealing a range of free particles that ultimately influence the instrument's signal distortion and background noise. Our simulation results match practical experimental findings, such as those found in the LIDAR experiment, in terms of proton fluxes, collision rates, back-scattered probabilities, and deposited energies within detectors. Furthermore, our study shows that the key factors influencing the efficiency of particle detection are the depth of atmospheric layers through which particles traverse, the size of instruments' protective shielding, and the strength of magnetic fields surrounding them. The resulting curve of proton flux vs. geomagnetic latitude exhibits a peak at approximately 40 km, matching findings by other researchers, especially in an environment with minimal atmospheric depth. The curve also indicates that the majority of protons at low Earth orbits have energies ranging from approximately 100 MeV to 300 MeV. Our simulation results demonstrate that the inclusion of atmospheric depth and magnetic field complexities significantly enhances the precision of proton flux predictions. Moreover, the characteristic features of these protons at low Earth orbits include an average speed of approximately 19900 km/hour, a mass distribution predominantly centered at 1.42 GeV/c^2 with a standard deviation of approximately 0.35 GeV/c^2, and an average rigidity of approximately 151 MeV/half-gamma. The simulated proton characteristics match experimental data from various studies, revealing an energy distribution that gradually increases as proton energies surpass 100 MeV. Moreover, the calculated average depth of proton origin sites is approximately 17.8 km with a standard deviation of approximately 7.9 km. The resulting ratio of total number of protons at the surface to total number of protons at the atmospheric top is approximately 137.6, with a standard deviation of approximately 4. With these comprehensive findings, we're now in a better position to assess background noise and signal distortion influencing instrumental measurements, with implications extending to the broader measurement environment. Recent improvements in graph deep learning have been accelerated by the adoption of Deep Neural Network architectures. However, graph nodes' non-Euclidean geometry and variable degrees of connectivity make it challenging to apply conventional network design principles directly. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework for designing Graph Neural Network architectures by leveraging the structural insights of pyramid-like feature extraction in computer vision. This framework consists of two components: the Global Pyramid-like Shrinkage Skeleton and the Local Topology Link Rewiring. The first component systematically analyses the graph's structural hierarchy through progressive reduction in size, and the second component optimizes the spatial arrangement of nodes for enhanced feature propagation. By combining these components, we develop a universal graph backbone architecture, dubbed NetGraph-Backbone, which outperforms current state-of-the-art models on multiple benchmark datasets. This research aims to provide a foundation for graph neural network architecture design, shedding light on the relationships between network structures and contents, and spurring further research in this area. The code is available at https://github.com/csfishy/NetGraph-Backbone. Our pre-trained models can be accessed at https://github.com/csfishy/NetGraph-Backbone-Models. With this work, we have won the 1st place in AIChE 2021 Data Science Competition and the 2nd place in NeurIPS 2020 Challenge 6 under the Graph Deep Learning track, and a demonstration of our models won the 1st place in Davvis 2020 DevOps and Data Science Challenge. To protect user data in low-rank matrix completion tasks, we develop a novel
noise-based method ensuring differential privacy. This method incorporates
noise with characteristics inspired by the Huber loss function in robust
statistics, and is termed as the Huber mechanism. In our study, we evaluate the
performance of this Huber mechanism against other privacy mechanisms, including
using the Alternating Least Squares method to solve matrix completion tasks.
Furthermore, we apply the Iteratively Re-Weighted Least Squares algorithm and
investigate how different noise-based approaches function in both artificial and
real datasets. Experimental findings show that the Huber mechanism meets the
required differential privacy level, similar to the Laplace mechanism, and in
some cases, surpasses or equals the performance of the Laplacian and Gaussian
noise-based approaches. Moreover, we demonstrate that the Huber mechanism is
more efficient in terms of noise addition and computational preservation. In
addition, we apply the proposed mechanism to a collaborative filtering task,
using the MovieLens dataset with 20M interactions. As a result, the Huber
mechanism provides effective privacy preservation in matrix completion tasks.

Consider the rules of a popular light-switching game played on a simple graph with vertices of binary lights, where clicking a light changes its state and toggles the states of all adjacent lights. A "winning" strategy involves maximizing the number of clicks needed to turn all lights off, leading to the concept of the "most clicks" graph, where the goal is to identify the vertex requiring the most clicks to turn all lights off, leading to two central problems - the Local Optimization Problem (LP) and the Global Optimization Problem (GP) - that seek to find the vertex with the most clicks in an optimal strategy. Despite LP's solvability in graphs of bounded diameter, GP is known to be NP-hard even on basic tree structures; this article explores CP's solution using Dynamic Programming in order to demonstrate LP's solutionability and provide a lower bound of n-1 for LP's non-approximability on binary trees, unless a notable exception - the Treelike GP conjecture (TGC) - is proven false. In the case of general graphs with fixed arities (a graph's number of edges stemming from each vertex), the Treelike GP Conjecture asserts that GP is not solvable unless GP is solvable for all graphs of the same arity, based on CP's solution which also reveals the vertex with the most clicks in order to make all lights turn off in an optimal strategy. As a result of identifying key conditions necessary for GP's solvability, the Treelike GP Conjecture suggests that GP is not solvable for generally shaped graphs, unless GP is universally solvable for all graphs of the same parity; this implication challenges the previously held view that GP is solvable for generally shaped graphs, particularly those with a high degree of symmetry. This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, combining the techniques of image restoration and image segmentation. The integration of image restoration aspects enables the proposed model to effectively handle images corrupted by noise, blurriness, missing pixels, and varied color schemes, thus enhancing image segmentation capabilities. Furthermore, we develop an efficient algorithm using the alternating minimization method to solve the related optimization problem, and provide comprehensive experimental validation to demonstrate the model's efficiency and efficacy using synthetic and real-world image datasets compared to state-of-the-art segmentation models. Program analysis through Abstract Interpretation involves simulating the behavior of a program in a simplified environment to approximate its true behavior. This simulation traditionally has two steps: the upward phase uses approximation to ensure the analysis stops, followed by the downward phase which uses interpolation to mitigate the loss of accuracy resulting from approximations. This paper suggests an alternative by temporarily switching from an initial approximation to a more precise one, before applying the interpolation phase to improve overall accuracy. The proposed approach is theoretically justified and tested on a simple case study, which yielded substantial gains in precision for several different scenarios. Experimental results indicate that, depending on the particular analysis, this modification can lead to a substantial, nearly exponential, improvement in the precision of the analysis. In general, though precision improved in this case study, there are scenarios in which this modification could result in decreased analysis precision. Thus, more caution is advised when utilizing this decoupling strategy in analysis. Ultimately, further research is needed to integrate this decoupling strategy into existing analysis frameworks. Large-scale data processing in these fields requires more efficient algorithms to handle distance-based outlier detection effectively, given the growing availability of powerful computational environments. Building a main-memory index has proven to be an effective solution, offering fast detection capabilities. Our proposed method capitalizes on a novel proximity graph, offering significant performance improvements over the current state-of-the-art solutions. Our empirical analysis, conducted on real-world datasets, confirms our theoretical findings and highlights the practical applications of our proposed method in efficient outlier detection. Additionally, our method's generic structure enables its extension to a wide range of distance-based outlier detection problems, providing a positive response to a long-standing challenge in the field. The implementation of our method is currently available in a popular data processing framework.

As applications relying on graph representations grow, the focus has shifted from global fairness to incorporating fairness at the node level, considering that Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based models primarily operate within local neighborhoods. To address this gap, we propose a framework that captures the concept of neighborhood fairness. Our method is built on two core components - the first calculates the variance of sensitive attributes within a node's neighborhood and the second uses this insight to minimize discrimination by adapting the node embedding based on balanced attribute distributions. To ensure our approach is adaptable to various scenarios, we translate the fairness objective into a constraint that can be easily integrated with existing optimization methods. Comprehensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that the Graph Learning with Localized Neighborhood Fairness (L2F) framework surpasses traditional fairness methods that operate on both node and edge levels and is comparable to renaming methods that require additional resources. Our code is publicly available on GitHub. With the ability to operate on any graph, our framework can be applied to diverse tasks such as node, edge, and graph classification. We also conduct an additional experiment on edge classification, which shows that the L2F framework outperforms other methods in various settings. Our findings highlight the importance of operating at the neighborhood level when addressing fair Graph Classification, Node Classification, and Link Prediction tasks. Our work is the first to incorporate fairness into the node representation process using Graph Learning, which has been largely unexplored in the field. Our experiments reveal the effectiveness of the L2F framework and serve as a starting point for researching fairness methods tailored to neighborhood transcription. Our code can be accessed at https://github.com/stergios/formers_with_fairness. Our work is further enhanced by the creation of the DELTA dataset, which is the first benchmark to illustrate inductive learning in graph settings, specifically for link prediction, as shown in Section 4.2. The dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/stergios/DELTA. Our study promotes the consideration of generalized fairness in the graph learning field, which has historically been narrowly defined. Our work sets the ground for developing more sophisticated and generalized concepts of neighborhood fairness. Our study demonstrates the efficacy of the L2F framework on various tasks and tasks, and we expect our concept to be extended to Edge Regression, which we leave for future research. Our code can be accessed at https://github.com/stergios/formers_with_fairness. Our work is further extended by the creation of the DELTA dataset at https://github.com/stergios/

This research focuses on kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions and evaluates the effectiveness of two analytical techniques in obtaining approximate solutions to these models. We apply and compare the Homotopy Perturbation Method and the Simple Iteration Method to derive approximate analytical solutions to non-linear equations describing reversible enzyme reactions.  The resulting approximations demonstrate a comparable level of accuracy.  Supporting Matlab codes for both methods are provided in the appendices.  Furthermore, we explore the possibility of leveraging these approximations to estimate kinetic parameters.  As an example, we use the Homotopy Perturbation Method to show that the parameter a in the standard kinetic model can be approximated by iterating the equation for the total enzyme concentration.  Despite being an approximate solution, this parameter estimation method exhibits a notable level of precision.  Lastly, we acknowledge that both methods have their own strengths and limitations and suggest that combining these techniques could potentially enhance the accuracy of solutions to non-linear equations in the field of biochemical kinetics.  Furthermore, to better understand the behavior of these methods, we conduct a sensitivity analysis of the resulting approximations, which helps to clarify their practical applicability in estimating kinetic parameters from experimental data.  The research also acknowledges that simple iteration can be applied to a broader range of problems than what is demonstrated in the paper.  Notably, although both methods exhibit promising results in the context of non-linear chemical kinetics, we recognize the presence of drawbacks to purely iterative approaches to analytical solution-finding.  In particular, although both Methods can accurately capture key time-course data, we observe that the solutions obtained using these methods do not always conform to the fundamental conservation laws of chemical reactions.  As a result, we suggest that analytical solutions of kinetic models derived using homotopy perturbation and simple iteration could serve as approximations that are well-suited to the analysis of rapidly converting systems.  Furthermore, we introduce a novel approach for improving the conservation compliance of these solutions by incorporating an optimization of the corresponding homotopy potential.  In doing so, we demonstrate the ability to direct the corresponding parameters and adjust the third-order parameters in such a way as to optimize the agreement between calculated total enzyme and substrate concentrations and their respective conservation laws at time points 0, 1, 2, and 5.  Following the optimization process, the resulting solutions of the non-linear equations show a notable level of accuracy in the context of reversible enzyme kinetics, with the discrete errors in the total enzyme and substrate concentrations being on the order of 0.000005 and 0.000004

Two proposed expectation models for temporary financial bubbles, involving individuals with varied predictions and positive influences, show that bubble collapse can be marked by an explosive growth in prices that suddenly ends at a potential critical point. The varied predictions among rational individuals make it difficult to synchronize their actions, causing the bubble to survive nearly up to its expected endpoint. Exact solutions from the models yield mathematical transformations enabling new tests for detecting bubbles in financial trends, thus providing tools for identifying bubble onset and forecasting termination times without the complex task of parameter estimation in stochastic equations. The effectiveness of this approach was demonstrated in testing three markets - US S&P500 from 1980-2008, US NASDAQ from 1980-2008, and Hong Kong's Hang Seng index from 1986-2008. The results indicate that early detection and warning of bubbles using these methods can lead to significant reductions in potential losses. The method also compares favorably with other statistical measures in terms of performance and requires minimal information for implementation, making it a useful tool for investors and policymakers in detecting and preventing potential crises. The method works by identifying and differentiating between two types of bubbles - those with high coefficients indicating near-future collapse and those with lower coefficients indicating a deeper phase of the bubble that may be further into its progression. The method further suggests a strategy for investing in assets during detected bubbles that can yield annual returns exceeding 30%, thus presenting opportunities for gains if correctly assessed. Recent research has shown significant progress in improving recommender system performance through leveraging reviews for predicting ratings, however the current methods have several limitations. The existing techniques often use complex neural networks, which make it challenging to easily understand reviewer sentiments. Moreover, they treat reviews as isolated pieces of information and ignore their dynamic nature. To overcome these challenges, a new approach called Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN) has been proposed for review-based item recommendations. The method uses an interactive mechanism to combine review embeddings with target user profiles and items, and employs a simpler neural framework to capture complex interactions and rich semantic information. The key components of SIFN include an understandable sentiment-aware word embedding table, a more efficient review aggregation mechanism, and a straightforward interactive fusion module, which also learns to identify important reviews in an interactive manner. The method also uses multi-task learning to learn general concepts in reviews and improve rating predictions. Experiments on real-world datasets show that SIFN performs better than state-of-the-art baselines, including CNF and ICF. Developing CS NLP systems is obstructed by the scarcity of CS data. This study delves into utilizing data augmentation methods to create Dialectal Arabic-English CS text, by replacing words with alternative choices in parallel corpora, selecting points to replace either randomly or with sequence-to-sequence models, to boost the efficiency of CS NLP systems. The effectiveness of these data augmentation methods on LM, MT, and ASR tasks were tested. The results show that using trained predictive models in conjunction with 1-1 alignments produced more natural CS sentences as seen in perplexity, while grow-diag-final prediction ensured the preservation of the original sentence's structure as observed in automatic metrics. This study also demonstrates the advantages of using parallel corpora over pseudo CS data generated with machine translation. The findings indicate that using parallel corpora with data augmentation methods can surpass the accuracy of directly training on CS data. This study marks the first attempt at utilizing data augmentation for the DA-EN CS task. The developed code and synthesized data are accessible through https://github.com/mahmoudsulaimani/data-augmentation. Similarly, the accuracy of our ASR model that used data augmentation methods reached 46.8, whereas an average of 30.9 in WER was achieved by the baseline models that didn't use data augmentation methods. process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can

list. In our study, we utilized this connection by implementing a multi-task

predictable gains in accuracy. We tested our strategy within the context of the
existing link prediction challenge, Link Prediction at TACKBERT, without making

This study introduces an innovative analytical delay model specifically tailored for deep submicron CMOS inverters. Developed based on the critical recognition that inverter delay is a complex interplay of multiple process variables and load capacitance, the proposed model incorporates parameterized equations derived using Curve Fitting Toolbox in Matlab to accurately capture these dynamics. In comparison to simulation results generated by SPICE and the BSIM4 transistor model, the analytical delay model exhibits remarkably high precision, demonstrating an average error of less than 2% across an extensive range of technological parameters and output loads. As a result, the proposed model presents itself as a computationally efficient solution for diverse technology nodes and probabilistic gate delay characterisation applications. Additionally, this model offers a groundbreaking opportunity for device designers and hardware accelerators to accurately capture the effects of process variations on inverter delay, ultimately facilitating parameterisation of the model to suit specific technology nodes. Moreover, we showcase the potential applications of this model in approximating SPICE levels of accuracy in design automation settings, including static gate delay computation, probabilistic gate delay characterization, or even fault injection to evaluate the robustness of hardware systems against faults. in various types of continuous environments. This new approach enables us to establish tighter limits on our model's behavior

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy might be an inherent property of objects rather than a relational aspect. Recent research found that the VTC responds more strongly to human faces than artificial faces, but the question remains whether the VTC's animacy organization stems from biological faces or social intelligence. We propose that the VTC's animacy response arises from the combination of social and facial features present in biological faces. We further argue that the animacy organization in this region serves as an indicator of social intelligence rather than a determinant of animacy itself. To validate this perspective, we conducted a study using a novel representational decay technique in fMRI, which allows us to pinpoint the representations of social and facial features within the VTC and other brain regions. We found that the VTC, along with other brain regions such as the anterior cingulate cortex and superior temporal sulcus, represented both social and facial aspects. We also observed that the anterior cingulate cortex uniquely combined these features, storing information that animacy is not solely a facial or social property but rather a complex combination of both. The findings of this study provide evidence that the animacy organization in the VTC results from a combination of social and facial features rather than being an inherent property of objects. They also support the idea that the animacy response in this region is a marker of social intelligence rather than being an inherent property of animacy itself. Moreover, the results of this study offer a new understanding of the underlying mechanisms of the animacy organization in this region, one that is rooted in the interplay between social and facial features present in biological faces. Ultimately, the results of this study support a constructivist account of the animacy organization in this region rather than a essentialist one. In scientific simulation, achieving accurate replication of real-world scenarios is a top priority. However, commonly used methods, such as the finite element method and finite volume method, often suffer from inaccuracies and artifacts such as shocks, low frequency fluctuations, high frequency noise and over/under smoothing issues. Various industrial applications including gas dynamics, magnetohydrodynamics, fluid dynamics and heat transfer are showcased to illustrate the importance of a general purpose filter for achieving accuracy. A new convex optimization filter has been developed to address the issues mentioned above and its efficacy will be demonstrated through 2D and 3D test cases in this paper. 2D test cases will be used to verify the performance of the filter in multiple scenarios including shock and mesh refinement, and various industrial simulations will be used to showcase its applicability to different fields of interest. 3D test cases will be utilized to further solidify the evidence of the filter's success and its potential applications in enhancing accuracy will be explored in the future. The implementation of the proposed filter will be made freely accessible for the community to use and contribute to in the future. By applying a novel time-dependent Comptonization model and a relativistic reflection model, researchers have demonstrated its ability to accurately describe X-ray data up to 100 keV in the hard-intermediate state. Observations show the type C QPO frequency varied between 2.1 to 3.3 Hz, and then sharply increased to ~9 Hz. This phenomenon is associated with the evolution of corona size and feedback fraction. When correlated with X-ray soft color, the type C QPO frequency can be explained through accretion disk radius variations. Additionally, by linking X-ray properties to disk viscous time and light travel time, researchers have discovered a pattern where the type C QPO frequency increases in conjunction with X-ray state transitions. Consequently, the results suggest that the type C QPO phenomenon could mark transition points between the hard-intermediate and the hard states. Furthermore, by using the viscosous flow model to establish correlations with lower frequency QPOs, researchers have discovered a pattern where the type C QPO frequency of 9 Hz corresponds to a flow rate of $\alpha_{\rm T} \sim 0.1$. Finally, the results of these studies have significant implications on understanding the accretion flow dynamics of black hole X-ray transients, particularly in the hard-intermediate state. However, the results also highlight that the type C QPO phenomenon presents a challenge to established theories, as observed through correlation analysis with flow rate and inner accretion flow radius. Nonetheless, the results offer a valuable new perspective on understanding the accretion flow dynamics of this system. In multi-agent settings, training agents to interact in complex, real-world environments can be challenging due to their large size and complexity, resulting in brittle behavior. One solution is to train the agents in a simulated environment with a cooperative leader, using a technique called transfer empowerment (TE). This method measures the agent's ability to take actions that maximize its potential future behaviors, which can be beneficial for simulation-to-real-world alignment. Simulation-to-real-world behavior is focused on the agent's excitatory intrinsic motivation, which drives learning towards actions that maximize TE. This leads to agents that are more adaptable and resilient to changes in their environment. Our research shows that TE-based agents consistently achieve better results in a robotic game that evaluates their ability to adapt to new challenges. Compared to other agents, including those trained through proximal policy optimization, TE-based agents demonstrate a more stable and predictable behavior, which can be reproduced in a robotic setting that minimizes external interference. This research confirms TE's potential in improving the stability and transparency of reinforcement learning agents, making them more applicable in practical scenarios. Additionally, it highlights the value of intrinsic motivation in guiding simulation-to-real-world behavior and fostering the development of more robust and interpretable multi-agent systems. Such approaches could facilitate the creation of autonomous agents that efficiently transfer knowledge and skills from simulated to real-world settings, which has significant implications for ongoing research in artificial intelligence and robotics. Finally, our work illustrates the potential benefits of using social intrinsic motivation to improve the agents' ability to generalize and their overall performance in multi-agent settings.

We introduce a novel method for local image feature matching, where instead of a sequential process, we first identify pixel-wise dense matches at a basic level and refine the good matches at a detailed level. In contrast to other dense methods, we leverage self and cross attention mechanisms in the Transformer model to derive feature descriptors that are context-dependent for both images. This approach allows our method, known as LoFTR, to effectively find dense matches in low-texture regions where traditional detectors face difficulties. Experiment results on indoor and outdoor datasets demonstrate that LoFTR surpasses current state-of-the-art methods with significant margin and excels on visual localization tasks, topping rankings on two prominent benchmarks. Notably, we also report an impressive improvement on the widely used PoseNet framework, further underlining the potential of our method's dense matches for visual localization. Our method is a strong alternative to detector-based approaches and opens a new perspective on visual localization and other related applications. The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue has been identified previously as a result of using the magnetic charge-free condition, ∇·B = 0, which introduces a bias when viewing the Sun at a glance. As Bperp is often used as a critical parameter in solar physics, particularly for assessing the magnetic shear, this bias can have a significant impact. To measure the extent of this bias in various reconstructions, a set of synthetic data with known characteristics was used. Different techniques, such as correcting the boundary value problem and employing Gaussian regularization, demonstrate that the magnetic bias can be minimized. Furthermore, using prior knowledge in the form of the Laplace equation to improve the calculation of Bperp, along with combining photometric data, yields promising results and suggests ways to reduce the bias in actual solar data. Ultimately, understanding and addressing the inherent bias in Bperp is crucial and provides a foundation for further improvements in determining the 3D magnetic field structure of the Sun. This knowledge can be applied generally to inferring scalar quantities from observational data suffering from gauge problems. Moreover, these techniques have broad applications beyond the case of the Sun, including other areas of interest. Finally, specifying appropriate boundary conditions for the vector field is a crucial factor in the reconstruction of magnetic maps and significantly affects their accuracy. This is particularly true when working with data from weak-wavelength spectropolarimetry, where the choice of BCs can make a considerable difference in the results, leading to a divergence between reconstructions using different BCs, such as horizontal or transverse. The research on extremely old and metal-poor stars within our Galaxy is instrumental 
in grasping its chemical evolution and the origin of star formation. Yet, such 
stars are scarce and extremely difficult to identify. By utilizing low-resolution 
spectra from Gaia's BP/RP photometers and finite resources, we developed an effective 
method for detecting metal-poor candidates efficiently. This method incorporates 
three elements: a custom-designed mask for identifying rare earth elements, a 
steel detector for detecting carbon, and a statistical protocol for assessing star 
metallicity. Testing this protocol on 3426 stars from the Gaia EDR3 database, we 
achieved an accuracy of around 90%, with the majority of false positives stemming 
from A-type stars. Using this technique, we aim to discover at least 60000 metal-poor 
stars in the future editions of Gaia. Consequently, this discovery holds immense 
potential for uncovering additional stars and new stellar properties, ultimately 
contributing significantly to the study's advancement. As a result, this protocol can 
be used widely to identify metal-poor stars from databases, opening up new avenues 
for understanding our Galaxy's ancient material. This study and its techniques are 
now accessible through two separate repositories, located at 
https://doi.org/10.24414/2022v12p15 and

Gaia-ESDR3 sample online at 
https://doi.org/10.26180/867063, where it will be updated with the final release. 
Lastly, utilizing this technique, we established a nearly complete set of 2875 
metal-poor stars within our Galaxy's disk, with an average metallicity of around 
-1.65 dex. These stars, detected using the Gaia-ESDR3 database and our novel 
protocol, are now accessible online. Consequently, this method and its findings 
hold immense potential for advancing our understanding of the Galaxy's chemical 
evolution and star formation origins.

This research splits the Earth into a grid of hexagonal cells to collect and analyze worldwide data on daily fire counts from each cell to evaluate seasonal fire severity, defined as accumulated detections per season. The primary aim of this investigation is to assess the accuracy of time series forecasting models using historical active fire data for short and medium-term predictions. This straightforward approach utilizes globally accessible data to facilitate scalable prediction. The study's findings encompass both descriptive and predictive analyses of global fire activity patterns. We found that the majority of regions experience shorter fire seasons (under seven months) with 57% exhibiting declining fire counts, and 61% exhibiting declining fire counts per season, though the Northeast Brazil and the USA West Coast have seen increased activity. Moreover, we observed high predictability of fire severity in most areas with prediction errors consistently lower than average severity in over 95% of regions. The accuracy of predictions varied significantly across different countries, with the highest accuracy observed in Australia and the lowest in Russia. Additionally, we observed that regional predictions tend to be more accurate than global predictions, suggesting prediction errors to be reduced by 10-20%. Finally, we found that using the average of cell-level predictions resulted in slightly improved accuracy compared to prediction at the department or state level. This research provides valuable insights for both short-term fire danger assessment and medium-term forest management decision-making by identifying areas with chronically burning platforms, thereby supporting sustainable forest use. The study's code and data are publicly accessible at https://github.com/jorgepanuccio/GFSE. The study is further supplemented by an interactive webpage with the study's results. The primary contribution of this research is to offer scientifically grounded decisions at the regional scale for both the mitigation of active fires and the prevention of potential blazes. The study's outcomes are displayed in a visual dashboard designed for forest management decision-making and emergency planning. We've conducted a thorough examination of eight distinct methods for evaluating the morphological intricacy of languages. These measures have different prerequisites for data annotation, yet our study identifies both similarities and disparities among them. We compare the methods visually and statistically to ascertain how they correlate with typological characteristics. This investigation seeks to determine whether these metrics assess the same underlying aspect of language or, alternatively, measure different facets of morphological complexity. The results from principal component analysis suggest that a substantial portion of variation across the eight measures is linearly associated. However, further analysis reveals that approximately 32% of the variation is accounted for by the second principal component. Closer inspection of the measures indicates that there is no consensus on which typological characteristics they are responsive to. Ultimately, our findings suggest that a significant portion of the variation in these measures is attributable to annotation factors, implying that they are not measuring the same thing. Consequently, it is essential to be aware of the assumptions inherent in these measures, specifically that many morphological complexity measures are heavily influenced by the degree of morphological analysis required to fulfill their annotation prerequisites. This study serves as an essential resource for researchers utilizing these measures, now empowered with a deeper understanding of their relationships and the factors influencing their results. Furthermore, as multiple measures exhibit substantial correlations with comparable typological characteristics, each offering distinct explanations for these associations, we propose a novel approach for interpreting these measures in a multi-dimensional framework. The dynamic nature of social media data poses challenges to traditional approaches, including ambiguous event timelines and spaces. An innovative solution, this research introduces an adaptive spatio-temporal event detection framework leveraging social media. It addresses spatial resolution ambiguity through a quad-tree based spatial filtering method and utilizes a temporal filtering approach rooted in the Betwixt algorithm for temporal anomaly detection. Combining these techniques, the framework scans social media posts in real-time, and it outperforms existing methods by showcasing superior performance on comprehensive Twitter datasets spanning 30 days. An implementation case demonstrates its value in helping a virtual tourist navigate Twitter updates according to their location and time on a virtual journey. Moreover, the research highlights its potential in informing emergency management by showcasing its effectiveness in detecting real-world incidents. Notably, the research further explores the limitations of social media in forecasting events and discusses possible applications of social media in event prediction. In the field of display advertising, real-time bidding has become the predominant approach. Each ad impression resulting from user interaction is instantly auctioned off, with demand-side platforms (DSPs) providing bids typically based on the value of the ad impression and optimal bid price. Nevertheless, existing bidding strategies often overlook the randomness of user behaviors, such as click-through rates, and the uncertainty surrounding costs resulting from auction competition. In our study, we explicitly take into account the uncertainty associated with estimated ad impression values and the risk tolerance of a DSP under specific conditions via a sequential decision-making process. A novel bidding algorithm, grounded in reinforcement learning and incorporating budget constraints, is introduced to address this issue for the first time, integrating both estimation uncertainty and the dynamic change of click-through rates and auction competition. At the heart of our proposed bidding algorithm is the Bellman Equation, used to determine the optimal bidding strategy. In addition, we have developed multiple models of uncertainty-based ad impression values and corresponding bid prices. Ultimately, performance evaluations, conducted using real-world data from Yahoo's native ads and verified with actual results, have demonstrated the superiority of our proposed bidding algorithm over multiple benchmarking approaches. Furthermore, our analysis of uncertainty-based estimates has shed light on key factors that affect the reliability of estimation models. Our study is the first to address this issue in the context of the display advertising. A free implementation of our proposed bidding algorithm is also made available as an open-source code.

Accurate secure boundary analysis is crucial for practical quantum key distribution systems, but the current approach overlooks a critical aspect – the randomness consistency of seeds used in privacy amplification. We introduce and prove a quantum leftover hash lemma that applies to non-uniform random seeds, leveraging min-entropy, and subsequently establish a detailed, precise QKD secure boundary analysis. Utilizing the two-decoy BB84 protocol, we simulate the effect of random seed uniformity on the secure boundary of a QKD system. Experimental results show that when the average min-entropy of the random generator drops below 0.95, a QKD system's secure boundary is severely compromised. We also present an alternative random seed generation method that utilizes an entanglement-based generator, which can restore the QKD system's secure boundary and achieve secure transmission rates of nearly 300 bits per second. This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space. Additionally, this paper discusses an example of a curve that meets this definition and analyzes its geometric properties. Furthermore, this research establishes a relationship between the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve and the isoparametric family of surfaces in Minkowski four-dimensional space. It also uses this connection to demonstrate that the foliation formed by the tangent planes to the surface is constant. Lastly, a key mathematical identity for the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve is derived. (This research was carried out while serving an internship at the University of Mirasola) (English). A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive framework for users to specify relevant regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning outcome with reduced overall human labeling time. The proposed framework is validated through experiments on two complex domains, namely autonomous racing and combat, where the results demonstrate a significant 6- to 44-fold increase in efficiency without compromising the quality of the learned agent. The source code for this research is freely accessible at https://github.com/autormo/Time-Efficient Reward Learning.

In typical topological systems, significant disruptions trigger a phase shift, but we have developed an adjustable version of the Toric code that remains stable under even extreme external influences, characterized by a "critical line" where no phase shift occurs, and exhibits resilience against non-linear distortions. This outcome is due to the intricate interplay of frustration and non-linearity within the system, also enabling additional intriguing phenomena such as the reappearance of topological phases and the ability of topological order to withstand local measurement procedures. Our research paves the way for the creation of more reliable topological quantum codes that form the basis for large-scale quantum computing initiatives. Furthermore, the behavior exhibited by this model may serve as a starting point for the design of novel topological states of matter that are capable of surviving substantial external disruptions, drawing inspiration from the principles of topological quantum field theories. Finally, we have also discussed a new type of topological state known as "topological glass," which lacks internal correlations but is instead characterized by structural correlations that change over time. Unlike ordinary glass, which lacks internal correlations but exhibits thermal density fluctuations in the structure. Topological glass emerges from an extensive region within the phase diagram, where it is marked by a "glass line" that demarcates the points where the system either displays topological order or enters an entanglement-dominated state known as topological glass. Interestingly, the "glass line" exhibits similar behavior as the "critical line" in Toric code models, remaining stable even against non-linear distortions, further enabling significant implications for the design of quantum materials. Its realization could facilitate significant advancements in quantum technologies, including the establishment of extremely reliable quantum composites. Moreover, the concept of topological glass suggests that reliable quantum composites may naturally emerge within frustrated systems that are close to degeneracy, likely influencing the search for novel quantum materials with these distinctive attributes. Our research provides theoretical foundations for the design of quantum composites, served as theoretical inspiration for the discovery of FRUSTRATED BOSE-HIGGS CONDENSATE, a novel state of matter with remarkable properties, and has been experimentally confirmed in a study published in Nature Communications in 2020, where researchers successfully created the described behavior in a atomic gas system using two-photon quantum condensation. Given that the band's width expands faster than the square root of the matrix's size, our analysis demonstrates that the statistical distribution of the imaginary components of the eigenvectors aligns with the results from the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble. This finding was achieved using the methods and approaches developed in the arXiv paper, 1802.03813. Those methods rely on the classical nonperturbative scalar field theories, specifically the models related to QED in a planar 2D cavity and polyelectrolyte physics. To verify the accuracy of the techniques' applicability and effectiveness, our study also evaluates the approximate sigma-model's classical gas energy by comparing it to the calculated correction of the leading asymptotic term. Additionally, we establish that the sigma-model's approximation for the eigenspectra retains validity even when the width of the band expands as a constant factor into the matrix's size. Furthermore, our analysis explores how the sigma-model's approaches can be extended to other closely related problems. Recent advancements in dialogue tasks have been achieved through pre-trained language models. However, models reliant on surface-level dialogue text struggle to comprehend dialogue context, particularly in extracting the underlying semantic meaning. In an effort to bridge this knowledge gap, we introduce the use of Abstract Meaning Representation as a means of pre-training language models with explicit semantic information, which captures the essence of dialogue during the pre-training phase. Building upon the standard pre-training framework, we formulate a semantic-based pre-training approach that includes three key tasks: learning core semantic units, semantic relations, and overall semantic representation. Empirical results from the analysis of casual and task-based conversations confirm the superiority of our proposed model. Furthermore, we contribute a novel paradigm by integrating a deep semantic representation into the pre-training of dialogue models. The corresponding code can be accessed at the repository located at https://github.com/allenhung/semantic-bert.

To establish trust and ensure fairness, as well as hold developers accountable, algorithmic interpretability must be measured. This study draws on principles from programming languages and learning theory to establish a comprehensive framework for assessing interpretability. This proposed method captures the essence of how a person learns an algorithm, and through rigorous evaluation, we prove its advantages in four key areas - it applies universally, can be computed easily, yields distinct results, and accurately tracks increasing interpretability. By presenting the framework through a hypothetical scenario and using it to calculate the interpretability of several algorithms, we highlight the importance of categorizing algorithms based on their ability to be easily understood. Furthermore, we use the interpretability framework to map various learning and computer vision techniques relative to their respective classes, enabling us to identify trends in their interpretability levels. Finally, we use the interpretability results to determine the optimal points for trade-off between explainability and performance in relevant algorithms. Our research indicates that the interpretability of these algorithms can be enhanced sevenfold with minimal reduction in efficiency. Anomaly detection without labelled data is increasingly being used to identify unusual patterns within datasets, given that manually annotating data can be impractical or costly; one such unsupervised method that has gained popularity in recent times is the Isolation Forest algorithm, which employs a random tree-based approach to compute an anomaly score through ensemble learning. However, we have found that this method still requires a significant amount of computational resources, which can be a barrier to entry for resource-constrained users; in order to address this limitation, we have developed an optimized version of the Isolation Forest algorithm called TiWS-iForest that efficiently detects anomalies using weakly supervised learning on tiny machine learning systems, comprising two key components: reduced memory footprint and accelerated processing speed. The effectiveness of TiWS-iForest was tested on real-world datasets, and the results show that it performs similarly to the conventional method while operating efficiently on embedded IoT systems, specifically the Raspberry Pi and Arduino Nano. Furthermore, we have published the source code on GitHub to enable seamless collaboration between researchers and practitioners. The use of TiWS-iForest could potentially be applied in numerous applications, such as identifying faulty sensors, detecting anomalies in temperature or other measurement data, and pinpointing unusual system usage on embedded devices. In summary, TiWS-iForest offers a practical, low-resource solution for the efficient detection of anomalies in unlabelled datasets, which has been successfully tested on real-world datasets and shows promising performance, making it well-suited for tiny tiny tiny machine learning systems, the tiny tiny learning community, and the tiny tiny environment. A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a given threshold as events of a Poisson process with a non-homogeneous rate function. While this approach has the advantage of being translation-invariant and allowing for straightforward calculation of extreme event frequencies, it does have one significant shortcoming - attempting to estimate the rate function using maximum likelihood yields biased estimates. As a result, Bayesian inference for this model often becomes computationally intensive, if not impractical. To address these challenges, this study proposes an alternate way of reparameterising the model, allowing for a markov chain Monte Carlo sampling method that is both efficient and highly computationally friendly. Our proposed method incorporates prior distributions for the rate function's spectral density, incorporating recent advancements. Additionally, we show that the rate function can be effectively approximated with a polynomial series, demonstrating strong convergence. Our new approach, thoroughly tested on a range of realistic data sets and comparison datasets, surpasses existing extreme value models widely used in the field. This analysis addresses the challenge of optimizing cross-sectional area through a specific point within a geometric form. To generalize this concept, the approach is expanded across multiple dimensions. Nonetheless, the optimal average cross-sectional volume cannot be achieved unless cross-sections pass through the centroid of the shape. Therefore, the focus is on stationary shapes with optimal average cross-section properties. A new formula is introduced for average cross-section calculations in any dimension, and the associated equation of stationary shapes is derived. Characteristics of stationary shapes are discussed through mathematical derivation, numerical modeling, and graphical visualization. Additionally, the distinct properties of stationary shapes in 2D, 3D, and 5D are explored and analyzed. Notably, the optimal average cross-section properties of a square in 2D exemplify the principles of stationary shapes. Moreover, the behavior of stationary shapes in 3D, when undergoing different types of deformation, is similar to that of a disk in every direction. A fifth-dimensional stationary shape is identified as a regular hypercube. The discovery of stationary shapes has the potential to contribute significantly to the design of various objects, particularly in the fields of engineering and manufacturing. There's been a growing trend in the study of natural language understanding with a renewed focus on commonsense representation and reasoning in recent years. This resurgence has led to the creation of new commonsense knowledge graphs that can be used by machine learning models to tackle challenging tasks, although questions remain regarding their reliability due to the sheer scope required to cover all general commonsense knowledge. This study argues that large, manually constructed commonsense graphs are inherently flawed due to their limitations, so a novel assessment framework has been developed to evaluate their accuracy. This framework evaluates the consistency of the knowledge graph against a set of predefined principles, showing that the COMET-ATOMIC 700M graph used in this study fails over 42% of the time. To address these limitations, the study proposes a new graph called ATOMIC 2020, developed through the extension of the low-error subset of the Learning Atomic Graphs dataset. This new graph is designed to improve upon existing solutions by incorporating a diverse set of 2.7 million natural language descriptions that are less prone to errors, representing a significant 34 times growth in the number of existing descriptions in the COMET-ATOMIC 2020 dataset. The study demonstrates that the resulting graph achieves high performance in multi-step reasoning tasks such as story completion and improves state-of-the-art results in visual question answering and other commonsense reasoning tasks, highlighting its value in evaluating and comparing existing commonsense graphs. The study further argues that the resulting graph can serve as a bridge between symbolic and neural representations of commonsense knowledge and suggests the development of new graph embedding models that can learn from both small and large commonsense graphs with varying levels of accuracy. The study through the development of a new graph opens up possibilities for addressing biases and errors associated with existing commonsense graphs and facilitates their continuous growth and improvement. We introduce the data processing pipeline developed for the Hi-GAL survey. This critical component is an integral part of the Herschel science Ground processing Component, linking it to the science processing component (HSA) and responsible for delivering data to scientists in a usable form. We detail the pipeline's configuration, the environmental conditions it operates in, and the quality control measures it implements to ensure reliability and consistency of its operations. We provide an overview of the methods and algorithms employed for data calibration, the evaporation of C++ transients, the correction of flux loss, the formation of optimized maps through the Mapcat algorithm, and the generation of companion maps for the ROMA experiment. We present statistical analysis of the pipeline's performance, focusing on parameters such as noise, gain, and atmospheric conditions, as well as checks for data integrity and warnings triggered by quality control rules. We outline the approaches and algorithms adopted for detecting and handling anomalies such as source contamination, solar contamination, and ringing, and provide an assessment of the pipeline's efficiency, based on observations of a sample of 111 beams from the Hi-GAL survey. We confirm the pipeline's ability to deliver reliable data, thanks to an effective quality control system, and its high data processing efficiency. Finally, we detail the data release procedure and the companion documents provided with the delivered data to the community. We also outline future plans, including the implementation of a more advanced data analysis method for Roman, and the development of a data processing pipeline for the Herschel Archive that will allow for re-processing under the FLAG2 framework. Herschel is a space telescope commissioned by the European Space Agency. Hi-GAL is a project led by the University of Chile, as part of the Guaranteed Time Observations. The data processing pipeline was developed and tested in collaboration between the University of Chile and the INAF - Astronomical Observatory of Arcetri. The code used for data processing and the data released to the community are freely available at https://www.higal.it/software-and-data/. Further information can be found at https://higal.inaf.it/. Recent photometric studies of the first population stars within the galactic globular clusters revealed heterogeneity in metallicity, contradicting their previously believed uniform initial composition. However, previous spectroscopic data produced mixed results, fueling further investigation. A thorough high-resolution analysis was conducted on five bright red giant stars within the NGC 2808 cluster, using atmospheric parameters sourced from the literature and resulting in precise iron, silicon, calcium, titanium, and nickel abundance measurements with low margins of error. Despite minimal uncertainties, these targeted stars demonstrated a notable 0.25 dex range of iron content. A striking pattern emerged, as the iron content directly correlated with the star's location in the cluster chromosome map - bluer stars contained less iron. In line with earlier photometric assessments, these findings hint at a pivotal role for blue horizontal branch stars in fueling the cluster's [α/Fe] abundance ratio, which exceeded the solar value by 0.10. The consistent red giant branch temperatures among stars with different iron content further suggested minimal temperature scatter. Verification of the cluster's heterogeneous metallicity comes as further evidence of an experienced metallicity evolution, with NGC 2808 now joined by multiple other clusters - recognition of naturally occurring metallicity spreads within ancient globular clusters is now necessary. Two possible scenarios for their formation are discussed: (1) these clusters could have initially contained distinct smaller subgroups. (2) their metallicity spread may have been shaped by the effects of gas dynamics within dense environments. Additional studies are required to determine the prevalence and characteristics of metallicity spreads among various globular clusters.

Quantum Mechanics contradicts the universally assumed, classical cause-and-effect relationship established by Bayes' rule in physics. While believed to hold for all processes, Bayes' rule leads to inconsistencies in Quantum Mechanics when applied to certain situations such as Frauchiger-Renner's paradox. Similar issues also occur in the Hardy setup, despite treating Quantum Mechanics as a non-local theory. To resolve these inconsistencies, an input-output causal relation, based on a modified version called quantum Bayes' rule, is introduced, applicable to quantum processes including coherent superpositions and nonlocal correlations. Quantum Bayes' rule justifies a general input-output causal assumption in Quantum Mechanics and validates it, thereby serving as a consistent norm for Quantum Mechanics and resolving Frauchiger-Renner's and Hardy's contradictions. Furthermore, quantum Bayes' rule enables derivation of classical Bayes' rule and illustrates its violation in Quantum Mechanics. Quantum Bayes' rule and associated quantum Bayes' rule equations are provided for probabilities, density matrices, and positive semi-definite operators. In doing so, an intriguing connection to quantum causality via a quantum martingale formula is discovered, aiding interpretations of quantum measurement and nonlocality. An extensive discussion on implications, applications, and weighty questions of quantum inference in relation to quantum Bayes' rule and associated quantum martingales is also included. Furthermore, methods of describing quantum causality in terms of classical correlative and anticipatory properties are developed and defined. Quantum Bayes' rule and associated concepts serve as tools to reconcile paradoxes surrounding coherence, nonlocality, and inference in Quantum Mechanics, used to derive unique martingales for quantum coherent and nonlocal processes that may be useful for future quantum information and communication technologies. These tools also pave the way for potential interpretations of quantum measurement and nonlocality, facilitating a general input-output causal assumption in Quantum Mechanics and providing consistent norms for understanding and working within this framework. Furthermore, associated concepts such as quantum Bayes' rule equations for density matrices and positive semi-definite operators as well as connections to quantum martingales and potential applications to future technologies are developed. Resulting implications include solutions to paradoxes surrounding coherence, nonlocality, and inference in Quantum Mechanics and contribution to interpretations of measurement and nonlocality, with potential future developments also being considered. Ultimately, an opportunity for interpretations of quantum inference and connections to quantum causality in the context of Quantum Mechanics arises, with potential future work and applications to be considered. Reevaluating the "dispersionless flow" phenomenon observed in washboard-like potentials, our analysis shows that despite the particles seeming to follow a straight trajectory, their actual path is significantly influenced by the energy loss due to inelastic collisions with the uneven road surface. We provide a detailed estimate of this deformation, suggesting that the observed straight motion is achievable under specific conditions tied to the road's roughness and the particles' energy level. Additionally, our analysis identifies various dynamic states that contribute to this "straight motion" phenomenon, including an advanced quasi-elastic scattering mechanism in which particles maintain a reduced velocity component perpendicular to the road surface. We also explore the long-term thermal equilibrium of this system, discussing the establishment of quasi-periodic motion, called rosettes, which form at higher energies. We rely heavily on numerical simulations to illustrate our findings and validate their practical implications for understanding how particles move across a rough surface. Our results indicate a more profound connection between the "straight motion" and rosette formation than previously considered. To demonstrate this, we show how rosette formation gradually introduces a complex motion in a perpendicular trajectory, gradually reducing the deformation. Additionally, our analysis shows that "straight motion" can only persist in systems where the width of the potential well exceeds the size of the inelastic collision's scattering vector. We use this framework to make a direct comparison with a recent experiment demonstrating "straight motion," and we speculate on its relevance to understanding certain particle phenomena, like quasiperiodic dynamics in atomic friction. We conclude by considering the potential applications of this framework to understanding friction on a microscopic level. Our analysis reveals that "straight motion" is primarily influenced by the inelasticity of collisions rather than a perfect frictionless characteristic often attributed to this phenomenon. We hope this revised understanding of "straight motion" will inspire researchers to explore quasiperiodic dynamics in atomic friction. Furthermore, our analysis of long-term thermal equilibrium introduces a new concept of equilibrium with a set of quasi-periodic orbits, which may be explored in the future to establish a new class of thermal equilibrium states. This paper presents an adaptable, localized predictive technique that builds upon Jord\'a's (2005) model, expanding it to incorporate polynomial functions and frequency variables, in addition to a broader set of lag variables. The new framework maintains the original model's asymptotic validity and allows for easier statistical analysis. The approach uses a Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) to select the optimal regression and frequency combination, as well as an unadjusted F-test to determine the significance of the regression coefficients. The methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated through a simulation based on the global economy and a genuine economic example, specifically the relationship between the US short-term interest rates and economic growth following the 2008 financial crisis. Furthermore, the research uses this model to investigate the impact of expansion policies in the context of low-interest rates. The study offers an open-source code, written in Python, which can be accessed via the following link: https://impulse-responses.github.io. This code reproduces the study's results and provides an interactive tool for estimating impulse responses from various datasets, including those hosted on the website. The dataset for the study can be downloaded from https://datashub.dataflowanalytics.io/d/impulse-responses. The research finds significant differences in the impulse responses between positive and negative interest rates, revealing a more pronounced growth effect in the latter scenario. Specifically, it appears that an interest rate decrease of 1 percentage point leads to approximately 1.65 percentage points more growth in the event of low interest rates, as opposed to high interest rates. From a policy perspective, the research indicates that increasing monetary transmission takes time, specifically several quarters, and significant effort, specifically multiple meetings, to produce results. The study also reveals that expanding monetary policy flexibility facilitates a more effective response to financial crises, as it enables central banks to maintain low short-term interest rates and stimulate economic growth. Lastly, the research shows that central bank credibility and trustworthiness are essential factors influencing the impact of monetary policy interventions. A credible central bank is characterized by consistent price control and limited political interference, which ultimately attracts public trust. We investigate the influence of the electromagnetic quantum vacuum on the angular momentum of a charge q moving in a uniform magnetic field. The orbital angular momentum generated is due to photons in the vacuum that emit an energy back to the charge in proportion to n^2, a greater increase than that of the -2n\hbar of a charge in a Landau level. Alternatively, a charge moving in a uniform electric field and undergoing Brownian motion generates a comparable amount of orbital angular momentum. The orbital angular momentum generated is in the same order of magnitude as that produced by a spin-locked two-photon process where one photon has spin 1 and the other spin 0. The possibility of detecting the orbital angular momentum generated is discussed. The electromagnetic quantum vacuum influence on a charge moving in a combined magnetic and electric field is also explored. Finally, the implications of the findings are considered. The primary goal of Fine-Grained Named Entity Typing (FG-NET) is to accurately classify various entity types, and significant progress has been made in this area through the application of neural network-based methods. However, the FG-NET task is hindered by two main challenges: 1) the scarcity of comprehensive training data, and 2) the competition among entity types during prediction. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel hyperbolic learning approach called FGNET-RH, which leverages the efficient hierarchical structure of hyperbolic space to enhance representational learning and promote more effective classification. Furthermore, FGNET-RH's integration of entity type refinement is shown to significantly outperform existing FG-NET models, and our analysis highlights the method's strong potential for further adaptation and development in this area. Unlike the traditional post-migration approach which is high-risk and time-consuming, a proposed prepartitioning (preplan) approach successfully balances the workload before migration occurs, thereby ensuring seamless and high-quality services during the process. In this study, a defined schedule and partitioning strategy along with a green migration technique are presented to demonstrate how to efficiently balance workload while reducing energy consumption. Additionally, the study refines the partitioning strategy using real-world data and illustrates its effectiveness in reducing load variance through simulation results, showcasing improved performance compared to postpartitioning (postplan) techniques. Furthermore, the study examines the complementary nature of partitioning techniques and quality of service (QoS), exploring factors such as convergence speed, energy consumption, and migration technique influence on QoS. In contrast to prior studies which categorized QoS into two categories, this study complements this research by considering multiple criteria including migration technique, convergence speed, and performance, thereby offering a broader understanding of QoS in cloud data centers. In addition, the study extends from previous research in several key areas including energy consumption optimization and convergence speed. Ultimately, the study demonstrates the feasibility of achieving near-optimal workload balancing with minimal additional overhead. The study's results can be applied in real-world settings where users are concerned with achieving near-optimal workload balancing while preventing service disruption and minimizing energy consumption. In modeling systems of rival agents as games, assuming each party makes rational decisions, the probable outcomes can be identified using equilibrium concepts like the Nash equilibrium. In various real-world scenarios, factors like weather, traffic or fiscal policy, beyond the agents' control, can impact game dynamics. Often, the equilibrium observed doesn't align with the actual cost functions of the agents. This research proposes the use of Nash Fixed Point Networks, a new class of neural networks, capable of predicting game equilibria using context. N-FPN architecture integrates data-driven approaches with constraints related to available agent actions, making it more efficient for learning and prediction tasks. N-FPN models can also leverage a recent backpropagation method and utilize novel techniques for avoiding computationally costly operations. Experimental results illustrate N-FPN's effectiveness on both atomic and non-atomic games. N-FPN demonstrates that, even in complex scenarios with limited access to agent actions, it's possible to align game equilibria with the agents' optimal action sets. Furthermore, N-FPN demonstrates its utility in finding and validating actual Nash equilibria. N-FPN's success highlights its potential as a decision-making tool for learning and predicting game equilibria under various, often practical conditions. Significant physical harm can result from cyber assaults on Industrial Control Systems. Although in-person assessment can reveal vulnerable system components, it's expensive and time-consuming. We introduce a method that allows operators to efficiently identify cyber assault risks to Industrial Control Systems without needing to physically visit the site. Our method utilizes model-based predictive monitoring to identify attack risks while minimizing computation requirements. We address two assault scenarios: one where an adversary is unaware of system constraints but seeks to minimize their detection to remain'stealthy', and another where the adversary has complete knowledge and control over the system. For the'stealthy' assault scenario, we develop a set of potentially malicious control inputs that could compromise system safety if combined, and demonstrate that these inputs are the only possible ones that could lead to attack. When the assault scenario involves all-system knowledge and control, we develop an optimization problem that identifies the least restrictive attack strategy that could go undetected. We demonstrate that these approaches can be efficiently applied to large-scale systems without increasing computation requirements. Additionally, we show that they can be applied to any Industrial Control System modeled as a linear time-invariant system, and we validate our methods using an example model representing a Nuclear Power Plant's liquid cooling system. Our method is successful in identifying and prioritizing cyber assault risks that would otherwise go undetected. For instance, in the case of our Nuclear Power Plant model, our method identifies 56 possible assault strategies that could maintain the plant's cooling system within specified temperature limits while still allowing the adversary to manipulate the system to meet their'stealthy assault' requirements. These assault strategies are then revealed to be significantly more cost-effective and efficient than the previously proposed 'watering can' policy, saving the plant approximately $2.5M in annual operational costs. Furthermore, our method is shown to outperform the attacking adversary in terms of efficiency by a factor of approximately four. Secondly, we seek to establish whether dependent S-rings of type A can be characterized as rings with unbounded conductor sequence type. The objective of this research was to identify and characterise potential substellar companions associated with five rapidly accelerating stars using data obtained through the Sydney Institute of Astronomy's MOOG_AB code, which utilises spectra from the Hobby-Eberly Telescope and the 2dF spectrographs for high-resolution data analysis. Adaptive synchronization in interactions, or entrainment, involves the participants in a conversation adapting or matching each other's distinctive vocal traits. To measure this adaptive synchronization in unsupervised conditions, researchers first need to establish a metric that can identify similarities and differences in vocal patterns. A Gaussian Mixture Model-based deep neural network is trained to create a distance metric from audio signals, which is tested on two datasets. Analysis using intraclass variability measures shows the potential of this approach to capture adaptation in conversations, serving as a method to quantify entrainment. Performance evaluations confirm the effectiveness of this method in identifying similarities and differences in vocal patterns using a supervised version of the same network. Moreover, experiments on multiple datasets reveal that deeper networks lead to greater separation between classes, while adding a binary label to input data slightly improves performance. Importantly, this approach delivers comparable results in unsupervised conditions, making it a promising candidate for entrainment measurement without the need for manual labeling. Further investigation is needed to assess its applicability to various areas of study, such as the connection between adaptive synchronization and an individual's personality traits, as well as its potential in detecting interpersonal abuse in conversations. Classifying every frame of a video into its corresponding action is difficult, especially when long and complex actions are involved.  Most existing methods create artificial boundaries to segment and categorize actions, but this is not accurate since some actions are smooth and undivided.  Furthermore, most methods rely heavily on the quality of the annotations in the training set and become easily distorted as a result.  We're proposing a new method, known as SSCAP, which analyzes videos at their natural flow by extracting coherent action segments based on the understanding of the context.  Unlike other methods, SSCAP is able to detect actions with ease without relying heavily on the annotations of the training set.  Instead, SSCAP utilizes self-supervised learning to recognize repeated actions and their significance in the video.  We're also proposing a new Co-occurrence Action Parsing (CAP) loss to monitor SSCAP's ability to categorize action segments effectively.  Tested across various scenarios, SSCAP outperforms other existing methods, delivering superior results across multiple datasets.  You can access SSCAP's source code via the following link: https://github.com/sterlin/SSCAP.
