Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-defined test cases that a student has overlooked. While this feedback has some value, it can lead students to rely on guesswork rather than organized testing methods. Moreover, this feedback style does not educate students on how to design effective test cases. To improve testing education, we developed an innovative approach that not only provides coverage insights but also offers conceptual feedback to enhance understanding of the testing process, test planning, and software quality. Through a pilot study involving 83 students, we compared our new approach with traditional feedback and found that students preferred the new implementation and noticed a significant improvement in their understanding of testing concepts and quality assessment. Empirical evidence from three other studies supports the effectiveness of this approach in improving testing education outcomes and demonstrates the value of empirical education research in this field. By using this approach, instructors can gain a better understanding of what actions their students are taking during lab sessions and how this can benefit both the instructors and the students. Furthermore, this approach has the potential to be applied across a variety of subjects and study areas. To support the findings of our research, all of our code and data are publicly available online. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first empirical study to explore the effectiveness of innovative educational tools in testing education. Our results demonstrate that educational researchers must conduct thorough assessments to validate the impact of their tools on students' knowledge and skills. While there are various evaluations of testing methods, most have not prioritized this aspect, which is why empirical education research is essential to establishing a connection between the effectiveness of these tools and students' outcomes. By promoting further investigations in this field, we can create a more rigorous body of evidence to support testing education. Ultimately, this research has the potential to contribute positively to the testing and quality assurance communities by showcasing the significance of implementing and evaluating novel educational tools and methods. As a result, testing education professionals and researchers can revise and refine these tools to better serve their students and the testing community as a whole. Domain adaptation has received significant attention for enhancing model accuracy across different data domains. However, the challenge becomes more complex when source data cannot be accessed directly due to privacy constraints or data transmission limitations. To overcome this obstacle, we propose a novel method that adapts a pre-trained model without using the source data itself by transferring hypotheses derived from the source data through a multi-cycle process with pseudo data creation and refinement. By utilizing pseudo data, we develop a discriminator that aids in refining the target model's domain alignment in a self-guided manner. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach with experimental results from three benchmark datasets in different adaptation scenarios, achieving a notable improvement in average accuracy by 8.5%, 6.5%, and 5.9%, respectively, compared to other adaptation methods. A comprehensive analysis of nuclear power systems designed for Deep Space transport is presented, utilizing a cutting-edge Gas Core Reactor (GCR) integrated with a magnetohydrodynamic generator. A novel GCR design with enhanced characteristics compared to existing models is proposed and validated, capable of generating 200 MW of electricity within a 200 ton system. This power system functions in tandem with a fuel depot space platform to enable a spacecraft to remain in orbit indefinitely, powered by virtually unlimited energy. Furthermore, this GCR power system is applied to a Europa lander mission, demonstrating its potential to significantly increase mission duration. By utilizing a fuel efficiency ratio, the cost-effectiveness of the GCR depots in orbit around Mars and the Moon is evaluated and assessed. Ultimately, the potential benefits of the GCR power systems are identified: indefinite mission duration, unrestricted choice of destination, and reduction of speed to low costs. Key advantages of the GCR systems over other nuclear power systems are their lightweight design, minimal thermal radiation, and high thermal to electric efficiency. A fundamental shift in space exploration approach may result from the availability of GCR power systems, potentially leading to high-speed missions between Earth and the Mars orbit. Following a thorough evaluation of the GCR systems, suggestions for future improvement are provided, guiding development toward integration into Lunar and Deep Space missions. Lastly, the feasibility of integrating GCR systems onto nuclear thermal propulsion systems is explored, potentially resulting in increased specific impulse values of the integrated systems. A comprehensive assessment of the GCR systems reveals their highly promising nature and likely future integration into Deep Space missions. The analysis demonstrates that these systems effectively mitigate the critical challenges of spacecraft propulsion and orbit maintenance, potentially enabling a wide range of innovative space exploration applications. The work presents a new perspective on the fundamental problem of transiting through and exploring other celestial bodies with human-made vehicles. In order to bridge this gap, we compiled a vast database of atomic and molecular absorption cross-sections within EXOPLINES, extending its scope to cover 425 distinct molecular species, 42,000 transitions, and spanning a wavelength range from 0.9 $\mu$m to 1.5 mm. We build upon ASP's modeling language semantics to define a formal description of grounding algorithms using (fixed point) operators. Central to this are well-established, fixed-point operators providing models that offer semantic insights into the outcome of grounding as well as facilitating simplifications during processing. We address a broad range of logic programs that incorporates recursive aggregates and extends the reach of existing ASP modeling languages, complemented by an algorithmic framework outlining the process of grounding recursive aggregates. These provided algorithms correspond closely to those utilized by the ASP grounder, gringo. To represent information in a random variable with a specific probability distribution relative to an information source with a known distribution at another point, we examine several candidate measures based on finite combinations of cumulants and the central limit principle. Among these, the cumulant caterpillar appears to offer the most balance of practicality, efficiency, and broad applicability. Its computation requires calculating the n-th cumulant of the target random variable divided by that of the source, where the degree of this division varies in a growth rate of n with each division providing an improved refinement of the target distribution at the cost of more complex computation and higher memory demands. Furthermore, we extend existing calculations of mutual information based on the central moment problem to include higher orders of cumulants and show that the results from these calculations converge to the known Shannon mutual information formula as the number of cumulants approaches infinity. The mutual information values obtained from the first four cumulants differ from the true Shannon mutual information value by less than one percent when the signal to noise ratio is greater than five, indicating that the fourth cumulant already achieves a high level of accuracy. Lastly, we illustrate the applicability of our approach to the analysis of time series data by comparing it with the widely employed Shannon mutual information formula in the field of neuroscience where the time series data describes neural spike trains and the source describes a Poisson process representing the underlying neural activity. Despite being unresponsive to discrepancies from its idealized model, the Shannon mutual information formula is shown to be highly sensitive to the alterations in model parameters when using our proposed cumulant approach, revealing new insights into spike adaptation, negative feedback, and neuronal irregularity. Consequently, we believe that the cumulant-based information measures offer a powerful tool for studying the mechanisms of neural populations, regardless of the distribution of the target random variable with a specific probability distribution relative to an information source with a known distribution at another point. A new method allows us to make this analysis without knowing whether certain assumptions hold or even what values some important statistics have. By using information about the matrix of average relationships among these time series, we create an estimator of how many common random patterns there are, even in cases with extreme data fluctuations. As sample size increases, the rates of divergence for the matrix's key properties are significantly faster than others. This, combined with analyzing a modified version of the problem, helps us make accurate estimates of this number with probability one, under certain conditions. Additionally, we apply our findings to estimating the number of states in a Markov chain. A novel set of quantum low-density parity-check codes is introduced, incorporating explicit designs that enable linear time decoding processes. The construction is based on a specific combinatorial structure involving vertices, edges, and faces, defined within a Cayley complex framework. A key aspect of this structure lies in the utilization of constant-size random codes mapping weights of small sizes from the torus to the sphere. A crucial property resulting from this is a rigorous proof that establishes a lower bound on the smallest distance between points on the torus and its randomly projected image on the sphere, achieving the optimal asymptotic exponential rate $\Gamma^{-1/2}$. Having addressed the distance gap issue, we further develop and apply two distinct approaches for correcting quantum errors. The first approach involves using a list-decoding method, coupled with a structural tree-based algorithm, which together ensure the capacity achieving property of the constructed ensemble under the symmetric error model. The second approach, inspired by the Baldi-Moss algorithm, yields a more efficient decoder with reduced time complexity, although falling short of meeting the exact requirement. Despite this, it's demonstrated that this modified list-decoding method can still provide practical performance under practical scenarios. Furthermore, an alternative variant of the original ensemble is proposed, featuring reduced message size in the decoding process, yet retaining the capacity achieving property for the symmetric error model. The paper's supplementary materials include detailed supporting data and figures. The work presented here addresses a pressing need for time-efficient quantum LDPC codes that can handle diverse error patterns, a crucial aspect for near-term quantum computing architectures requiring resilient storage of several hundred to several thousand qubits. The development of these codes is set to be part of a groundbreaking quantum error correction library for practical application in the field. The authors also outline a subsequent plan to develop a parallelized implementation of the tree-based algorithm, aimed at further optimizing performance and speed, with the goal of integrating it into the Quasaki quantum error correction library. The development of these codes represents a collaborative effort between the quantum research community and the machine learning community to advance practical quantum computing. The distance-$r$ dominating set problem, a close variant of the well-known dominating set problem, has received significant attention due to its broad applications across multiple fields. Notably, it has strong connections to the clustering and fault-tolerant coverage problems in wireless sensor networks, as well as crucial infrastructure maintenance tasks in computer networks, such as upgrading key equipment to ensure network stability. While the problem is known to be NP-hard for most cases, it is surprisingly solvable in polynomial time for certain sparse graph types with limited diameter and high generality. Our study extends existing work by providing a distributed algorithm for finding the minimum distance-$r$ dominating set in sparse graphs with a high generality property, varying independent of $n$, and a maximum degree of $\Delta$. Our algorithm is capable of achieving a 2-huge factor approximation in the O($\log(n)$) time frame for $r\geq 2$, provided that $r$ remains a constant. Conversely, we have established that reducing the approximation factor to $2+\varepsilon$ would necessitate a staggering $n^{\varepsilon/4}$ factor increase in time, assuming the One-Way LOFAR Communication Complexity Hypothesis holds true. For the specific instance where $r=1$, we have devised a distributed algorithm that is capable of producing a $(1+$\varepsilon)$-approximate distance-$r$ dominating set in the $t$ time frame for $n$ vertices, where $t$ is in the order of $\log(n)^{O(1/\varepsilon))}$, provided that $\varepsilon$ and $t$ are in the order of each other. Our results mark the first instance of a distributed algorithm for this specific problem variant and are further accompanied by a lower bound demonstration of its tightness, thereby highlighting a critical barrier to progress in this area of study. Our algorithm design techniques are versatile, encompassing potential applications in other problems, such as the distributed Independent Set and Vertex Cover problems, thus serving as an innovative foundation for future research in these areas. Our results provide a significant performance improvement relative to the independent sets produced by the recent work published in FOCS'21 and are, in fact, complementary in nature, thereby expanding the reach of that work while addressing a crucially distinct variant of the problem. This research examines the properties of bulk and boundary states in topological insulators that exhibit higher-order topology and disorder, using the effective low-energy theory of the strong topological insulator HgTe. We demonstrate the protection of bulk and boundary states against randomness using the bulk-boundary correspondence principle. We then verify the stability of corner states by calculating the Green's function of the system and show that corner states contribute to the appearance of bulk bound states within the bulk insulator. Furthermore, by incorporating the effect of surface disorder, we derive a surface version of the bulk-boundary correspondence and identify the possibility of implementing the bulk-boundary correspondence as an inequality for the zero-energy surface states. Our findings could potentially lead to the realization of corner transport in experiments involving high-mobility materials that exhibit topological properties. Additionally, we provide a conceptual understanding of the bulk-boundary correspondence in terms of the long-range interaction between bulk and boundary modes. We identify the long-range potential as a result of edge or corner states influencing the bulk and generate the required interaction by adjusting the boundary conditions to demonstrate the bulk-boundary correspondence as an equality. We also show that the long-range interaction disappears when the boundary contributes no charge, thereby simplifying the bulk-boundary correspondence to its original form. This research opens up new avenues for studying topological insulators that exhibit higher-order topology and may inspire innovative experiments in the field of topological insulators. Novel view synthesis with light field rendering traditionally requires accurate geometric and appearance reconstruction. However, since there is no explicit geometry, analysis-based methods often employ rough estimation and iterative refinement. In contrast, data-driven approaches depend on pre-trained models encoding 2D images to reconstruct 3D scenes. Yet, these models struggle to generalize beyond specific scenes and contexts. Our work challenges this assumption by developing a data-driven, end-to-end approach to light field rendering, initially trained on rendered data rather than actual scenes. This allows our model to handle novel view synthesis across a wide range of scenes. Additionally, since no real-world scenes closely resemble the training dataset both visually and statistically, we incorporate several key regularization techniques. These include geometry and appearance regularizations derived from 2D object detectors, as well as a novel temporal regularization based on video object affinity detectors. Our model successfully renders high-quality 4D light fields from diverse real-world datasets and even generates novel views from actual video clips. The model's code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/dianaalex/e2lf. Our research demonstrates the potential for end-to-end, data-driven light field rendering on real-world scenes and highlights key regularization techniques that facilitate generalization. Furthermore, this work may lead to further research in deep rendering and novel view synthesis. An associated video is accessible at https://youtu.be/dGyvQy4oY6w. A powerful and dynamic solar eruption triggered by shock waves emanating from the Sun's corona can accelerate electrons, resulting in the formation of type II radio bursts. Although these bursts have been observed extensively, researchers continue to investigate their origin. To address this, we studied a notable solar eruption on October 16, 2015, that involved an EUV jet, a streamer in white-light, and a type II radio burst observed through simultaneous data from LOFAR, the WIND spacecraft, the K-c coronameter, and the Solar wind Ensemble. By examining the data, we found that the radio burst's forward shock appeared at altitudes ranging from 1 to 3 megameters and moved at speeds between 570 and 980 km/s, indicating that it originated in a low-density region of the corona. We further analyzed the jet and streamer systems, finding they shared the same speed, trajectory, and timing indicators, suggesting the eruption of a coronal stream due to the propagation of a jet-driven piston shock. This finding has implications for how we interpret observations of similar events, particularly the complex interplay between shock waves and streamer formation. Additionally, we found evidence that the low-coronal type II radio burst's forward shock was driving the streamer forward. Consequently, we believe this event provides strong evidence for a piston-driven shock mechanism in the formation of a coronal stream, and that this type of shock drives the streamer forward through the propagation of a jet driven piston shock. Furthermore, this type of shock was generating the observed type II radio burst. It is suggested that this type of solar phenomenon, an eruption of a streamer through shock waves, typically produces type II radio bursts and therefore should be a primary driver in the formation of streamers via shock waves. This study introduces a unique, self-contained three-dimensional random vortex system that mirrors the behavior of the Navier-Stokes equations for non-viscous incompressible fluid flows. The newly developed random vortex system incorporates a stochastic differential equation that interacts with a finite-dimensional functional differential equation, contrasting it with earlier two-dimensional random vortex dynamics equations. The creation of this random vortex system lays the groundwork for developing innovative numerical techniques, known as random vortex methods, for solving three-dimensional incompressible fluid flow equations through Monte Carlo simulations. In order to establish the three-dimensional random vortex dynamics equations, we have formulated two influential methods: first, the duality of the conditional distributions of two interconnected Taylor diffusions, offering an integration by parts technique in the context of path space; second, a forward type Feynman-Kac formula that expresses solutions to nonlinear parabolic equations as a form of functional integration. The technical strategies employed here could have potential applications in solving other nonlinear problems. In addition, we have demonstrated that when using a finite dimensional approach the random vortex dynamics equations converge to the exact solution of the incompressible Euler equations, providing a theoretical framework for the random vortex methods in this context. In order to establish this convergence result, we have incorporated a rather unique argument involving the interpretation of the random vortex dynamics equations as a continuous time Markov chain on path space. The random vortex dynamics equations provide a connection to the random hyperbolic systems, enabling us to extend our approach to develop random versions of other hyperbolic equations, such as the wave and Schrodinger equations, in a separate study. In order to extend our random vortex dynamics equations to include viscous effects, we have introduced a new method for including a diffusion operator into a stochastic differential equation, allowing us to derive a random version of the Navier-Stokes equations through functional differential equations. The random vortex dynamics equations provide significant value in the areas of random differential equations, random functional differential equations, random hyperbolic systems, random hyperbolic equations and Navier-Stokes equations, contributing new techniques to the random functional integration, random integration by parts, conditional distribution and Feynman-Kac formulas used in the random differential equations and partial differential equations literature. The creation of this random vortex dynamics equations also provides an opportunity to develop random vortex methods in three dimensions, enabling a future Monte Carlo simulation of turbulent fluid flows. The state vector of a boson sampling process can be precisely generated using S single photons passed through beam splitters with M modes, facilitating a description of its initial state using generalized coherent states. Due to its polynomial scaling with M, it is now possible to study Renyi entanglement entropies for systems containing large numbers of modes and moderate numbers of particles. Our findings include the existence of Renyi index-independent, symmetric Page curves, where maximum entropy occurs when the partition is even, as well as the linear increase in asymptotic entropy values with S in the collision-free subspace. Moreover, it is observed that the cusp in asymmetric entanglement curves appears at the exact subsystem size equal to S, whereupon maximum entanglement occurs before the entire system's mode population is reached. Additionally, it is found that the cusp depth is directly proportional to S and linearly increases with S when S is large, while the width of the cusp, occurring immediately after the critical subsystem size, narrows as S increases. These theoretical findings are consistent with numerical simulations in dimensions up to 5 and are expected to remain relevant for increased dimensional systems. Our work may be expanded to other models featuring similar entanglement characteristics, such as frozen states, where the cusp persists even under arbitrary S growth. It is also shown that the cusp can be removed through repeated copying of the local subsystem, whereupon entanglement increases continuously without restriction to the system size. Our work is further facilitated by the creation of an open-source Python package, PyMBOS, for efficiently computing the state vector of a boson sampling process. This tool allows for the generation of analytical wavefunction files for subsequent use in Monte Carlo sampling or numerical resolution of the Schrodinger or Liouvillian equations. Furthermore, it is shown that the cusp can be efficiently eliminated in the linear Gaussian model, where the resulting entanglement exhibits smooth, differentiable change with respect to the system size, and this approach may be extended to more complex Gaussian models featuring arbitrary quantum noise. As an alternative solution, we also demonstrate the exponential suppression of the cusp using a simple decoherence channel. Our work is further supplemented with several illustrative boson sampling visuals and related discussions. Temporal sequence analysis typically employs spectrometric or gene expression profiles with limited time points and a high number of variables. Due to this, existing methods face significant challenges, often relying on classical expression differences or wrapper techniques for predictive variable identification. A key issue lies in the small sample size common in such studies. In contrast, our proposed supervised learning approach, Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time, successfully tackles these challenges by creating a low-dimensional grid mapping for temporal sequences. A hidden Markov model and relevance learning technique allow it to handle time-dependent data, prioritize predictive feature dimensions, and prune irrelevant dimensions that introduce noise. As a result, our system excels in learning and interpreting temporal data patterns on low-dimensional grids, focusing on key features over raw data. R's source code for STMTT is publicly available at https://github.com/andreashellwig/stmtt. Using three real-life studies – breast cancer ARID1 mutation, colon cancer TCGA, and MCF7 ER-positive cell line – our approach demonstrates superior diagnostic accuracy, effectively identifies relevant features, and facilitates data interpretation. All related data and results are available at https://andreas-hellwig.de/stmtt. Notably, our results show that the accurate prediction of diagnostic outcomes through our approach is largely independent of grid size, highlighting the importance of hyperparameter tuning in topographic mapping. Furthermore, our technique outperforms established methods by producing feature-oriented explanations that explain patient diagnoses better than the baselines. A comparison of diagnostic accuracy and feature explanations for the three real-life studies is shown in Figure 7. Finally, our approach expands the concept of explanatory supervision in the analysis of high-dimensional temporal sequences. Visual summaries of the top 20 HMDT features for the three real-life studies are provided in Figure 6. Additionally, our analysis generates survival trees that produce probabilistic predictions for patient diagnoses based on the relevant features identified by our approach. A graphical representation of these trees is available in Figure 8. Ultimately, our results show that the application of Supervised Topographic Mapping for Temporal Data Analysis yields better diagnostic outcomes, more interpretable results, and the ability to provide feature-oriented explanations. The implementation of our technique is available in the form of publicly accessible R code at https://github.com/andreashellwig/stmtt. Using this code, one can easily reproduce the results presented in this study, as well as apply the technique to their own data. Reinforcement learning seeks to develop the most effective strategies through interactions with complex systems, even when the underlying rules are unknown. Many successful methods use a valuation function approximation to determine near-optimal approaches. However, in partially observable systems, these valuations are dependent on an extensive sequence of past events and previous actions. Recent research demonstrates that neural networks specifically designed to approximate these valuations are found to internally calculate a probability distribution of the present system state given its history, or belief. Notably, studies have revealed that, as these networks learn and adapt, their hidden states increasingly become intertwined with key state variables necessary for making optimal decisions, exhibiting significant correlation while diminishing in relation to less critical variables, or noise. Furthermore, our findings indicate that a well-trained network's hidden state can effectively serve as a reliable representative for the system's temporal information required for informed decision-making. Consequently, our work suggests that these networks' hidden states can be viewed as a form of temporary storage for the system's information. Moreover, our analysis shows that, as these networks learn and adapt, their hidden states increasingly become more informative, or utilizable, while diminishing in its unpredictability or randomness. A new simple algorithm was also formulated to enhance information utilization by adjusting the network's parameters in accordance with its current predicaments, resulting in its improved performance using partial information. Ultimately, our work's main objective is to clarify how these networks' hidden states evolve and contribute to belief formation in partially observable environments, while also providing practical applications for their effective application. In video action detection, current research often relies on classifying actions based on spatial and temporal features extracted from 2D or 3D convolutional networks.  However, we believe that understanding an action involves also making sense of its context, like who else is in the scene and what actions they are performing.  This paper proposes a new method where we utilize a graph convolutional network to learn context information, and to reduce the need for expensive annotated data, we introduce two new weakly-supervised approaches.  First, instead of relying on frame-by-frame annotations, we convert action classifications into node attributes in a graph, making it possible to transfer knowledge across actions.  Second, to leverage expert annotations more efficiently, we turn expert annotations into expert graphs, allowing the model to learn from multiple experts more effectively.  Our approach outperformed previous state-of-the-art action detection methods on HMDB51, UCF101, and Kinetics400 datasets.  Code for our method is available at https://github.com/mayfly/zr_c3.  Our code is built upon the PyTorch framework.  This research will be presented at the CVPR 2020 conference. This work delves into the dynamic cognitive hierarchy theory, introduced by Lin and Palfrey (2022), within the context of multi-stage incomplete information games. In such scenarios, players simultaneously uncover peers' relevant characteristics and problem-solving abilities as the game unfolds, providing an efficient framework for analyzing recurring interactive situations. Building on this foundation, we demonstrate that common payoff functions in incomplete information variants of well-studied complete games result in the dynamic cognitive hierarchy providing an accurate characterization of the equilibrium strategy profile. Furthermore, we establish that certain unilateral deviations remain unprofitable when an infinite array of skilled players is included in the considered set of potential cognitive types. Our study offers novel insights into the dynamic cognitive hierarchy theory and verifies the theoretical efficiency of this tool in generating actionable insights. Moreover, we provide groundbreaking conclusions by showing that some common unilateral deviations remain unprofitable even when players can only distinguish between each other's skill levels; this remains applicable for a wide range of games and cognitive hierarchy models. Lastly, we contest the assumption of lin and palfrey's assumption assumption that players can always engage in the final stage of a game. Instead, we argue that a specific minimum skill threshold is necessary to participate in these games, and this threshold is dependent on the specific game being played. Our results are based on three common games such as matching, auction and bargaining, that have been modified to fit within the dynamic cognitive hierarchy framework. Precise and continuous population estimates are crucial for policy decisions surrounding vaccination initiatives and infrastructure development planning. As local governments rely on outdated censuses for resource allocation, we investigated whether contemporary deep learning methods could enhance traditional sign-based estimation techniques. We adapted the General Estimation Net (GEN) model, initially successful in Rwanda, for application in Mozambique using similar remote sensing data. In a case study in Mozambique, we found that GEN produced a highly accurate population density map with an correlation coefficient of 0.91, closely matching the results of an independent accuracy assessment. We also evaluated local telephone data as a potential measure of population size, yielding an annual growth rate of 3.5% for the study area. We discovered significant eleven-year and thirteen-year periodic patterns in the time series, attributed to the extended birth cycle and the time it takes for villages to emerge as distinct urban centers. Furthermore, we found the study area to be undergoing rapid urbanization, with urban centers gradually transforming from discrete entities to interconnected parts of a broader urban landscape. Additionally to GEN, we analyzed the add-on module for urban extent extraction based on built-up areas. However, due to the absence of detailed, pixel-level data on cadastral information and urban planning, we could not accurately assess the urban area. As a result, we cannot rely solely on the urban extent module for precise population estimates in this study area. On the other hand, GEN's ability to utilize a broader range of data sources provides a more comprehensive population estimate. Therefore, it can be used in conjunction with the estimated density maps and source data of the built-up module to generate more accurate population estimates. To achieve sustainable, census-independent estimation, we recommend integrating these estimated population maps into local and national resource allocation processes. Also, we advise the Mozambican government to consider collaborating with the relevant administrative and scientific communities to implement this approach. Finally, we suggest training models on data from a variety of sources and populations to broaden the applicability of estimation methods, complemented by additional statistical analysis, such as household sampling, to validate the accuracy of the estimates and correct biases. Over the past ten years, substantial advancements have taken place to minimize the occurrence of incorrect positive results in data retrieval systems. These developments led to the creation of approximate filters with enhanced capabilities to reduce false positives. Current approximate filters can exclude a portion of the data keys, but they cannot eliminate the risk of generating incorrect positive results altogether. This study proposes a new data retrieval method known as the CP-set, which incorporates a novel approach using a combination of hash tables and a set of specific data keys to eliminate the likelihood of incorrect positive results, thus enabling users to place a lower bound on the number of incorrect positive results in data retrievals. Furthermore, the CP-set allows for online data insertion and querying, with an online time complexity of O(d) and query time complexity of O(d^2), where d represents the number of data keys. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of our CP-set approach through experiments showcasing its performance advantages over traditional approximate filters. These experiments were conducted using datasets with high-dimensional characteristics that have become prevalent in recent years, specifically datasets with 128-bit and 256-bit strings. These studies revealed that, compared to other methods, our CP-set approach successfully minimizes the occurrence of incorrect positive results by as much as three orders of magnitude, while also outperforming other methods by achieving online querying time reductions of 45% and query time reductions of 40% on datasets with 128-bit strings, and further improving these performance metrics to a 25% time complexity decrease when applied to datasets with 256-bit strings. By doing so, our CP-set method has effectively bridged the gap between its own time complexity limits and optimal time complexity bounds, thereby bringing us closer to eliminating the risk of incorrect positive results in data retrieval systems. These CP-set method experiments were conducted using Google's Benchmark suite, a scientific framework. This work marks a significant breakthrough in our understanding of how to effectively manage and prevent the occurrence of incorrect positive results in data retrieval systems, with the CP-set method having been open-sourced on GitHub. Its storage efficiency and fast query processing capabilities make it suitable for deployment in a wide variety of applications, with its potential uses spanning application domains such as enterprise computing, network security, search engines, video streaming, medical imaging, scientific computing and related data retrieval systems. This research develops a novel fuzzy k-means approach to cluster high-dimensional data across multiple subspaces. The algorithm is specifically designed for high-dimensional data sets where features can vary in relevance and importance, affecting the quality of the cluster. To overcome this limitation, our method modifies the traditional fuzzy k-means objective function using two distinct entropy terms. The first term optimizes cluster compactness by maximizing inter-cluster separation and minimizing within-cluster variance. The second term dynamically weights features according to their unique contributions, promoting better data partitioning. The effectiveness of our approach is evaluated through multiple datasets and comparisons with established state-of-the-art clustering methods. Our results indicate significant improvements in clustering quality and Centrality Clustering Score compared to baseline algorithms. Notably, our algorithm outperformed existing methods by achieving lower within-cluster variances and the Silhouette Index, which measures clustering quality and bias scores. The associated source code is publicly accessible at the following link: https://github.com/samehshakal/Entropy-FK-Means. The experimental outcomes strongly support the use of our algorithm for clustering high-dimensional data across multiple subspaces. The research investigated the impact of parameter sensitivity, feature weighting, and clustering quality in comparison to established state-of-the-art methods, showcasing the superior performance of the Entropy Variable Feature Weighted Fuzzy k-Means algorithm under various data configurations. The research also highlighted the practical implications of using our algorithm to improve clustering quality in real-world applications. Notably, the approach has broad potential applications in diverse domains such as computational biology, computer vision, drug discovery, and information retrieval. The research strongly advocates for the use of our algorithm to enhance the quality of clustering in multi-aspect data sets characterized by shifting dimensions and variable feature weights. The approach produces high-quality clusters by rewarding compactness, separability, and informative feature selection without requiring any prior knowledge of cluster structures or conditions. The research presents a comprehensive evaluation of the algorithm in a variety of data configurations, leading to a deeper understanding of the algorithm's mechanisms and a thorough analysis of the possible outcomes. Notably, the approach achieves competitive results in multi-aspect clustering and outperforms existing methods in density-based clustering by promoting more accurate and informative cluster structures in multi-aspect data sets. The research informs future research directions in clustering algorithms and provides valuable insights for method application and data analysis in multiple aspects. While quantum gravitational effects generally break global symmetries, their presence may hold significant value in understanding both particle physics and cosmology. Discovering well-maintained global symmetries could provide a valuable insight into the properties of gravity. Researchers have recently suggested the existence of an axion-like particle derived from a broken global $U(1)$ symmetry, essential for explaining cosmic birefringence observed in the Cosmic Microwave Background. We investigate the consistency of this proposal by examining the possibility of unbroken $U(1)$ symmetries in an effective quantum gravitational theory. We demonstrate that the existence of unbroken $U(1)$ symmetries puts constraints on the cosmological constants in the form of an effective field theory of QCD. Notably, the existence of a stable global $U(1)$ symmetry results in a lower threshold on the cosmological constant, approximately $m_\phi^4\gtrsim(2\pi m_\eta)^4$. Assuming the $U(1)$ symmetry involves a lepton number, we show that its existence puts constraints on the observed birefringence, with a 30% reduction in one case. While the existing Cosmic Microwave Background data does not meet these constraints, the forthcoming CMB-S4 experiment is expected to set a significantly more stringent upper limit, with planckian masses for the $U(1)$ symmetry. We discuss the implications of these findings and suggest that the forthcoming large-scale experiments may be able to discover the existence of well-maintained global symmetries in the quantum gravitational theory and its impact on the early universe. Furthermore, we propose that the well-maintained global $U(1)$ symmetry may underlie the observed anomaly in the moon's rotation rate. We outline a more detailed study in the moon's global symmetries and its relation to the effective quantum gravitational theory. In particular, global $SU(2)$ times may provide a new mechanism for explaining the observed decrease in the moon's rotation rate. Similarly, global $SU(3)$ times may lead to the existence of long-lived gravitational waves from the Big Bang. Our research presents new findings based on far ultraviolet (FUV) observations of the globular cluster NGC 4147 obtained with three specific filters onboard the AstroSat satellite. These findings were further confirmed by cross-checking the source's cluster membership using Gaia data and proper motions. Our FUV-optical analyses allowed us to identify numerous variable stars, three blue straggler stars, and 23 candidate blue horizontal branch stars, marking a first for NGC 4147. Additionally, our investigation into the FUV-bright members of this cluster showed a higher concentration in the central regions, indicating that these stars are primarily white dwarfs in the post-atomic hydrogen stage. Our data also provided a FUV-FX, FUV-FV, and FUV-FG color-magnitude diagram for NGC 4147, yielding over a hundred FUV-bright member candidates, giving us a valuable inventory of the cluster's blue and very hot stars. Furthermore, our investigation into the FUV-X, FUV-FX, FUV-FV, and FUV-FG color-magnitude diagrams helped us understand the characteristics of NGC 4147's BHBs, giving us key insights into this cluster's horizontal branch morphology. The goal of deep transfer learning (DTL) is to empower deep neural networks (DNNs) with the ability to draw from past experiences like humans. This report presents three key findings from analyzing the utility of pre-trained DNNs: an investigation of their structural properties, a study of their training dynamics, and evaluations of their capacity for information retention. These results shed new lights on two widely accepted conclusions within the DTL community: the claim that fine-tuning pre-trained DNNs leads to better results, and the assertion that the outcomes of DTL are largely influenced by the similarity between the source and target data. Our study indicates that these assertions require refinement. This work also introduces two methods aimed at improving the transferability of DNNs, enhancing their potential for utilization in a wide range of applications. Theses methods can be used independently or in combination to enhance DNNs in various ways. At present, the trial data for these findings is limited to the ImageNet dataset; however, the proposed methods are suitable for general application. We anticipate that these findings are likely to be widely applicable. The code for these methods is currently publicly accessible on GitHub, but it needs to be further refined. At present, the code does not reflect the most advanced version of these methods, but rather an early version of the algorithm. Nonetheless, the code should be easily modifiable by other researchers. This work is primarily based on a theory of representation, suggesting that DNNs strive to develop a universal set of features with broad applicability. However, this may not always be the case. For instance, it has been demonstrated that the features learned by VGG19 are better suited to the performance requirements of CIFAR100 than those of ResNet120, despite the latter being reported to outperform VGG19 on MNIST and ImageNet. This is to suggest that the success of DTL is not always the result of transferring a pre-trained feature from one task to another, but rather sometimes requires adapting the structural properties of the DNN itself. This is an area for further research. Furthermore, it has been discovered that the outcomes of DTL are not always the result of similarities between the source and target data, but rather in some cases the success of DTL is determined by which data is more easily represented by the DNN. This is an area for further research. These research questions are of the type that require little or no prior expertise in the subject matter to understand. In various scenarios, such as mobilization, pandemic mitigation, and advertising, the swift dissemination of information and social behaviors are paramount. Despite thorough examinations of massive cascade dynamics across multiple contexts, few have scrutinized how information propagation is influenced by complex network structures. Our research explores the impact of network modularity on information spread, proposing a model that incorporates both structured and unstructured information dissemination mechanisms. We demonstrate that a significant enhancement in network modularity leads to increased efficiency in information dissemination, enabling a larger cascade to emerge within a shorter time frame. Moreover, our results indicate that high-modularity networks facilitate targeted information dissemination, allow for controlled timing of the information release, enable simultaneous cascades, and make it more challenging for others to initiate comparable events. These findings are consistently validated through extensive simulations and analyses. Our study reveals the inherent connection between network structure and efficient information spread, offering a new perspective on target-oriented information dissemination. The application of our model to real-world social network data further corroborates our theoretical predictions, providing a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between network structure, information spread, and efficient information dissemination. Our research develops and theorizes a novel target-oriented information dissemination model that showcases the significance of network structure in information spread, contributing meaningfully to the existing literature in theoretical modeling. Additionally, it is successfully validated using extensive data analytics. Based on these insights, we suggest that boosting network modularity could be an effective strategy to facilitate information dissemination. To further contribute to the field, we publicly release our code for data analytics and simulations at https://github.com/mateus-resende/info dissemination. Service-oriented computing utilizes services as building blocks for constructing distributed systems. Traditionally, orchestrating cloud-based services centered around business process execution, particularly with BPEL's focus on services as processes. However, recent shifts towards alternative service motivations such as XaaS and RMAD require a revised approach. Although conceivably, diverse services can be converted to WSDL/SOAP formats, such a strategy is overly complex and impractical for industries to adopt. As a result, treating a service solely as a business process proves restrictive. Conversely, we view a service as a procedure that is technology-agnostic and agnostic to implementation, encompassing both advanced and low-level elements. Underpinned by this definition, we introduce Ozy - a modular, adaptive orchestration framework - enabling users to incorporate custom elements when necessary. We validate Ozy's potential through real-world deployments of two cloud-based services: Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure. Our experiments confirm Ozy's effectiveness in including both pre-built and custom elements, enhancing simplicity and efficiency. In summary, we redefine the concept of a service as a procedure, propose a corresponding orchestration framework, and provide an exemplarily efficient solution in comparison to standard approaches. Additionally, we provide users with the freedom to tailor the framework according to their needs and preferences. The accompanying code is openly accessible for users to implement custom solutions according to Ozy's definition. The comprehensive framework is available at https://github.com/bestflow/ozy, comprising both source code and deployment materials. However, these rings are not necessarily a direct result of planet formation as excess material can arise from other phenomena such as the de-stabilization of global disc dynamics, shock waves, and correlated gas and dust density fluctuations. We utilize a simplified disc model and include statistical noise to mimic the inherent fluctuations in the system, representing the effects of external factors on global disc dynamics. We observe that in regions with increased density fluctuations, planet accretion rates significantly surge during the early formation stages, with these variations dependent on the level of perturbation. Ultimately, these findings suggest that ambient density fluctuations could substantially alter a planet's mass in its formative stages, with the potential for its impact to be similar to that of existing pebble accretion mechanisms in later stages of formation. A natural follow-up would be to incorporate these factors into numerical simulations for a more in-depth understanding of planet formation. In recent times, heavy-heavy hadronic molecules have garnered significant interest within the hadronic physics community. A comprehensive review of heavy-heavy hadronic molecules, including their theoretical and experimental status, is provided in this paper. The review begins with an exploration of the underlying QCD long-distance physics, specifically focusing on the creation of quark-antiquark pairs and color exchange between the constituent quarks. It assumes a simplified, long-distance quark model for its analysis and addresses the challenges associated with it. The characteristics of heavy-heavy hadronic molecules, such as the bottomonium-like entities Uss, Bodge, etc, and tetraquarks like double bottomoids and double charmonoids, among others, are also examined in the review. The vast spectrum of heavy-heavy hadronic molecules offers valuable opportunities for exploration through theoretical decay widths and phase shift analyses, in addition to potential detection using experimental methods such as Belle II, LHCb, and other experimental facilities. The review delves into the experimental identification of heavy-heavy hadronic molecules using experimental approaches, discusses the significance of recently identified heavy-heavy hadronic molecules, and discusses future research directions in the field. Ultimately, the review concludes by highlighting the pressing questions regarding long-distance quark-gluon interconnections in heavy-heavy hadronic molecules and calls for further investigation into the subject. The review concludes by highlighting future research directions and calling for exploration into the mysteries of heavy-heavy hadronic molecules at the quantum chromodynamic level. It is hoped that the survey will stimulate interest in the subject and encourage young researchers to delve into the subject, its challenges, and its complexities in the future. To address this, we directly fitted synthetic Ly$\alpha$ correlation functions, including cross-correlations with quasars, without compressing the data, and then compared the results to the conventional method. Our approach provided significantly more precise measurements, constraining the matter density to 3.5% and outperforming the conventional BAO method. A fundamental component of various technologies, including surveillance, robotic navigation, and self-driving systems, is pedestrian trajectory prediction, and significant advancements have been made in this field. Nevertheless, past studies still have two main weaknesses. Firstly, as time progresses, prediction accuracy significantly degrades, and little consideration was given to the initial sequences of past trajectories. Secondly, although socially-aware models aim to capture complex interactions among pedestrians, they often overlook the fact that these interactions are dynamically altered as time advances, resulting in reduced effectiveness. To address these issues, a new trajectory prediction method called TSAR is proposed, involving a multi-layered encoding structure that reexamines past trajectories in a sliding sequential manner. This method also incorporates a socially-aware model with time-varying influences called SVR, which utilizes inter-pedestrian distances at different time points to estimate future trajectories. Additionally, CVAE-based encoders and decoders in the proposed TSAR structure leverage invariant and variant features to generate accurate and informative sample trajectories, ultimately enhancing trajectory prediction. Experimental outcomes have shown that TSAR surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques by producing more accurate, collaborative, and informative trajectory predictions, ultimately leading to enhanced interaction outcomes. An attached code is available on https://github.com/jeongyoonlee/TSAR.

A key advantage of counterdiabatic protocols in driving quantum states involves the use of a supporting, auxiliary gauge potential. However, determining this potential requires the full quantum Hamiltonian, posing a significant challenge for complex many-body systems. A recent approach, proposed by P. W. Claeys et al., involves using a variational method to derive an effective, efficient gauge potential. This method can be applied to prepare equilibrium states in quantum simulations. As a proof of concept, our research demonstrates the efficacy of this approach when using a variational combination of nearest-neighbor hopping and on-site terms to drive the two-dimensional Hubbard model. Our results show that the time-dependent evolution of local observables closely matches the target state's evolution, with minimal diabatic error for various target states within the Hubbard phase diagram. This method offers a promising route to efficiently preparing a wide range of many-body target states with high precision. Its applicability extends beyond the specific case of the Hubbard model and can be adapted to derive efficient gauge potentials for any quantum Hamiltonian representing a set of locally conserved quantities. Additionally, our approach allows for the determination of optimal gauge potentials that yield exact, analytic solutions for specific target states. Furthermore, it provides an alternative to existing methods for calculating properties or performing simulations of the Hubbard model. Since our approach only requires efficient algorithms to propagate the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, it can be adapted for use with various types of quantum hardware and simulated using classical resources alone. Finally, extending our approach to account for extra conserved quantities in the Hubbard model allows for the efficient preparation of target states representing entangled condensates, even when the extra conserved quantity cannot be locally represented. This method offers a new perspective on using counterdiabatic protocols as a framework for understanding and optimizing quantum driving in quantum simulation. Its applicability to complex many-body systems presents an opportunity to efficiently prepare a wide range of quantum target states, even those protected by hidden symmetries. Of course, our very best results are achieved when we use the full quantum Hamiltonian to derive the supporting gauge potential, representing the best possible outcome. However, the variational method proposed here represents a significant step forward, offering a promising solution to one of the key challenges associated with counterdiabatic protocol implementation. Its efficacy in the Hubbard model serves as a strong starting point for the efficient driving of quantum states, potentially expanding to include a wide range of complex many-body systems in condensed matter, cold atomic, and quantum optical systems. Color-neutral images are a cornerstone in various image processing applications such as image compression, feature extraction, and printing due to their role in tone mapping. However, valuable image data gets lost when transitioning color images to their grayscale counterparts. In this study, a streamlined, efficient, and high-speed image decolorization approach based on color temperature perception is developed. A comprehensive assessment conducted on seven widely used techniques in the field has revealed that our novel method not only compares favorably to existing solutions in terms of visual quality and time efficiency but also significantly outperforms them in terms of metric scores and time consumption. Furthermore, our approach demonstrates adaptability in various image processing scenarios including both raw and JPEG images across different resolutions. We anticipate that this recently proposed technique will serve as a reliable alternative to existing decolorization methods. Inspired by the principle that the perceived color temperature as described by the HSB color space accurately represents the natural way in which the human brain processes colors, our approach decolorizes images in three distinct stages. First, it identifies regions with high color temperature and converts them into their grayscale equivalents through a weighted average of the RGB channels. Next, it identifies colors closest to the neutral colors in the HSB color space and converts them into their grayscale equivalents. Finally, it reinserts the color information absorbed during the first and second stages by combining the RGB components of the grayscale image with the HSB components of the colorized image. The proposed algorithm has a complexity of O(N^2), making it highly efficient in terms of processing time. A comprehensive assessment of the technique has been carried out on seven leading image decolorization techniques in terms of SSIM, MS-SSIM, and time complexity, where it is observed that our approach compares favorably to existing methods and even outperforms some of them by a wide margin. In addition, our technique has been applied and successfully improved the performance of LDR to DR image conversion. In particular, our results show that when our image decolorization technique is combined with the learned DCR model, it significantly improves the score, outperforming leading tone mapping methods. In addition, our approach inspired the development of LDR to DR image conversion, significantly improving the score when compared to leading existing techniques. A new field of shape-constrained nonparametric regression is rapidly growing across various disciplines including economics, statistics, operations research and artificial intelligence. Recent advancements in the analysis of productivity and efficiency now bridge a significant knowledge gap in this field. The application of these techniques has been hindered in the past due to significant computational requirements and limitations imposed by existing software. In an effort to address these challenges, a new Python package named pyStoNED has been created, offering a user-friendly solution to implement a range of nonparametric techniques based on piecewise linear functions. This tool allows users to easily calculate and analyze key performance indicators such as average products or profit functions. Below is a brief introduction and a live demonstration of pyStoNED showcasing its main features through an example related to the analysis of productive input combinations. The live presentation will focus on the usage of pyStoNED's main functions including the definition of a Productivity Data Framework and the application of its key methods including adding new units and handling missing values, the calculation of a production frontier and the estimation of productivity growth rates. Additionally, a range of visualization tools available in pyStoNED will be quickly presented. The presentation of pyStoNED is intended for a broad range of users including those with little or no experience in the analysis of shape-constrained nonparametric data. The presentation will be accompanied by a fully documented Python code that can be accessed and run by attendees to understand how pyStoNED works. The analysis used in this presentation is based on a dataset containing cross-country and over-time production data from 19 countries within the European Union over the period from 1995 to 2018, obtained from the AMELIE dataset hosted at https://amelie.io. The presentation's main codes can be accessed at https://github.com/axilrod/pyStoNED-livesheet_2022/tree/main/v0.4.1-livedemo. The official release of pyStoNED can be downloaded at https://github.com/axilrod/pyStoNED/releases/tag/v0.4.1. A comprehensive user manual of pyStoNED is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/ternep.129. The presenters' email addresses are Tomax Axilrod (axilrod@u.nl) and Casper de Vries (devriescas@u.nl). The presentation is based on a live demo presented at the 2022 SciDataCon

By employing a novel method of mass reconstruction, it has been demonstrated that a resolution of at least double can be achieved in the lower mass region, maintaining a comparable level of resolution to existing methods in more favorable production environments. Furthermore, it has been shown that a parton-shower-induced smearing effect significantly impacts the mass reconstruction resolution, with amounting to approximately 5 MeV for both CM energy of 13 TeV and 27 TeV, and 10 TeV, 15 TeV, and 20 TeV for 35 GeV and 50 GeV, respectively. Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture syntactical information, as established in previous studies [Tenney et al., 2019, Jawahar et al., 2019, Hewitt and Manning, 2019]. This work presents two unsupervised constituent parsing models, UPOA and its enhanced version UPIO, both of which use the syntactic distance from self-attention weights in pre-trained language models to evaluate sentence structures. Further experiments demonstrate the significance of linear layers in capturing the parsing details. Consequently, the unsupervised model UPOA leads to improved benchmark results, and when combined with minimal annotations, it outperforms other shallow parsing methods in cross-domain and few-shot parsing tasks. Additionally, the fast parsing capability of UPOA makes it suitable for applications in other fields. Ultimately, the results show that linear layers in pre-trained language models are invaluable and that incorporating self-attention weights can yield superior parsing results in unsupervised and few-shot settings. The accuracy of speech-based applications heavily relies on high-quality Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR). Despite having access to advanced ASR models for English, German speakers often face difficulties due to the lack of modern ASR models in the public domain. In an effort to address this issue, we compiled a large-scale speech dataset comprised of 146 hours of spoken German, where speakers read news articles aloud. To further improve performance, we developed a two-stage training approach that leverages a combination of self-supervised and fully-supervised techniques. Notably, this method achieved an impressive average word error rate of 4.67% on three rigorous evaluation benchmarks, significantly outperforming existing German ASR models by over 1 point. Our proposed framework and training strategy have promising implications for advancing German ASR and creating valuable resources for the NLP community. The resulting models and associated dataset are openly available to facilitate future research and development. Furthermore, we have publicly released our code and guidelines in the hope that they can be adapted and repurposed for other low-resource languages. The research was conducted in collaboration with the German company Tengai GmbH, a leading developer of interactive speech-based games and applications. We are pleased to report that our research has successfully lowered their word error rates, resulting in improved user engagement and productivity. Ultimately, the advancements made in this research have the potential to dynamically adjust system parameters based on user performance, thereby enhancing overall user experience. The research was presented at the 21st Workshop "Syntaktische Analyse" (Syntax analysis) at the Universität des Saarlandes in December 2020. Beyond their interesting evolutionary process, these stars also possess a rapid rotational motion which significantly influences their spectral pattern and produces unique characteristics such as strong absorption of blue light and weak emission of red light.  Our study has used a spectroscopic method to identify 26 candidate Be-type stars within 30 Doradus and has also found that these stars have a higher abundance of being binary stars compared to the broader Wilkins-Sosa sample, with a notable interrelation between their spectral characteristics and binary status.  The resulting data set provides a foundation for future studies, including detailed analysis of these stars such as determining their age and comparing their movement patterns with predicted models of single star evolution.  The associated data includes high resolution images and spectroscopic classification of these stars in 30 Doradus and can be accessed through the DOIs https://doi.org/10.26180/97223 and https://doi.org/10.26180/97224 respectively. This paper demonstrates a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue 
of the Hermite operator when subject to Robin boundary conditions, showing 
that the optimal configuration is a half-space, and investigates the conditions 
under which equality occurs. Additionally, related problems involving Robin, 
Neumann, and Dirichlet conditions are explored. Our approach relies on a new
Sobolev inequality tailored to the given Robin condition and tailored for half-space geometries. 
Moreover, it involves the use of Fourier and periodic functions in multiple dimensions. 
In the case of equal volume regions, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition 
for the equality of Neumann and Robin problems by translating it into a problem of 
matching functions in L^2 spaces, and applying a Radon inversion theorem and Fourier analysis. 
Lastly, similar results and procedures are considered in Dirichlet scenarios. 
This research reveals that when the Robin condition's parameter λ and the dimension n are 
perpendicular, half-spaces achieve the best possible outcome in the Dirichlet case as 
well. However, the inquiry as to whether this phenomenon holds true across all cases remains an open question. 
All other cases exhibit stability in the best possible outcome in the Robin and Neumann cases.

μ respectively, do not differ significantly, half-spaces achieve the best possible outcome in the 
Neumann case as well. Whether this phenomenon holds true across all cases remains an open inquiry.

well. Whether this phenomenon holds true across all cases remains an open inquiry.

This interpretability issue severely hampers their use in critical areas like medical imaging or self-driving vehicles. A promising approach to tackle this challenge involves neural tangent networks, which exhibit similar behavior to linear models while maintaining the efficiency of fully connected neural networks. Nevertheless, they fall short in image classification tasks, primarily due to their inability to capture global average pooling operations. This study presents a novel method called non-fungible tangent kernels to overcome this limitation in CNNs, yielding an average test accuracy of 89.8% on CIFAR-10 and 93.13% on CIFAR-100, significantly outperforming the neural tangent network baseline by more than 6% on both datasets. By utilizing this insight, we can associate each model output with training data points, enabling accurate feature visualization and attribute explanation. We evaluate our model's feature extraction capabilities on visual concept learning and attribute explanation, achieving superior performance on both tasks. Additionally, the proposed methods allow for the design of planar GCAs with 1, 3, 5, or 9 ones per row and column, which can be used in omnidirectional precoding applications, including beamforming or omnidirectional precoding. A comprehensive study examines the connection between residual entropy and viscosity using an extensive, high-accuracy dataset. The concept was first introduced by Rosenfeld in 1977; this research demonstrates that scaling leads to a nearly linear correlation between residual entropy and reduced viscosity across a broad range of substances (argon, methane, CO2, and several others), including different model potentials. The initial "universal" correlation of Rosenfeld was found to be limited, yet adjusting the density can successfully relate the viscosity of non-associated fluids to idealized models. Consequently, this comparison generates a length that directly relates to the liquid's cubic root volume. Furthermore, this research develops a novel, easy-to-use model for examining viscosity, which accurately predicts visited states in phase space in relation to volume and temperature, accurately predicts viscosity within experimental error, and effectively simulates dynamics that are close to real. In contrast to current models, this research reveals a significant difference in the dependence of viscosity on the distance between molecules for supercritical fluids. It also proposes a novel definition of an idealized fluid that is based on entropy rather than intermolecular interactions and demonstrates the existence of an almost linear relationship between this ideal and normal fluid. Lastly, this research explores implications for understanding transport processes during fluid demotion. It develops an additional, easy-to-use model for examining entropy production in transients, which effectively simulates the development of entropy production in the correct proportionality constant. Additionally, this research reveals that with sufficient precision, experimentally obtained viscosities are sufficient to demote the fluid to its corresponding reduced state and extract relevant length parameters. However, such a procedure fails for current model potentials with known potential forms. Consequently, further refinement of these model potentials is necessary. In conclusion, this research emphasizes that there are many paths to developing effective models for complex properties. It also explores some potential applications of this research, including examining the dependence of viscosity on the direction of flow in electric and magnetic fields. However, further studies indicate that viscous effects in these fields are extremely minimal, and in any case, they do not affect main-correlation features. However, similar research on similar problems with high accuracy may uncover more critical influences in these fields in the future. In any case, such a possibility demonstrates the current importance of examining viscosity in relation to the concept of superfluidity. In addition, further studies are needed to effectively simulate dynamics for flows in parallel to velocity in non-associative fluids. The possibility that our Universe undergoes a periodic expansion led us to develop the Lambda CDM periodic model (ΛCP), which combines the widely accepted Lambda CDM model with a periodic expansion schedule. In the ΛCP model, the universe expands normally in the Lambda CDM phase, but at certain times it contracts and then re-expands in a way that challenges the conventional understanding of the cosmic timeline. To explore the implications of this periodic expansion, we examined alternative big bang theories and tested the ΛCP model using Hubble data from 500 galaxies, as well as constraints on the universe's present-day state derived from the cosmic microwave background and Baryon Acoustic Oscillations. Our findings indicate that the periodic expansion of the Lambda CDM model is consistent with current astronomical observations, without requiring additional assumptions, for a range of cycles. In particular, we found that the universe has likely experienced one or more expansion cycles in the past and may be approaching the next contraction phase soon. Conversely, our analysis also shows that the standard Lambda CDM model provides a sufficient match to the available astronomical observations, suggesting that the periodic expansion scenario is a plausible, albeit not necessary, explanation of the universe's behavior. We have further validated the viability of the Lambda CDM periodic model through four distinct physical arguments: the challenge to the traditional notion of the cosmic timeline; the need for matter to slow down the periodic expansion; the potential significance of an intercycle 'dark age' for understanding the universe's present state; and the possibility that the periodic expansion could be caused by a cyclic model's steady-state bubble. Ultimately, our research indicates that the Lambda CDM periodic model offers an innovative solution to cosmological problems and provides a foundation for fresh discussions about the universe's behavior. It represents a departure from the standard Lambda CDM model in a way that is consistent with astronomical observations, and it paves the way for novel investigations into the fundamental nature of gravity and the universe's birth. This idea brings concepts from areas like chaos theory and dynamical systems into the study of quantum foundations. Despite this, developing a clear hidden-variable model for it has been a challenge, making it hard to properly evaluate. In this piece, a hidden-variable model for the theory is developed and several aspects of the theory are analyzed with it. Our model indicates that the original formulation of the theory likely incorporates an unrealistic requirement. Even with a more relaxed approach, multiple issues with the theory become apparent, including the substantial fine-tuning needed to align the theory with known quantum phenomena. In particular, the theory's prediction of an infinite correlation function for specific product states cannot be reconciled and appears to be a universal property of any superdeterministic hidden-variable model for quantum mechanics. In general, generating realistic models that accurately replicate quantum behavior is a significant challenge for superdeterministic approaches. In light of these findings, a modified version of the theory called Stable-set theory is proposed as an alternative, where realism is preserved without necessitating superdeterminism. We examine Neural Networks (NNs) for keyword spotting on devices such as smart speakers and wearables. Our focus is on NN execution within devices with limited resources; thus, we suggest a Compact Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture. This CNN features (i) reduced computation with fewer multiplications and inputs, (ii) thinner layers with fewer parameters, and (iii) a smaller kernel size for each layer to mitigate computational costs. Compared to current state-of-the-art keywords spotting models, our proposed CNN exhibits superior performance with significant reductions in computational and storage requirements. We assess our model's resilience through various forms of noise simulation and adversarial testing, showcasing its potential as a reliable and efficient solution for real-world IoT applications. We further provide a general framework for resource-constrained NNs, allowing for easy adaptation and improvement of the model's design. This framework integrates enhanced initialization for reduced storage needs and employs loss functions for enhanced robustness. Finally, the code and models are made accessible through a public repository at https://github.com/NVIDIA/FAST. To address these problems, we can utilize the Group Lasso method, which encourages regularization in the context of categorical variables. However, the existing Group Lasso approach often results in the incorrect identification of groups due to its estimation bias, particularly in high-dimensional scenarios. To overcome this limitation, we have developed the Dual Form Group Lasso method, which determines variable selection in an efficient manner by taking advantage of the structural characteristics of categorical variables. By reformulating the Group Lasso problem as a linear programming issue and introducing the dual form, we can obtain multiple optimal solutions, leading to a higher probability of achieving accurate results, especially when dealing with complex data sets. Our proposed method has been evaluated through extensive numerical experiments, which demonstrate its superiority over existing techniques. Notably, it performs significantly better in scenarios involving large datasets, demonstrating its potential as an effective tool for high-dimensional categorical data analysis. Lastly, to illustrate the practical value of this method, we have applied it to the analysis of customer purchase history in the retail industry.
