In recent years, the needs of embedded systems have grown more complex.  These systems not only require reliable, hard real-time capabilities but also diversified functions like network capabilities.  Implementing virtualization using hypervisors has emerged as a suitable solution to address these demands.  Unfortunately, existing hypervisors, which were designed with general-purpose computing in mind, come with a considerable system overhead that is not suitable for mixed criticality embedded real-time systems.  Moreover, the schedulers within embedded hypervisors fail to account for the diversity of real-time demands as well as the rapidly evolving nature of scheduling principles.  
  This paper presents T-Visor, a custom-made hypervisor designed for mixed criticality embedded real-time systems.  Built to support the ARM architecture, T-Visor achieves full virtualization by utilizing the capabilities provided by the ARM Virtualization Extensions.  Ensuring real-time performance, T-Visor's scheduling framework is flexible, allowing it to be tailored to various types of embedded systems.  Through our evaluation, T-Visor demonstrates its ability to deliver high system efficiency while ensuring real-time dependability and network reliability.  These results validate that T-Visor is an appropriate choice of hypervisor for mixed criticality embedded real-time systems.  The source code of T-Visor is publicly accessible on GitHub at the specified URL.  This research contributes towards understanding hypervisors in mixed criticality embedded real-time systems, its application, and its technical implications.  Furthermore, our study is the first of its kind to apply real-time scheduling theories to a commercial-grade hypervisor supporting the ARM architecture.  As a result, this paper is expected to offer valuable insights to software developers working with hypervisors and embedded system designers. Our results, obtained from robotic tasks, demonstrate that the traditional method is susceptible to performance degradation in response to environmental shifts, whereas a probabilistic model that considers various environmental profiles yields controllers with enhanced robustness and adaptability. This process enables the creation of such algebras in the form of matrix and tensor products of lower-dimensional algebras. Consequently, it results in equivalence of module categories for certain types of quivers and n-dimensional algebras. Furthermore, we can use multi-layer quivers to express the higher dimension (n+1) algebras as slices of larger, infinite-dimensional algebras known as higher dimension YD algebras. Earth's life is defined by lasting connections over time. Organisms' material arrangements, present-day forms of which are contingent upon events from billions of years ago, represent the most evident example of this. In biology, information that's passed on through generations not only explains species' current states, but also their gradual evolution, which is the fundamental driving force behind the tree of life. In this context, understanding how matter systems in biology convey information is crucial for insights into both the natural world and Earth's history. We develop a basic approach to determine the amount of information that's contained in matter systems that are governed by probabilistic rules and connected over time generatively. We also demonstrate that systems that operate in this way can, in fact, store and transmit reliable information across infinite periods of time, but only if the processes that govern them remain unchanged. We then show, using fractal dimensions, how the number of possible states in such systems grows when new generations are added. Furthermore, we verify that this growth defines a unique set of exponential functions, which effectively determine the amount of information that's contained in these systems. We then use this approach to explore the amount of information that's contained in Earth's history, including the emergence of complex life forms, which is the subject of significant debate among scientists regarding the nature of this information and its role in the processes by which life evolved. We demonstrate, through an application of our approach and using calculations for self-similar systems, that systems in this context not only retain information about their past states, but also significantly contribute to their future forms through the amount of information that's contained in them. We then make calculations regarding the amount of information that's contained in the transition from non-life to life on Earth, which effectively defines the nature of Earth's primordial conditions that led to the emergence of its most complex life forms. We also demonstrate, through an application of our approach and using fractal geometric data for the tree of life, how the natural history of this information defines the development of the natural world. Researchers have suggested the application of quantum interferometry using Bose-Einstein condensates to develop versatile interferometers, potentially surpassing traditional photonics in applications like quantum communication over long distances. Although atom interferometers have shown significant progress, the integration of quantum information into their design is still in its infancy. In our work, we develop a plan for creating a wide range of nonlinear quantum gates that can operate within the current technical limitations of cold atom interferometers. Our approach leverages the collective interactions between atoms to apply controllable phase shifts during the interferometer's operation. In addition to theoretical advice, we outline an associated experimental protocol that details the required adjustments to existing atom interferometers. By implementing this modification, researchers can generate various quantum operations, including entangling gates, to explore the capabilities of cold atom interferometers in quantum information processing. Our methodology offers an efficient method for simulating any quantum circuit using a maximum of three Fock states. In experiments involving low-lying modes, we demonstrate the feasibility of implementing accurate nonlinear gates with fidelities exceeding 99%. These advancements could contribute to the growth of quantum networks based on cold atom technology. Our work ultimately aims to bring quantum information processing closer to the realm of multi-atom experiments. In support of future research, we release the associated code at github.com/LukeTewari/Nonlinear-atom-gates. In the accompanying supplemental material, we outline the asymptotic analysis of the gates as the number of atoms approaches infinity. An extended discussion on related work is also provided in supplemental notes. In a related development, we demonstrate the application of atomic quantum gates to cold atom interferometry, effectively merging the fields of quantum information processing and cold atom interferometry, a trend that has since been replicated by other researchers. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although the detector operated within expectations during Phase 1 experiments (2010-2018), it experienced higher-than-anticipated levels of radiation than expected, resulting in increased readout noise and systematic errors in its measurements. This research paper focuses on the identification and subsequent analysis of the causes behind noisy pixels and pixel splits detected within the pilot blades of the detector during this period. Through in-depth analysis of the data, researchers were able to determine that the majority of these issues were the result of ionization damage rather than random noise. Furthermore, the study provides an estimation of the damage's half-life, offering insights that could be crucial in predicting the detector's performance during Phase 2 and beyond. As this work has direct implications for the future operation and maintenance of similar detectors, it is particularly significant for the ongoing upgrades of the CMS pixel detector. Moreover, the methods and techniques used in this investigation can serve as a model for the analysis of detector issues in the future, especially during the current CMS pixel detector upgrade. This research has been performed using real-world data from the CMS pixel detector. As such, it has been submitted for publication to the Journal of Instrumentation. The accompanying figures include graphical representations, while the associated code may be accessed on the GitHub repository under the name 'PixelPilots'. The relevant CMS software was also utilized in this study. Both the CMS-associated resources and the detector itself are managed by CERN. The target audience for this work comprises members of the particle physics research community involved in the detection, analysis, and interpretation of particle physics data, particularly those specializing in the operation and maintenance of the CMS silicon pixel detector. The study offers valuable insights into the performance characteristics of the detector during previous experiments. C. Jones and S. This research introduces an open-source framework for developing and training hybrid Quantum-Classical classification algorithms. Ultimately, the research reveals the potential for scalable, stable, and accurate hybrid Quantum-Classical classification algorithms. Interpreting teaching instructions with natural language can be compromised by the complexity of meaning, often leading to misunderstandings. Learners may misinterpret the intentions behind teacher-provided information when object characteristics are ambiguously described, a problem known as referential ambiguity. We explore how principles from cognitive sciences can inform our understanding of natural language guidance in reinforcement learning, with a focus on object induction. By implementing teaching instructions that take into account both the object's properties and the context in which it is taught, we improve the learner's object representations, overcoming referential ambiguity and resulting in better generalization. We evaluate our approach through experiments designed to test induction, with human trial-based trials confirming the effectiveness of our object induction methodology. We further demonstrate our method's applicability to multi-goal reinforcement learning tasks. Training agents using our induction methodology reveals them to be more efficient and effective, with a preference for using learned object representations that reflect their underlying context. We validate our results through a series of manipulation and observation experiments, supporting our approach and the cognitive efficiency of our training methodology. Our research demonstrates that by addressing referential ambiguity, natural language guidance can yield robust object representations in reinforcement learning. Training agents using induction results in efficient and generalizable behavior in a variety of tasks, making our methodology an important contribution to goal-conditioned reinforcement learning. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/comallino/overcoming-ambiguity.

In this study, we explore a UAV model that serves a maximum number of users at various locations within a set time frame by optimizing its flight path. Data security and user privacy concerns loom large over the IoT landscape, where devices operate on low power. The Ramsey sequence serves as a prime illustration of quantum phase measurement for a spin qubit, and its efficiency in measurements can be enhanced by strategically choosing the duration of phase accumulation, $\tau$. A sequential Bayesian experimental approach is employed to determine this duration in low-accuracy Ramsey measurements, and its results are compared to a prior adaptive heuristic method and a randomly selected setup. An efficient process that enables simultaneous measurement-taking and design calculations greatly minimizes the computational overhead associated with measurement time. When the precession frequency is the sole parameter being estimated, the Bayesian method exhibits significant improvements over the adaptive heuristic and random protocols, resulting in computation time savings of two and four orders of magnitude, respectively. Furthermore, the Bayesian method exhibits robustness to a variety of prior distributions for the unknown precession frequency. And interestingly, we find that for certain cases, using the Bayesian method and random protocols can yield identical accuracy as the adaptive heuristic method. Finally, the Bayesian approach has been extended to consider multiple parameters and various prior distributions for the unknown parameters with comparable performance results. Network centrality metrics quantify node importance using various geometric and diffusive characteristics, focusing on distinct scales. From a geometric perspective, a multi-scale centrality is defined by Gromov's definition of a metric space's filling balance, measured as the infimum of conformal cocycles exceeding a geodesic distance threshold. This metric is demonstrated on a network's geometric representation, and an algebraic formulation is introduced as the spectral extension of a multi-scale network centrality (GSE) based on the Laplacian matrix, which determines the optimal scaling for a network's strongly connected diffusive process. Additionally, Gromov Centrality is derived as the limiting case of a reweighted random walk model, which also enables the incorporation of additional data and signals onto the network. Centrality analysis is then applied to a large social network, a nearby highway network, and a microcredit network to evaluate its practical applications. Results show that Gromov Centrality's properties enable its use for identifying nodes at specific scales, handling network data with uneven distribution, and proposing multi-scale evaluation frameworks. The framework's generality is demonstrated on a network's strongly connected diffusive process and a network's network diffusion model. The GSE and Gromov Centrality encourage the development of new geometric network analysis methods and the recovery of a network's underlying geometry. Subsequently, in an attempt to apply this new equation, we discover that it yields a solution identical to Schrodinger's equation for a bound state electron, achieving unification of quantum mechanics and general relativity. Furthermore, we apply the derived equation to model the behavior of a planet in a central sun system, revealing a newly discovered pattern of planetary gaps, which can explain numerous astronomical findings such as the Goldreich-Barber gravitational resonance, as well as the mysterious Mars Spinning Spin Pattern. Finally, we use the newly derived equation to model the behavior of gravitons in a linearized context and demonstrate that it results in a new model of quantum gravity that fundamentally differs from the established approach established by Hawking and Hartle. Additional potential applications of this new theory are outlined at the end. The supplementary material discusses the theoretical underpinning of this new approach as well as a long-standing pattern of periodic planetary rotation observed in the solar system, solar system, and other planetary systems, which serves as the foundational component of this new azimuthally symmetric theory of gravitation. Sets of matrix pencils sharing the same Kronecker canonical form are classified under strict equivalence into infinite groups called bundles. Introduced in the 1990s, this concept is an extension of the earlier idea by Arnold in 1971, relating to matrices under similarity transformations. Despite substantial research on the topology of bundles of matrix pencils, some key issues remain unresolved. Specifically, open questions include characterizing closure inclusions among bundles and determining whether these bundles are open within their own closures. This paper addresses these queries, revisiting existing notions and offering proof of the openness of bundles for matrices, as well as matrix polynomials within their respective closures. Additionally, we establish descriptions of these bundles using attributes like subspaces, solvable systems, and rank functions. Furthermore, we examine closure inclusions among bundles of matrix pencils, including special cases like lines of matrix pencils and curves of matrix polynomials, and explore the related topology. Finally, we explore potential applications of these findings in parameter estimation problems. The accompanying thesis provides further detailed analysis. The presented research incorporates its validation into the existing topology of bundles framework, representing an extension of previous works by the first author. The potential of using noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers with the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) lies in molecular simulations, where accurately constructing an ansatz using a shallow quantum circuit is key to successful implementation. Instead of employing fermionic-excitation evolutions to create ans\"atze, our approach utilizes qubit-excitation evolutions, which adhere to qubit commutation relations. By doing so, qubit excitation evolutions can accurately construct ans\"atze with fewer qubit rotations, even with only single-qubit rotations, resulting in reduced computational cost. Furthermore, to adapt to changing circuit structures, we suggest utilizing qubit-excitation-based evolutions that are independent of qubit indices, allowing the evolutions to be applied simultaneously to any qubit. This offers a more flexible framework for exploring different excitation patterns and circuit structures. With this method, our wavefunctions outperform those obtained with fermionic-evolution-based VQE in cases involving N=4 and N=8 qubits, even when utilizing fewer quantum operations. The suggested method provides an essential foundation for the research and development of ansatz circuits in quantum chemistry simulations on NISQ devices. Its potential applications also extend to other quantum algorithms that benefit from qubit-excitation-based circuit designs. Additionally, our approach can serve as a prototypical model to illustrate the fermionic-excitation-based VQE, allowing researchers to create ansatz circuits with lower costs or better resilience to noise. Such a study could contribute to a deeper understanding of the characteristics of fermionic-excitation-based VQE and may uncover further improvements to this algorithm. Finally, although our suggested method is focused on quantum chemistry simulations, its underlying principles can be applied to other domains where fermionic-excitation evolutions are used to create ans\"atze, potentially leading to novel developments in related quantum algorithms. A new VQE approach called fermion-to-qubit VQE was recently proposed, offering improved resilience to qubit errors by translating fermionic evolutions into qubit-excitation evolutions with fewer qubit rotations. Similar to our algorithm, this method can accurately construct ans\"atze with reduced computational costs, offering promising prospects for implementation on noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers. The main difference between our work and fermion-to-qubit VQE lies in our research goals, as our approach is focused on developing ans\"atze for quantum chemistry simulations, whereas the former algorithm is more general and can be applied to any fermionic system. A key characteristic of deep generative models is the interaction of representation, its distribution, and a neural network mapping, with techniques like variational autoencoders (VAEs) often applied, but posing significant optimization challenges. Specifically, the inclusion of an encoder introduces complexity, particularly in terms of the amortization gap and the uncertainty of the variational approximation. Furthermore, the balance between model complexity and fitting accuracy in the latent distribution often proves difficult to achieve. In response to these issues, we propose an alternative approach, replacing the standard encoder with a maximum aposteriori (MAP) estimator for the latent representation. By integrating this modification into existing frameworks, including VAES and normalizing flows, we derive a unified framework, which we refer to as the Deep Generative Decoder. Furthermore, we provide a mathematical justification for the efficacy of this MAP estimator in maintaining the underlying structural properties of selected representation learning methods and introduce an extension of the existing KL-divergence based learning objective to our new setup. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the DGD counterpart to VAE, with reduced optimization gap and latent variable variance across multiple different configurations. Additionally, the DGD PNF model displays superior performance, improved fidelity and more realistic sampling behavior, relative to the standard NF model. Finally, the DGD PNF model is able to generate images of higher quality, with less reliance on overly complex models, when compared to the standard PNF system. In summary, replacing the standard encoder with a MAP estimator yields substantial gains in optimization simplicity, maintained structural consistency, and improved generative model quality. A comprehensive open-source implementation of the DGD framework is made available for the research community. Furthermore, the findings and results are further substantiated through interactive demonstrations.

The stochastic gravitational-wave background from inflation can be generated by quantum fluctuations during inflation and can be amplified by two less common cosmological theories: bransons and axions. These theories were previously less well-constrained, but recent results from NANOGrav precision measurements may have significant implications. The findings could indicate that the stochastic gravitational-wave background is consistent with current data, but only if the primordial gravitational waves are undetected and the common assumption that the state is Gaussian is incorrect. Alternatively, combining lower-frequency data with the assumption that the background is unpolarized could make the detection more feasible. In any case, the stochastic gravitational-wave background may help resolve the ongoing "Hubble tension," which persists despite the consensus on the cosmological constants. In fact, the proposed models could account for the observed tension if the stochastic gravitational-wave background is incorporated into the calculations, resulting in a more accurate understanding of the universe's spatial curvature. Consequently, the proposed models could serve as potential solutions to the "Hubble tension," and further data collections are expected to provide greater clarity on the feasibility of these solutions."

Our study presents the first survey of molecular emissions from a comet's volatile substances. We utilized standalone observations with the Atacama Compact Array (ACA) of the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA) of the comet C/2015 ER61, conducted shortly after its significant April 12, 2017, outburst. The data collected on April 15, 2017, included 8-hour tracks with a 30-km baseline sensitivity of 20 millijansky at  220 GHz, yielding the detection of carbon monosulfide (CS), carbon monoxide (C^34S), water (H2O), methane (CH4), cyanic acid (HNCN), and ammonia (NH3) emissions, as well as the non-detection of hydrogen sulfide (H2S) and H-D. The emissions detected were significantly broader than those typically seen in other comets, suggesting the presence of a global ring. Comparing the intensity of CS and HNCN to water, we noticed that CS's abundance dropped much faster than that of HNCN when compared to water, indicating that CS originates from the comet's gas-rich atmosphere, whereas HNCN likely comes from external sources within the solar system. This could have implications for the understanding of cometary chemistry. On the day of the outbreak, we found emissions that extended over 22 degrees in solar elongation, exceeding the comet's optical size, suggesting the presence of a broad ring. We estimated the volume of this ring, yielding a total gas amount of 1.1 x 10^11 mol, approximately five times that of the gas released by Hale-Boppe in 1997, supporting the theory of dynamic gas release. The gas release rate of  2.72 x 10^19 mol per day, rapidly overpopulated the space with C2S and CS, explaining their easy excitation and detection. This rate of gas release equated to  1.9 x 10^5 kg per day for carbon monosulfide, representing  4% of the non-ice mass of the non-ice portion of the snowless nucleus of the comet, indicating the presence of sulfur in the comet's ice. This work marks an important outcome from independent ACA observation, underscoring the value of the full ACA dataset, showcasing the remarkable sensitivity of ALMA's standalone interferometry to the study of cometary science. Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems frequently arise in real-world contexts, notably in mechanical engineering. A novel approach, combining multi-criteria branch-and-bound and non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm 2, is proposed for approximating Pareto fronts for such problems. A computational study, comparing this proposed hybrid method to non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm 2, demonstrates its efficacy with real-world and test cases. A new performance metric, investment ratio, assesses solution quality in relation to computation effort. Results from evaluating this proposed algorithm on five mechanical engineering and two mathematical test cases indicate its competitiveness for solving MO-MINLPs. A 5% lower investment ratio was observed for three test cases when using the new method in comparison to NSGAII. However, this new algorithm exhibits improved convergence properties, particularly in identifying a rich set of high-quality solutions in a relatively short time with low investment ratio, as exemplified in the computational study. Additionally, limit analysis is performed on a tight branch-andbound search tree generated using the proposed algorithm for solving STEQ to estimate minimum computation times required for achieving desired solution quality. A computational study demonstrates the practical applicability of this approach for dynamically adjusting computation times based on user preference for improved time efficiency and quality of solutions. Furthermore, employing the STEQ algorithm on the KSDP test case illustrates its potential in expanding the Pareto front without sacrificing solution quality, suggesting the potential for optimality in this test case with additional computation time proportional to the inverse of the lower bound on hyper-volume contribution. A detailed discussion on generalizing this approach for solving multi-objective computationally expensive optimization problems is provided in the thesis. A new algorithm, capable of handling expensive functions by using sampling and reduction techniques in addition to partial grading of solutions, is employed on the multi-objective non-convex post-hardening heat transfer test case and yields superior results when compared to branch-and-reduction paradigm. A comparative study of the proposed algorithms on four mechanical engineering and two mathematical test cases in terms of investment ratio and number of evaluations reveals their respective efficiency and effectiveness. A domain decomposition approach, used in combination with the proposed algorithms, demonstrates its potential for improving solution quality and computational efficiency. A new performance metric, geometric density, assesses solution quality in relation to computation effort, revealing that domain decomposition has negligible impact on investment ratio but significantly affects geometric density. Results from the computational study indicate that using domain decomposition yields higher solution quality and reduced computation times, thereby expanding the Pareto front and improving investment ratio. We refine and reinterpret the core principles of Lie theory, specifically Lie groupoids, through the lens of internal groupoids in synthetic differential geometry. Key concepts are re-expressed, including path sources and integrated $A$-paths. The primary findings demonstrate that a classical Hausdorff Lie groupoid's internal connectivity properties mirror those it satisfies as a classical connected Lie groupoid. Conversely, any internal weakly connected Lie groupoid hosts a unique, refined version of its 1-skeleton, which fulfills certain connectivity requirements. Additionally, we establish the internalization of the Gauchy-Nijenhuis theorem for Lie algebras and extend this to base change compatible morphisms of internal Lie algebras. Lastly, we discuss the internalization of foliation theory and prove the existence of a maximal integrable distribution for any pre-foliation. Moreover, we demonstrate that a pre-foliation is integral if its associated source 1-forms are zero. This is achieved by internalizing the holonomy functor for connected Lie groupoids and leveraging it to construct a foliation from an integral, connected Lie groupoid. Notably, the internalization process retains key classical properties including their functoriality and cohomological implications. However, the most critical aspect of this work is the emergence of a unique 1-skeleton for an internal weakly connected Lie groupoid, which serves as a fundamental, universally defined component in this setting. Furthermore, the internalization process makes the appearance of the 1-skeleton's transition maps, connecting its components, explicitly calculable. By synthesizing the simple, uniform structure of path spaces and their readout functions in synthetic geometry, this work's methodology can serve as a model for adapting and enriching classical algebraic and topological structures within internal geometry. Notably, the internalization process has an explicit and weakly explicit nature for the newly defined components, which is in line with the general principles of the synthetic approach. Moreover, the transition maps' expressibility in synthetic geometry for the 1-skeleton's components, which constitute the primitive elements of the groupoid's structure, is a novel aspect that distinguishes this setting from other homotopy algebraic frameworks. The simple, effective method employed in this paper could likely be applied to other structures undergoing a similar internalization process, which might lead to further research in the field of internal geometry. The Dynaswap project is focused on developing a robust, trustworthy architecture for safeguarding holistic workflows in cyberinfrastructures, allowing for deployment on virtual machines via cloud services such as JetStream. This cloud platform facilitates user-friendly access to dynamic computing and data analysis tools on demand. Dynaswap's security architecture incorporates role management, hierarchical access control, and transparent data encryption. This system is evaluated through various real-world scenarios, demonstrating its capabilities and limitations in protecting sensitive biomedical data. Additionally, Dynaswap's integration with a user-friendly interface on the JetStream gateway has streamlined user accessibility to the platform. Findings reveal that Dynaswap's data encryption approach is computationally demanding and requires further optimization for efficiency on JetStream. In contrast, the project's social impact could extend to supporting secure data analysis on diverse cloud platforms, contributing valuable knowledge to the Dynaswap user community. Furthermore, the project's analysis of holistic workflow protection, coupled with interaction between multiple cyberinfrastructures, is relatively unexplored in existing research. In particular, the JetStream gateway's ability to seamlessly move users through a series of configured virtual environments has posed a novel challenge in testing Dynaswap's security architecture. This complexity is acknowledged as the project's primary constraint in its research design. In contrast, the project's main advantage is the concept of platform agility, allowing users to conveniently transition between different cloud services and cyberinfrastructures. The project plans to contribute Dynaswap's source code to the open-source community and propose a future extension to the ESANN conference on Neural Networks Engineering, focusing on Agent-based Optimization of Cybersecurity Algorithms. The project's conclusions include identifying the importance of evaluating and validating Dynaswap's security architecture through controlled experiments, incorporating domain-specific data analysis and optimization techniques. In particular, the project recommends integrating Dynaswap's data encryption and decryption process with a distributed computing model to mitigate efficiency issues. In terms of future research directions, the project suggests exploring additional optimization methods for the data encryption and decryption tools, as well as developing cybersecurity models and simulators to assess the effectiveness of Dynaswap's security architecture in protecting against specific cyber threats. In contrast, the project plans to discontinue investigation of the Project Dynaswap Social Impact, given its secondary priority in the project's research design. Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the positive or negative sentiment of a particular aspect within product reviews. Approximately one-third of reviews lack explicit opinion statements, yet clearly convey sentiment towards an aspect. Identifying implicit sentiment is crucial for understanding customer opinions and making informed decisions during purchase decisions. Despite the effectiveness of supervised models for explicit sentiment analysis, they often struggle to capture implicit sentiment. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a new approach that leverages a significant amount of annotated implicit data through a supervised contrastive pre-training method, enabling the model to extract implicit sentiment from reviews. Importantly, our technique does not rely on any auxiliary tasks or extrinsic metrics to learn implicit sentiment. Instead, we utilize a self-supervised objective that contrasts implicit and explicit sentiment labels to distinguish between dominant and non-dominate sentiment orientations. To further enhance the model's performance, we employ a co-training strategy, involving two distinct models, to recover missing explicit reviews and facilitate the learning of implicit sentiment. As a result, our approach achieves superior results on the ImplicitASAP benchmark, outperforming existing state-of-the-art models by significant margins, particularly in identifying implicit sentiment. A thorough ablation study and various experiments validate the effectiveness of our supervised contrastive pre-training and co-training frameworks. The analysis also reveals that our methods are robust across different training data compositions, comprising varying amounts of explicit and implicit training instances. Notably, our results confirm that our methods are more effective at capturing implicit sentiment when the training data is predominantly comprised of explicit labels. Furthermore, our methods excel at identifying implicit sentiment when the majority of non-dominate instances are implicit in actual test scenarios. This research delves into secure communication systems for multiple users that utilize reconfigurable intelligent surfaces to compensate for hardware limitations.
We simultaneously adjust the base station's beamforming vectors and the phase shifts on the RIS to achieve the highest possible weighted minimum secrecy rate under constraints for the base station's power output and RIS element limitations.
To address this optimization challenge, we split the problem into two subproblems for subchannel allocation and phase shift optimization, solving each problem using mathematically feasible approaches.
A key subchannel allocation algorithm is proposed to handle the resulting combinatorial problem, while two efficient algorithms are developed to tackle the separate subproblems for phase shift optimization.
The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, which outperforms an existing benchmark method in terms of achieving the highest possible weighted minimum secrecy rate. Furthermore, the impact of RIS efficiency is considered, and the underlying principles are discussed. Additionally, the computational complexity of the proposed approach is investigated. Finally, the theoretical security gains of the proposed method over a relevant benchmark are examined via analytical expression. The findings confirm the validity of the proposed method and highlight its superiority to traditional approaches in various scenarios. Specifically, when the RIS efficiency is low, the proposed method still enables substantial improvement in the weighted minimum secrecy rate, thereby addressing a previously overlooked aspect. Moreover, the proposed method ensures a reduced error covariance compared to the baseline method. As the RIS efficiency and the number of users increase, the theoretical security gains exhibited by the proposed method also tend to increase. These findings illustrate the critical role of RIS that introduces significant performance advancements, thereby representing a promising enhancement for secure communication systems. The results suggest that the RIS efficiency significantly affects the secured throughput compared to the case when it's low, which leads to the conclusion that RIS introduces substantial improvements to communication systems. Consequently, the selection and design of RIS have a profound impact on achieving secure communication goals, which of course could also apply for regular non-secure communication goals, which is a subject for future research. The results suggest that when low RIS efficiency is achieved the secured communication goals can still be met with lower over all power consumption which is a subject for future research. Moreover, the proposed method provides reduced computational complexity compared to the baseline method, which makes computational efficiency a subject for future research. Finally, the proposed method enables further research for secure communication systems with lower error covariance, which is a subject for future communication systems. The code for the proposed algorithms can be found at https://github.com/AminKhosrav

Next, we create a predictive model, the contrastive value policy, to help the learner in this setting by producing a policy that compares old and new experiences and determines the value of each. This value can then be used to decide which perceptions to keep and which to discard in an iterative process. Additionally, we propose a method known as hindsight, which makes it easier to train the contrastive value policy by providing a more stable target for it to work with by combining multiple episodes and experiencing the consequences of different sequences of actions in reverse. With hindsight, we construct a training strategy for the contrastive value policy that uses an iterative process of labeling and resampling to optimize its performance in predicting future rewards. This approach can also be applied to other regression problems and serves as the foundation for developing a meta-learning method that is based on the concept of categorization. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the Sun, using data from the Parker Solar Probe, to better understand energy behavior and solar wind acceleration. The data, covering 12 close approaches to the Sun, included three-dimensional time-varying data on energy flux and temperature, and two-dimensional data on radial energy flux. We observed a distinct pattern of energy flux variability, linked to coronal mass ejections and high-speed streams, which showed intermediately high levels and increased intensity with distance from the Sun. Notably, energy flux at low altitudes was approximately 100 SW m^(-2), roughly double the value near the Earth during solar maximum. We also found that energy flux increased approximately 5.3x per radial distance, according to power law indexing. Moreover, temperature was found to follow a different set of rules, increasing at a rate of 1.6x per radial distance, and exceeding predictions in quiescent regions. These findings indicate a need to revise current models to accommodate observed energy flux behavior and nearby solar activity, particularly during phase 2 of the Parker Solar Probe's mission. By the end of this program, the ratio of energy flux to distance will be roughly 10 SW m^(-2), exceeding the current prediction of ~6.5 SW m^(-2) based on extrapolation and modeling. The data suggest that energy flux behavior changes at a distance of approximately 20 solar radii from the Sun. To gain a more precise understanding, the authors recommend publishing the full solar wind energy spectrum and speed, to better inform research and modeling initiatives. The findings presented resonate with the goals of the PSP mission and its collaborators, particularly the Solar Dynamics Observatory and other Keck Institute for Space Astronomy highlighted areas of study. The authors also acknowledge the support and resources provided by the University of Iowa's Earth and Space Sciences Division and the Iowa Space Grant Consortium, as well as the outstanding work and contributions of the data analysis team comprising Dr. Curtis Moore, Dr. Nathaniel Schuchijer, and Dr. Alan Patel. The authors appreciate the kind and professional support of Dr. David McComas and Dr. Craig Foster, who served as the reviewers of this article. The findings presented are even more significant in light of recent publications by the PSP team, particularly those that described the solar wind acceleration and the energy flux findings near the Sun. The article is complemented by an associated publication from the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which delves into the spatial structures and variability of energy flux within the near-Sun environment

A new method inspired by finite volume schemes leverages a cell-average based neural network to solve partial differential equations. By utilizing the weak formulation of these equations, the method trains a feed-forward network to accurately predict solution evolution between time steps, circumventing traditional numerical limitations. After offline training, the neural network model can be used in conjunction with a finite volume scheme, which requires mesh adaptation. One distinct advantage of this approach is its ability to eliminate CFL restrictions, permitting a wider range of time step sizes. Furthermore, when solving the Heat equation, convergence rates and error magnitudes show dependence on the spatial mesh size while being independent of the time step size. Moreover, the neural network model exhibits exceptional performance in simulating shock waves and rarefaction waves within nonlinear hyperbolic conservation laws with negligible numerical diffusion. Lastly, the neural network model demonstrates its capacity to handle complex problems by solving the Navier-Stokes equations using a previously established method. With further research, this approach has the potential to tackle more demanding applications such as turbulent Navier-Stokes equations and other high-dimensional problems. A related Python package, svneqn, provides an accessible and efficient implementation of the neural network method for solving PDEs. Moreover, the code is adaptable and can be integrated into the open-source framework PyCFD-Gurobics for deep integration with simulation tools. For additional details on the implementation, usage, and troubleshooting of the method, reference the accompanying guide. Furthermore, the analytical framework developed in this study has the potential to be generalized to other feed-forward network architectures, which may lead to separate investigations of alternative networks like ResNet, U-Net, and ChebNet. Following the framework established in this study, the implementation of these alternative networks would result in less complex and more efficient codes, which could lead to a deeper understanding of the relationship between network architecture and performance. A related Python package, neural-fv, facilitates this exploration by providing a unified framework for testing and evaluating the neural network method in its current form across various architectures. Ultimately, the approach presented in this study has the potential to serve as a starting point for the development of a wide range of neural network based finite volume schemes through systematic network architecture analysis. For direct access to the codes, data, and continuous integration setup used in this study, please refer to the repository provided. Furthermore, the user guide for the Python package svneqn and the PyCFD-Gurobics and neural-fv repositories has been made available for seamless continuation of the work as suggested. The Unruh effect can emerge not only through the entanglement of left and right Rindler regions, but also between forward and backward light cones. Our analysis focuses on the geometric phase associated with a massless scalar field's quantum state as it navigates a Schwarzschild black hole's background. We propose that the latter case represents a more fitting manifestation of the Unruh effect, as it avoids overlap issues between future and past domains and, we show, yields a comparable Berry phase to the Rindler case. Utilizing $2\times2$ Hilbert space spinor representations for both scenarios, we computationally verify that the generated entanglement is indeed the hallmark of the Unruh effect. Our work provides a template for experimentally verifying this phenomenon. Moreover, we've identified an approach to measure entanglement within the $2\times2$ Hilbert space, as existing methods to do so rely on infinitely differentiable models. Our analysis resolves a critical problem in this regard. A broader interpretation of our findings is also explored, including their applicability to the global phase of a quantum state in the Schrödinger picture. Our approach to the Unruh effect differs from traditional methods based on accelerating observers or linearized gravity, as we've used geometric optics to derive the future and past light cone's geometric phase. This task has received significant research attention, yet efforts focused on non-English languages remain largely underrepresented due to a lack of quality datasets required for model development and evaluation. In this work, a open-source Python framework called laserbench is introduced to design, optimize, and reverse engineer HPFS. By leveraging established thin film propagation equations and incorporating a diverse range of amplifier models, laserbench enables users to build, configure, and analyze virtual HPFS configurations. The framework utilizes the free, open-source Pysphera tool for automatic code generation and the AdaM framework for closed-loop optimization. Furthermore, it includes a new inverse modeling technique for reconstructing HPFS amplifiers from experimental data. The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.
While Delegated RingCT may not possess the same level of anonymity compared to other RingCT implementations, we propose that its ability to be compatible with DPoS consensus mechanisms provides a reasonable trade-off for enabling faster and more efficient transactions for anonymous users. Furthermore, additional measures such as Delegated RingCT token creation and redistribution for rewarding security Delegates can also be incorporated into the protocol. As such, Delegated RingCT represents a middle-ground solution for achieving a delicate balance between anonymity and transaction verification speed. This paper presents a novel optimization technique called AskewSGD to efficiently train deep neural networks with quantized weights. Initially, we transform the quantized neural network training into a sequence of constrained optimization problems that can be iteratively refined. Our method, AskewSGD, is an efficient first-order stochastic approach designed to solve each optimization subproblem. Unlike conventional algorithms, AskewSGD circumvents computationally expensive projections or quantization operations within the iteration process. AskewSGD's convergence properties are rigorously analyzed and we provide empirical evidence that confirms its superiority over existing methods. Extensive testing of AskewSGD on multiple networks, datasets, and quantization schemes demonstrates significant reductions in training time, averaging an impressive 3.5 times speedup. Furthermore, AskewSGD produces results comparable to the state-of-the-art approaches both in terms of performance and consistency. These findings highlight AskewSGD as a versatile method that can be adapted to various quantized neural network training tasks. Moreover, we show its potential extension to train neural networks with learned constraints on weights and activations with a notable improvement in the existing literature. Finally, we release AskewSGD's implementation on the public GitHub platform for the community to use and benefit from. It's composed of two parts: the $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ subgroup and the $H_3(\mathbb{R})$-group, which is made up of 6-dimensional real-valued cochains on a 3-cube. In the past, finding the Lie algebra of this group had proven difficult. However, new research reveals that the Lie algebra of this group, known as $\mathfrak{g}^J_2$, can be easily identified as the direct sum of the Lie algebra of $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$, denoted $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})$, and the 3-dimensional real Lie algebra $\mathfrak{b}_3$. Additionally, the Lie group $G^J_2$ can be realized as a subset of the group $SL(2,\mathbb{R})\times B_3$, which is the product of the groups $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ and $B_3$. This research provides new representations of key units within $G^J_2$, including its cohomology and homotopy groups, which differ from previous results. As a result, $G^J_2$ can be realized as a subset of the group $SL(2,\mathbb{R})\times B_3$. Furthermore, $G^J_2$ can be realized as a subset of the group $T_2\ltimes P_2$, where $T_2$ is the 2-dimensional torus and $P_2$ is the 2-dimensional parabolic group. In addition, $G^J_2$ can be realized as a subset of the group $T_2\ltimes (T_1\times B_1)$, where $T_1$ is the 1-dimensional torus and $B_1$ is the 1-dimensional compact solvable Lie group. These new realizations allow for a simplified understanding of the group $G^J_2$. Initial breakthroughs in the field relied on unsupervised approaches, however, current advancements are primarily based on labelled data, leading to increased control, flexibility, and stability in the generated images. Notably, these supervised methods require substantial amounts of annotated data, posing a major challenge. Our proposed framework combines two powerful techniques: adversarial training and representation learning, ultimately contributing to the development of unsupervised conditional GANs. To perform Bayesian inference using nested sampling, a specific prior sampling approach must be used, which involves selecting prior samples that meet a minimum likelihood requirement. The design of these sampling approaches is crucial, particularly for complex cases involving Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms. Here, we present "wrigglers," a set of strategies that incorporate differential evolution, simple exploration, and other techniques to maintain diversity in the sampling set, surpassing traditional mesh algorithms that often struggle with local minima and leading to poor performance, specifically in terms of varying posterior volume exploration. We examine "differential reversal," which adds a new direction to escape local minima, and several other techniques, such as integrating differential reversal into the general mesh algorithm, replacing poor mesh iterations with divergent simulations, and implementing a simple, highly exploratory method, and compare them with mesh algorithms using realistic synthetic and astronomical data, then selecting the most effective method. This choice is then used to analyze a complex dataset involving the search for neutron star black hole systems. Our study indicates that the proposed "wrigglers" are valuable tools in nested sampling, allowing for the efficient exploration of complex, high-dimensional parameter spaces. Finally, we extend our approach by developing a meshless algorithm that maintains sampling diversity, effectively allowing for the efficient exploration of these complex spaces. A comprehensive meshless approach, effectively allowing for the efficient exploration of these complex spaces. A thorough investigation of its performance in a range of synthetic and actual scientific applications demonstrates that the approach performs well across different types of datasets, highlighting the benefits of exploring alternative sampling techniques to the traditional mesh algorithms used in nested sampling. Using this tool, we perform an exhaustive analysis of 1194 available TOAST simulations that searched for black hole-Neutron star and neutron star-neutron star mergers in the actual astrophysical parameter space, effectively allowing for the efficient exploration of these complex spaces. In this theoretical study, we explore two-particle correlations in time and frequency for a Bose-Hubbard model subject to external driving and dissipation, specifically at and around the point where dissipation triggers a phase transition. We calculate a temporal two-particle correlation function and observe oscillations that decline when the model's imaginary Liouvillian gap narrows, a behavior that indicates a transition is imminent. When parameters deviate slightly from this transition, our findings suggest that super-bunching and anti-bunching regimes coexist, a behavior revealed when the two-particle correlation function is transformed into the frequency domain. The resulting spectrum features multiple components, including a center peak that grows stronger as the transition is approached and two smaller peaks that remain evident on either side, with reduced amplitude, in the anti-bunching regime. The observed features are similar to those predicted for second-order phase transitions in conserved quantities. We also apply quantum-state tomography to examine how two-particle correlations are affected by non-equilibrium dissipation, a process described by a microscopic model where a Bose-Einstein condensate interacts with a bath of two-level systems. The resulting modifications to the spectral density are found to significantly decrease the imaginary Liouvillian gap, causing the transition to be first-order under certain conditions, a finding supported by classical rate equations that outline the evolution of quantum states. The reductions to the imaginary Liouvillian gap that occur at the transition point also strengthen the corresponding drift terms, leading to a longer-than-exponential decrease in the time-evolved spin polarization, with the associated decay constant proportional to the imaginary Liouvillian gap, implying that the drift terms significantly influence the model's behavior. Finally, we examine an alternative interaction scheme featuring a cross-coupling of counter-rotating terms and show that for sufficiently strong and shallow lattices, the resulting modifications to the two-particle correlation function do not substantially affect the model's predicted phase diagram. Quantum systems driven periodically exhibit unique traits not found in undriven or thermally driven systems, particularly in their response to noise and heat, with recent studies uncovering unusual behaviors in closed systems that challenge conventional beliefs, including the emergence of long-lived "scars" that resist decoherence. This research investigates whether the previously observed characteristics of open quantum systems using Floquet drives can offer insights into their dynamics and if "Floquet scars" are a realistic phenomenon in these systems. To explore this, a study on driven bosonic atoms in an optical lattice is conducted, using the superfluid phase and vorticity to understand how noise affects their behavior. Findings indicate that a specific drive condition can lead to the formation of Bose condensation in an edge mode by triggering heating, with "Floquet scars" no longer being a distinct feature but rather a component of the more complex phenomenon of Bose condensation. This research no longer relies on the absence of interactions to observe edge modes, making it more closely related to quantum-driven many-body systems where scar states may be embedded within bands. Furthermore, it outlines a broader framework for understanding and identifying "Floquet scars" in diverse quantum many-body systems. Study data and parameters are available online for other researchers to view. Using a density matrix renormalization group method to simulate the system, simulations reveal that a non-equilibrium steady state is achieved much faster in open systems under Floquet drive conditions compared to undriven or thermally driven systems, with degenerate edge modes being a common trait in these systems. With the help of the density matrix renormalization group, it's found that under Floquet drive conditions, it takes significantly fewer steps to reach a non-equilibrium steady state in an open system compared to undriven or thermally driven systems. To explain the phenomenon of the edge mode being stable for a long time, it's found that it's influenced by a complex interplay of level repulsion, dephasing, and the influence of the continuum. With the help of the similarity flow, it's found that under Floquet drive conditions, it's possible for the edge mode to develop as a result of heating and form a stable Bose condensation pattern. Study data and parameters are available online for other researchers to view. Using a method of self-consistent second-order perturbation theory to describe the influence of the continuum, it's found that under Floquet drive conditions, it's possible for the edge mode to develop as a result of heating and form a stable Bose condensation pattern.

Metric learning's pair-wise loss technique is centered around optimizing an embedding that maximizes similarity between images within the same class, minimizing distance between images in distinct classes. Various forms of pair-wise loss strategies have been proposed. To consolidate this diverse set of loss functions, we've isolated specific aspects that dictate how these functions manipulate the positioning of feature pairs. Breaking down pair-wise gradient updates this way enables a deeper understanding of the dominant effects and allows for the development of a streamlined algorithm, ultimately leading to better image retrieval performance across datasets like CAR, CUB, and the Stanford Online Marketplace. Our findings indicate that pair-wise gradient-based optimization can surpass the conventional triplicate gradient optimization method previously thought of as the standard. Additionally, we show that pair-wise gradient-based optimization outperforms traditional methods, like triplet, by incorporating not only positive samples with labels but also negative samples. Our analysis reveals that pair-wise gradient-based optimization essentially applies a soft gradient that blurs the distinctions between distinct classes, achieving a softer separation than the harder distinctions produced by triplet gradients. This is demonstrated by analyzing the gradients produced by pair-wise and triplet objectives in a two-dimensional plane; the results indicate that the pair-wise approach produces weaker class boundaries, allowing for the incorporation of more training data, leading to better generalization and more accurate image retrieval. Our analysis also confirms that pair-wise gradient-based optimization outperforms triplet gradients, which have been demonstrated to perform better than singular gradient optimization in the past. Our simplified loss function interpretation provides a clear structural understanding of the loss functions, facilitating direct comparisons between different gradient-dominated effects. In this context, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor networks, which can efficiently simulate various systems using the principle of minimization, serve as quantum codes to prevent information loss, and accurately describe phenomena exhibiting power-law behaviors. A key finding reveals that networks comprising a single type of tensor and possessing erasure correction capabilities can't simultaneously possess certain desirable traits - those that facilitate efficient calculations and handle diverse phenomena. This contradiction motivates the creation of network guidelines that maximize efficiency while approximating desirable characteristics. A specific set of networks, Hyper-Invariant MERA, serves as an exemplary model, demonstrating significantly improved performance in processing tasks and capturing long-range correlations when compared to conventional networks used in quantum physics and information applications. A concrete model was developed - the HMERA$(d,j)$ - consisting of a combination of projective and $d$-dimensional quantum tensors, arranged in a way that maximally utilizes the principle of minimization, resulting in efficient calculations through a process called multilayer optimization. A key advantage of this model is its ability to execute specific tasks - scaling advantageously with the size of data, precising relationships between data density and correlation length, and using a relatively small amount of data to predict outcomes. Furthermore, our model allows for the description of a specific type of quantum physics scenario - a 1D quantum system with interactions gradually intensifying. Through a comparison, our model was found to surpass conventional networks used in quantum physics and information applications for specific tasks. This study contributes the creation of a universal network model that efficiently simulates and preserves information, which can be widely applied to various fields such as quantum physics and information technologies. Additionally, our model may facilitate the development of a universal language to describe phenomena exhibiting power-law behaviors in quantum physics and information theories. A related Python guide is publicly available online for the implementation and usage of HMERA tensor networks. This study was conducted as part of the Milstein Foundation's Quantitative Methods in Artificial Intelligence Initiative.

Current text-generation algorithms in dialogue can be flawed. Specifically, optimizing task success using reinforcement learning alone often leads to low lexical diversity in task-oriented settings. The proposed reason is not an inherent property of using reinforcement learning, but rather a byproduct of limited goal definitions in task-oriented settings, which typically focus on task completion rather than the quality of generated text. Subsequently, investigations into the QCD phase diagram and the thermodynamics of hot, dense strong-interaction matter gained significant momentum. To ground the discussion in context, a brief overview of the underlying lattice QCD formalism is provided, followed by a focus on the numerical methods used to study QCD at non-zero temperature and density. Structurally, the review is organized according to the decreasing length scales of QCD, with the primary emphasis on the bulk properties of QCD thermodynamics. A separate section is dedicated to the use of lattice QCD results for constraining the equation of state and testing phenomenological models, particularly in relation to the QCD critical point's hypothetical existence. Furthermore, some current challenges in lattice QCD research on QCD thermodynamics are highlighted. This research focuses on analyzing Twitter posts related to the 2020 Izmir earthquake, aiming to leverage these insights to infer real-time public opinions. potential use cases for the SceNDD dataset, such as in modeling driver decision-
making and evaluating behavior prediction models. The SceNDD dataset can be

Nonetheless, the precision of channel estimation in such systems is significantly compromised by the increased risk of underutilized cyclic prefix resulting from additional cascaded RIS channels, the inherent inaccuracies inherent to hardware implants, and large phase shifts introduced by RIS elements. To tackle these challenges, we develop a novel enhanced Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) model based on the least square (ELLM-LS) approach, which incorporates an adaptive learning mechanism and efficient data dimension reduction through both maximum variance reduction and sparse reconstruction techniques. With the aid of an optimized matrix, the proposed ELM-LSS approach can minimize the effects of underutilized cyclic prefix, multiple hardware distortions, and large phase shifts, ultimately leading to significantly improved channel estimation and subsequently, the system's performance. Simulation results validate the superiority of the proposed ELM-LSS approach, which surpasses several established underutilized cyclic prefix compensation and imperfect channel estimation techniques. Furthermore, the dynamic underutilized cyclic prefix compensation mechanism of RIS-related data distribution adaptation (RDDA-ELLM) outperforms relevant benchmarks by expanding the underutilized cyclic prefix tolerance, thereby enhancing system robustness, while its data distribution and quality do not significantly depend on the underutilized cyclic prefix value. The performance of the proposed methods is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and experimental validation conducted with the aid of numerical simulations. We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the canonical connection on nearly G2-manifolds with a normal homogeneous structure of four dimensions. Additionally, we derive a necessary and sufficient condition for the canonical connection to remain metric-compatible. Our methodology involves the use of Dirac operators to define a Lie algebra and describe the space of infinitesimal deformations associated with the structure. We identify a specific subgroup of the group of automorphisms consisting of smooth transformations with linear effect on the fiber, and construct a particular normal homogeneous structure of three dimensions featuring non-abelian instantons and a one-dimensional deformation space. Moreover, we prove that the deformed connection corresponding to this specific example preserves the metric. Lastly, we present an example illustrating the connection's role in forming G2-instantons via the twisted Dirac operator associated with a line bundle and a connection. Our methodology combines classical mathematical concepts with modern operators and index theory. The analysis provides insights into the interlinkage between the deformation theory of instantons, the Dirac operator, and nearly G2-manifolds. We leverage spinors and spinor bundles to formulate the deformation theory. Throughout this study, our primary focus lies on the smooth, seven-dimensional manifolds that support G2-instantons, but the underlying theory is applicable to any smooth, seven-dimensional manifold possessing a G2-structure, including spin manifolds. We aim to expand our research in this direction in the future. The analysis reported here represents the first approach to the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds though the space of the title has been extensively explored on spin manifolds. We have made significant progress in this direction. The study reported here represents an independent contribution to the field. The central nervous system's underlying physiological processes that drive conscious experiences have long been the focal point of research in cognitive neuroscience. In contrast to classical physics, which initially seemed unsuitable for a role in causally effective consciousness, the indeterminacy and unique duality of quantum physics have opened doors for modeling consciousness. We utilize quantum principles, particularly the Schrödinger equation and Planck-Einstein relation, to investigate the relevant timescales of conscious processes and to understand how non-zero interactions between quantum components give rise to entanglement and correlations. We demonstrate, employing a measure of entanglement based on Schmidt decomposition, that interactions between quantum subsystems can generate both entanglement and decoherence, which in turn enable dynamic changes in the entanglement of composite states. In contrast, coherence of individual subsystems is insufficient for binding, whereas interactions and associated decoherence play a crucial role in shaping quantum entanglement and correlations. We draw upon this understanding of quantum phenomena to propose a measure of ordinal utility, drawing parallels to Allais' paradox in human decision-making, which in turn raises fundamental questions about the role of quantum dynamics in human cognition. Our analysis serves as a prelude to exploring the broader implications of quantum mechanics in the functioning of the human nervous system. In particular, we draw a parallel between binding problems in cognitive neuroscience and the freezing problem in the quantum dynamics of Fermion systems, highlighting the potential for new insights into quantum information dynamics in nervous systems. This research paper introduces a tool for automatically translating ACL2 representations of C code into executable C code and verifying its correctness through the creation of accompanying ACL2 theorems. The tool employs a shallow embedding of C within ACL2, which attributes a formal nature to C's syntax by treating it as a prefix of ACL2 terms. The implementation of this idea is built upon the foundation of a shallow embedding developed by Robert Goodman and Deepu Singh's ACL2fx extension, which facilitates the representation of C data structures. Utilizing this shallow embedding, a set of macro functions is implemented to translate C code, and the tool also creates corresponding ACL2 theorems to validate the generated C code's functional correctness. The generated C code is then proven correct through the application of the Deepu Singh's ACL2fx's extract-shallow function, which extracts the embedded C syntax from ACL2 terms, combined with the theorem-generating capabilities of ACL2's immutability properties. This approach was successfully demonstrated in the development of ACL2 optimizations for two core data structures: trees and lists. The resulting C code is compatible with both legacy C code and contemporary cstd extension code, which provides access to the C standard library, thus allowing for the verification of any C code, including that on which the standard library is based or that supplied with the cstd extension. The research presents a number of possibilities for further investigation into the expansion of this work to encompass other aspects of C's syntax and the development of ACL2 reasonings for the creation of new C code. We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^1-equivariant theory constructed in Bar22, share key properties for any finite dimensional representation V of a torus T. Predicting short-term traffic is a widely researched area within intelligent transportation systems. However, existing forecasting systems face significant limitations due to their reliance on real-time data. The 2022 Traffic4cast challenge at NeurIPS addressed this issue by using publicly available sparse data. Our team submitted a solution to the expanded challenge of predicting estimated time of arrival. Our method involves extracting multiple feature sets - node flow characteristics, segment-based attributes, and similarity-based properties, which we used to train a model based on decision trees with gradient boosting. Our results demonstrate exceptional predictive capabilities across three cities - London, Madrid, and Melbourne - and even surpass some graph neural network-based approaches in estimating travel times. Our source code is available at https://github.com/c-lyu/Traffic4Cast2022-TSE.

This work introduces VACA, a new family of variational graph autoencoders developed specifically for causal inference tasks where there are no hidden confounding factors, using solely observational data and causal graphs. VACA models key aspects of a Structural Causal Model (SCM) without requiring any assumptions about its underlying parameters. By leveraging these properties, it provides a unified framework for simulating hypothetical scenarios and making predictions based on hypothetical outcomes. We demonstrate that VACA's variational and hypothesis-testing objectives can effectively assess model fit and evaluate hypotheses about interventions or counterfactual queries in cases without hidden confounding factors, offering a useful alternative to traditional causal inference methods. Through both theoretical analysis and computational experiments using synthetic and real-world data, we verify the effectiveness of VACA's new family of graph autoencoders that use variational inference. One of the main benefits of VACA is that it can efficiently handle complex datasets with a large number of examples, like air quality measurements in a city, without the need for additional training on similar datasets. Moreover, it can accurately evaluate precise counterfactual queries in cases without hidden confounding factors, like what would have happened to my lung health if I had never smoked, by utilizing Structural Casual Models and observing how the variables change in response to hypothetical scenarios, without requiring additional assumptions about unobserved factors. We have released VACA along with additional information, data, and results at https://vaca-source.github.io. We have also obtained an US patent for this technology. As a result, CPS of Cs can be viewed as dynamic, distributed networks of CPS Cs, necessitating the incorporation of high-level decision-making and autonomous intelligence. Consequently, CPS of Cs are becoming intelligent entities, capable of independently navigating complex challenges and achieving desired outcomes, necessitating the exploration of advanced, decentralized algorithms for decision-making processes. In this study, a decentralized approach is considered for developing intelligent CPS of Cs, where the cyber component of the system is represented by a decentralized artificial neural network, functioning as a centralized decision-making tool, while the physical aspect is characterized by a utilization optimization problem focused on reducing CO2 emissions. Due to the complexity of the involved mathematical problems, two optimization algorithms are proposed, performing gradient descent operations at an individual vehicle level and utilizing a gossip protocol for data exchange among the cyber entities, with simulation results demonstrating notable improvements in CO2 emissions reduction and overall performance. In conclusion, our work has successfully incorporated decision-making and autonomous capabilities into CPS of Cs, offering a promising starting point for the design and development of highly capable, intelligent cyber physical systems of systems. This work is part of a larger project focused on the development of advanced, decentralized artificial neural networks for system-of-systems decision-making and has enabled the creation of intelligent CPS of Cs through the incorporation of DANNs as decentralized decision-making tools. However, the resulting high data volume, which is equivalent to video, poses a significant obstacle to widespread adoption. To mitigate this, our study presents an efficient light field image compression method that utilizes a disparity model. By incorporating knowledge about camera displacement in the structure, we can significantly reduce the 4D light field array while minimizing the impact on spatial quality. To support this approach, our model includes a disparity estimation module that can identify horizontal and vertical displacement directions. An adaptive predictor module is also developed to calculate angular data points based on known spatial information. Additionally, we have created a network called the 'Latent Disparity Guided Reconstruction' (LDGR) module, which helps in restoring distorted points during decoding. The effectiveness of our compression method was tested through experiments using light field datasets, which showed notable improvements over traditional compression methods.
