In cross-lingual information retrieval using vectors, two fundamental models, 
interactive and non-interactive, prevail with synchronous and asynchronous 
query-document embeddings, respectively. Weighed against retrieval accuracy and 
computational efficiency, each approach excels and falls short. This study combines 
the benefits of these two frameworks through the development of a semi-interactive 
mechanism that constructs a non-interactive framework but unites document embedding 
with multiple associated queries in parallel, thus enabling interactive-style cross-lingual 
feature acquisition. By leveraging the word embeddings and a distillation process of 
an interactive model, we augment our proposed semi-interactive approach and demonstrate, 
experimentally, substantial gains in 5-15% accuracy over non-interactive and 2-8% over 
interactive baselines across various multilingual and low-resource language settings. 
The source code and saved models can be accessed at https://github.com/ahmadale-sb/semi-interactive-klr. 
Our findings show that a semi-interactive model can attain similar performance to interactive 
models with significantly reduced computational and memory burdens. Additionally, it 
requires less human involvement than fully interactive models and excels non-interactive 
models in retrieval efficiency and accuracy. As a result, the semi-interactive model 
emerges as a robust cross-lingual information retrieval solution. 
Researchers and developers can utilize this approach to tackle challenges in vector-based 
cross-lingual information retrieval and adapt it to various data retrieval and other 
associated tasks. 
Lastly, it will be made available through the HuggingFace Transformers library. 
We intend to update the model and incorporate feedback from the research community. 
The model achieved the top rank in the 2021 NLPShare Shared Task on Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual 
Information Retrieval and we're excited about applying the semi-interactive mechanism 
across multiple natural language processing domains.  The NLPShare challenge report can 
be accessed at https://github.com/DeepLearnIndia/NLPShare2021-data.  We're looking forward to 
utilizing this model to enhance search engine listings and improve user experience. 
The related dataset is hosted at https://github.com/ahmadale-sb/5shot-adapters.  We're 
renaming it  NLPClarity - https://github.com/ahmadale-sb/NLPClarity - to facilitate 
easy accessibility.  The Model has been updated to provide additional support for 
zero-shot information retrieval

The urgent need for comprehensive health and demographic reports has driven an increased focus on geographic studies, often utilizing detailed, pixel-level maps, particularly in low-income and middle-income nations. A key source of this data comes from household surveys, usually employing a complex, two-stage sampling design that stratifies regions and urban areas. Obtaining accurate estimates is crucial for crafting precise policies, but many existing studies often neglect the significance of sampling design, resulting in inaccurate and biased findings. This study investigates how different statistical analysis techniques react to distinct survey designs, comparing results from two discrete approaches: incorporating considerations of sampling design and those that disregard it. A simulation-based analysis of the differences between these methods reveals that ignoring a complex survey design can lead to notably inaccurate and biased outcomes, especially in predictive studies. Furthermore, it is found that a simple, up to four-level finite mixture model is an effective technique for making precise, small-area estimates when the underlying assumptions of this model hold true. Where this is not the case, a step-by-step process for selecting an appropriate spatial regression model is outlined, with recent research suggesting that geographically weighted regression as a viable option. In our study, we utilize Uganda's 2016 National Household Survey as a real-world dataset to test these findings. Overall, the study highlights the need for an informed, design-based analysis in the publication of survey results. While there are multiple model-based approaches that can be effective in making these estimates, it is only through an aware choice of methodology that we can guarantee the level of precision and accuracy required for these reports. Ultimately, the study recommends a set of guidelines for choosing an appropriate model or design, with the end goal of producing more accurate, geographically-targeted estimates. These study findings and recommendations have been shared with and endorsed by the Ugandan Ministry of Health, with the ultimate aim of enhancing more effective, geographic-based health decision making. In addition to these study findings, we have also provided a series of step-by-step instructions and code for replicating these results using a combination of R and Python in the supplementary materials, with the long-term goal of promoting replicability and knowledge dissemination in the geographic studies field. Finally, the study suggests a range of potential future research pathways in spatial modeling and analysis, with the ultimate recommendation being that future studies integrate considerations of sampling design in the publication of survey results. A simulation study has also been conducted and the associated code is available via GitHub at the following repository: https://github.com/salimate/SPSS_R_comparisons/tree/2022

In the context of quantum betting, this research investigates how to achieve optimal returns in a game where the payout depends on the relative outcome of two quantum states, $\rho_m$ and $\rho_n$, with the bettor winning if $\rho_m$ exceeds $\rho_n$ for losing the opposite. We represent the payout as a positive operator, $(\rho_m - \rho_n)\rho_n^{-1}$. A critical finding is that the optimal participation factor, key to determining success and failure in the Kelly betting strategy, is now a function that depends on the trace ratio, $\mathrm{Tr}(\rho_m^{\dagger}\rho_n)$, as opposed to the previous discrete scenario where it was solely dependent on the bias parameter. We examine several test cases to illustrate how the trace ratio affects this optimal participation factor. Additionally, this study introduces a new approach to determining the optimal portfolio based on fractional betting, and we verify that our proposed method aligns with the standard formula in cases where the payout is represented as a scalar multiple. We also show that if the payout has an adjoint representation proportional to the identity, the optimal portfolio equation will have a simplified solution with a residual. As part of this work's contribution, it sheds light on the relationship between the optimal participation factor and the trace ratio, highlighting that the former increases linearly with the latter for the case of our test wavefunctions. Moreover, this study provides insight into the variance of the wealth when the initial investment is uncertain, an aspect addressed in the supporting document. Finally, to demonstrate its practical application, this study proposes a prototype of quantum betting based on a continuous variable and showcases its user experience through a web application, available at https://doris-sun.github.io/QuantumBetting/. Its results verify that the Kelly betting strategy is indeed the most successful and robust method among all others. We further conduct a comparative analysis with alternative betting strategies and find that it yields a higher success rate in most cases and a comparable success rate in the remaining cases. Its robustness is undiminished even when the bias parameter is relatively small. As the prototype's technology advanced, it has become possible to implement the optimal participation factor based on the trace ratio, thereby enhancing its performance. We have used the prototype to test the efficacy of the optimal participation factor, thereby contributing to a deeper understanding of its behavior. We have also explored its possibilities and limitations, thereby raising important insights for future development. Its success rate is impressive, and its applicability is seemingly limitless. The magnetic field and non-ideal factors are known to be significant in the process of stellar formation, causing the collapse of a prestellar core into a rotating disk. Recent numerical studies have involved examining the effects of various magnetic field configurations and non-ideal factors on protoplanetary disk formation. However, a comprehensive analysis of the formation process, particularly in the presence of non-ideal factors, is still lacking in the literature. Our goal is to present a detailed analysis of the formation process, focusing on the evolution of the angular velocity, density distribution, gas temperature, and ionization degree in the disk area. Our study reveals that the disk formation process is characterized by a series of events, starting with an outburst like activity in the core, followed by the weakening of the magnetic field, and finally the establishment of a nearly axisymmetric velocity pattern. During this process, radial density distributions and gas temperatures in the disk area increase, while the ionization degree in the disk is maintained at a relatively low level due to the presence of a critical radius. Within this critical radius, radially midplane gas temperatures increase, leading to a nearly axisymmetric velocity pattern and radial density distributions. As a result, two distinct areas emerge, characterized by a velocity shock and increased density behind the magnetic field line in the midplane, and a region with axisymmetric velocity and radial density distributions away from the magnetic field line in the disk area. Our study also indicates that the disk area in which the gold standard model holds is relatively small, particularly at early stages of collapse. As the disk evolves over a long period of time, the midplane temperature increases, potentially allowing for the formation of the disk area in which the gold standard model holds, thus facilitating planet formation. Furthermore, the presence of non-ideal factors is found to have a significant impact on the disk area and mass distributions during this process. In the case of turbulent transport, the non-ideal factor causes the disk area and mass to decrease, leading to a nearly axisymmetric velocity pattern and radial density distributions. In the case of anisotropic transport, however, the non-ideal factor causes the disk area and mass to increase, while the disk area in which the gold standard model holds decreases, leading to a nearly axisymmetric velocity pattern and radial density distributions. In summary, the formation process of the protoplanetary disk from a prestellar core is complex and requires consideration of various factors such as the magnetic field configuration and non-ideal factors, which in turn affect the velocity, density, and gas temperature distributions

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors are based on atmospheric models which have yet to be verified through on-site measurements. We've carried out the first detailed study of atmospheric dispersion by directly measuring the refractive indices of the atmosphere across various wavelengths under differing conditions, rather than relying on simulated data. This research is the first of its kind to examine the subject and we've applied the results to create an accurate atmospheric model, allowing for the characterization of dispersion and the evaluation of the effectiveness of ADCs in relation to their commercial counterparts. By comparing our results to existing models, we've found notable discrepancies, highlighting the need for atmospheric dispersion correction solutions to be based on scientifically validated methods. The findings of our study provide valuable insights for improving the accuracy of atmospheric dispersion correction methods. Moreover, since the refractive index of the atmosphere varies depending on atmospheric conditions such as humidity, temperature, wind and system aperture, we recommend that the dispersion correction should be adjusted in real-time in line with changing atmospheric conditions, further minimizing distortions. This research aims to refine the precision of the dispersion correction method, a key area of improvement for optimizing the quality of the system's images. The study's major achievement is the development of an accurate representation of the atmospheric dispersion, a crucial element required to produce sharp images of the sky when observing from the Earth's surface. The study demonstrates the potential for adaptive correction strategies that could significantly enhance the quality of the system's images. Ultimately, the results of our study provide valuable groundwork for developing novel generation Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors capable of operating in real-time. Such advancements in technology could open up new avenues for observational studies, for example the exploration of the deep sky. Furthermore, we suggest that the application of our method could be extended to the assessment of the system's focal plane, potentially leveraging a smaller region within the image, however this requires the integration of our method into a real-time observational framework. We've also demonstrated the effectiveness of our strategy by analyzing a subset of our data, a approach that could be utilized in the development of future ADCs. The study's final contribution is the distribution of its results through the creation of a publicly accessible repository, potentially sparking the development of novel applications in the field of ground-based observational astronomy. Despite significant advancements in object detection, current methods have limitations in detecting diverse object categories due to the labor-intensive process of creating training data with bounding-box annotations. Recent open-vocabulary object detection methods have been developed to address this limitation by training on a set of base categories, enabling detection of object instances outside of the base category set. However, their effectiveness is restricted by the relatively small size of the base category set and the absence of further pre-training on diverse data. To address this issue, we propose an innovative technique that uses massive image-text pairs in a self-supervised manner to generate pseudo bounding-box labels for novel object categories with minimal human supervision, effectively expanding the base category set to a larger size. Furthermore, we improve the method's ability to accurately localize object shapes by introducing a simple yet efficient approach to integrate the proposed pseudo labels into state-of-the-art object detectors. Experimental results on the ImageNet-1K and COCO datasets extensively demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed pipeline in open-vocabulary object detection. Our approach achieves superior results on various benchmarks, achieving an average relative improvement of 12.3% and 5.3% over state-of-the-art methods for single-stage and cascade detectors, respectively. Mortality forecasting models built on the classical factor framework, such as the Lee-Carter model and its variants, often oversimplify the complex relationships between demographic factors to a single set of static connections. In contrast, models incorporating dynamic factor connections offer more nuanced representations, like the state-space model and its state-space extension, the extended Lee-Cater model. Our study highlights the significance of model complexity in forecasting outcomes and suggests a third option, the extended extended Lee-Carter model, which has the capability to adapt factor connections over time yet maintains a simple model structure. Using historical mortality data from Switzerland and the US, we compare the effectiveness of these models in predicting long-term trends and short-term variations in mortality. The results indicate that models accounting for dynamic factor connections, particularly the EELC model, provide the most accurate forecasts among those tested. Notably, the EELC model outperforms the traditional Lee-Carter model in long-term predictions and delivers comparable or better short-term forecasting results to advanced models. Additionally, we observe that models incorporating an additional, time-varying parameter in the covariance structure of the state-space equation can enhance forecasting accuracy, and this enhanced accuracy holds especially for forecasts of extreme events. Our study also explores the practical feasibility of implementing these models using online tools, such as mortality forecasting platforms and software libraries, to facilitate widespread adoption and application in practical settings. Further analysis delves into the sensitivity of the EELC model to potential forecasting inaccuracies resulting from missing data and high initial mortality rates, and finds that these errors primarily affect accuracy in the short-term. Finally, the study demonstrates the capabilities of the EELC model's extensions, which can generate spatial forecasts and estimate various types of secondary mortality indicators with a high degree of accuracy. Overall, our study confirms the value of modeling complex demographic relationships through time-varying factor connections and provides evidence of the effectiveness and practicality of doing so in mortality forecasting. The study's findings were implemented using an open-source mortality forecasting platform, which is available at https://mortpy.github.io/ Mortal-forecasting-is-one-of-the-key-elements.html. The related Python code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/andreashb/mortpy_experiments. By developing simple yet adaptive models accounting for distribution shifts, we significantly enhance the feasibility of long-term planning and decision-making in fields heavily influenced by demographic changes. The study's findings and resources are intended to facilitate the integration of mortality forecasting models into practical applications, which in turn may ultimately shape the fields they affect

Reducing the cost of Neural Architecture Search (NAS) by sharing weights among different datasets is a key challenge, but these efforts are often hindered by interference from one dataset affecting another's results. This phenomenon has previously been studied in the context of training on multiple datasets, but its impact in the NAS field remains unexplored. In our research, we investigate the nature of interference in NAS and identify two primary effects: 1) biasing picks that favor better performance on one dataset over others; 2) amplifying noise in architecture evaluation caused by sensitivity to random weight initializations. By applying mathematical analysis and empirical observation, we reveal that shared weight models in NAS are prone to a 'tyranny of the majority,' where results for smaller datasets are overwhelmed by those of larger ones. To mitigate these issues, we delve into the technical requirements for mitigating interference in NAS and evaluate the effectiveness of three methods: 1) optimizing top-performing architectures for better generalization; 2) implementing dataset-specific regularization; and 3) using an 'influence function' to identify and avoid biased picks. Our research provides a comprehensive understanding of the counterproductive effects of dataset interference in NAS and introduces a simple method to overcome these challenges, allowing for more effective architecture search with associated cost reductions. By combining these techniques, we achieve nearly optimal results on several benchmark datasets using only 3 days of training, representing a 5x improvement in efficiency. Moreover, we apply our method to a state-of-the-art NAS architecture and achieve superior performance on a diverse set of 11 image classification datasets, outperforming a strong baseline with 110% higher top-1 accuracy and 93% lower training time. Time series data in various scientific disciplines are analyzed and measured. One common technique for evaluating the characteristics of these data sets involves computing multiple statistical measures or features, which can then be represented as a feature vector for analysis. This resulting feature space enables traditional statistical techniques like clustering, regression, and classification to be applied. When dealing with large datasets, though, selecting the most relevant features to use becomes a significant consideration. This paper introduces an open-source R package called theft, which offers a straightforward, high-efficiency interface for extracting notable time series features, selecting the most influential ones, and conducting supervised machine learning analyses. Additionally, the paper showcases the theft package through a demonstration of its use in astrobiology for identifying genomic motifs that are characteristic of Earth's microbial organisms and are also found in other extraterrestrial life forms, should it exist. This included using the theft package to perform feature selection on various Earth-based microbial features. Human-assisted Translation Quality Assessment (TQA) involves evaluating the accuracy of translations by either expert translators or language experts, drawing on their extensive experience in translation. By considering the collective views of multiple assessors, we can gain a deeper understanding of how reliable each translator is. From a Bayesian perspective, we've developed a method to determine reliability by averaging posterior distributions based on expert and translator agreement. This approach utilizes a dependently-ratioed model for translating pairs, effectively quantifying each translator's reliability through a single score. Furthermore, we've found that our method effectively identifies outliers and establishes confidence intervals for reliability scores. Although outliers affect reliability scores, they have minimal impact on the overall accuracy of translation. We've implemented and tested this method using a fully annotated corpus of translation evaluations, demonstrating its ability to accurately capture the reliability of translators and identify consistent translators with high reliability scores. Additionally, we've discovered that our approach is capable of accurately predicting translator reliability even when only considering a small number of evaluations. Finally, we've compared our Bayesian model to a traditional reliability measure and performed various experiments, confirming that our approach consistently surpasses traditional methods in assessing translator reliability and performing classification tasks. You can access the full source code and annotated corpus from our companion repository at https://github.com/alexey-guliu/bayes-reliability. From a practical standpoint, we've found that our approach is useful for both individual translators and companies, allowing them to identify and take action to correct flaws in translation and reinforce the skills of their translators. Ultimately, our research showcases the efficacy of a Bayesian method in assessing translator reliability and facilitating translation quality improvement. Although this research holds significant practical value, we acknowledge its limitations to theoretical advancement, as our primary goal was to bridge the gap between BPA and TQA. We hope that our study inspires further research in this direction and that you join us in exploring the integration of Bayesian probability and assessment theory to achieve even greater progress. You can access the full source code and annotated corpus from our companion repository at https://github.com/alexey-guliu/bayes-reliability. From a practical standpoint, we've found that our approach is useful for both individual translators and companies, allowing them to accurately and systematically measure translator reliability and take concrete steps to correct their errors. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the effectiveness of a Bayesian method in assessing translator reliability and showcasing its practical value in translation industry applications. increasing ticket sales can often predict a better return for individual tickets.
To boost the return on investment in a lottery ticket, we need to determine when to
purchase a ticket based on recent sales and jackpot growth. Our study focuses on
two leading US lotteries, using a combined statistical model to analyze sales and
jackpot advancements. By examining the interplay between the jackpot's current state
and player participation, we can identify the ideal time to buy a ticket to maximize
profits. Furthermore, we analyze the bimodal distribution of returns in individual
tickets and explore their underlying causes, using statistical models to establish
a connection between winning numbers and individual ticket winners. Our study
combines the patterns in winning numbers with overall lottery outcomes to assess the
expected profit from an individual ticket based on its unique winning numbers and
the jackpot's growth. By demonstrating that our approach effectively increases returns
in both the Powerball and Mega Millions lotteries, we demonstrate its practical
value in maximizing investment returns on lottery tickets. Ultimately, this study
reveals that using our methodology to align ticket purchases with jackpot growth can

profits based on an individual's willingness to take risks. Our findings highlight the
value of combining data analysis and statistical models to explore the complex
interactions between lottery outcomes and player behavior, particularly in contexts

accuracy, which has significant financial implications for individuals investing in

Specifically, SIAA leverages Swift-IAA's fully convolutional projection module paired with additional normalization and patch-based loss functions in an iterative process for better results. t-SNE is a widely employed method for reducing high-dimensional data to lower-dimensional representations, particularly in data visualization. Its core assumption relies on non-constrained data within Euclidean space, with proximity determined by Gaussian distributions. However, this premise doesn't always apply in real-world scenarios, as evidenced by data such as points on the surface of a sphere, which adhere more closely to von Mises-Fisher distributions. In response, this study develops a novel vMF-SNE algorithm tailored for embedding spherical data efficiently. Utilizing an extended gradient structure, vMF-SNE achieves notable performance enhancements over its Gaussian counterpart, with notable improvements in both simulation and real-world roboairing array applications, where embedding spherical data into 2D or 3D spaces. Notably, vMF-SNE produces more accurate embeddings and significantly accelerates computation by up to 40 times, with results corroborated across multiple initial placement options. Overall, vMF-SNE proves a more robust and efficient solution for embedding spherical data compared to its Gaussian counterpart. Its implementation is freely accessible on GitHub, with the name 'vmfsne' reflecting its core algorithmic involvement. Additionally, this study's results demonstrate that vMF-SNE outperforms its Gaussian counterpart by up to 40 times in terms of embedding accuracy and computational efficiency, with results further validated in a real-world application of the roboairing algorithm in section 4.3. Furthermore, to ensure reproducibility of the research, an additional study using synthetic data is provided in section 4.1 and supplementary results in section 5, with source code and data hosted on GitHub at the specified GitHub repository. As for the second question regarding the research domain, spherical data embedding finds its applications in diverse fields, with notable examples illustrated in this study, particularly its use in robotics, geology and medical imaging. In this hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing, any quantum algorithm can be implemented without traditional two-qubit gates by utilizing an inherent, always-active connection between qubits. Building on this principle, our research explores how digital-analog simulation can be used to study fermionic systems, specifically the Fermi-Hubbard model, using a fermionic SWAP network and a method to correct distortions. Focusing on the effects of qubit connectivity and the distribution of interaction coefficients, as well as the precision of entanglement-inducing operations, our results indicate that an optimal qubit connectivity arrangement for simulating fermionic systems of any dimensionality is a chain for systems without spin and a ladder for those with spin. This relatively straightforward connectivity arrangement makes the digital-analog method particularly appealing for fermionic quantum simulations. Furthermore, our study shows that accurate simulation of fermionic systems requires precise entanglement generation but is somewhat robust to distortions in connectivity, which in turn highlights the importance of starting from Hamiltonian representations and illustrates the unique advantages of the digital-analog approach. Finally, our results suggest that for fermionic systems with spin, the influence of interaction coefficients' distribution significantly affects entanglement development and, consequently, the quantum phase transitions' location and nature. Overall, our work demonstrates the digital-analog method's potential as a powerful tool for simulating complex fermionic systems on quantum computers. Additionally, we developed the HDAQROM algorithm, which utilizes quantum computers to determine the optimal entangling operation for efficiently and precisely correcting distorsion effects on quantum circuits. This algorithm's development is motivated by the current limitations of available methods for handling analog errors in multi-qubit quantum circuits, which typically only address a single type of distortion and hence can be applied only in specific situations, thus hindering their more widespread adoption. Graph polynomials hold significant value due to their potential to develop algebraic formulas describing various graph characteristics and encoding multiple graph invariants through their evaluation sequences. Certain graph polynomials also introduce novel invariants not captured by existing ones, highlighting their importance. This article provides a theoretical framework to illustrate how sequences of graph polynomials arise from invariants of labeled graphs. This framework involves translating invariants into formulas expressing the behavior of sequences of polynomials based on graph types. We also present a conceptual software implementation to facilitate this process. Additionally, this article establishes that any sequence of graph polynomials that evaluates to unique values for isolated graphs must itself be uniquely determined by the values of isolated graphs. As a result, we discover multiple previously unidentified sequences of graph polynomials. We analyze the chromatic polynomial, a known sequence, and several new ones, including a pair that may potentially lead to the development of a graph invariant similar to the treewidth. Our analysis also addresses the open question regarding the uncountability of sequences defined by the evaluation of graph polynomials. Finally, we provide a preliminary study on the computability of graph polynomials based on the nature of their defining equations. While some graph polynomials can be evaluated exactly with minimal computational effort, others fall within the NP-C or #P class, and a few others are non-computable. Notably, we found that while the non-computability of a graph polynomial may imply the non-existence of a polynomial expression for its underlying invariant, this is not always the case. We identified an explicit graph invariant with a known non-computable generating polynomial, suggesting the possibility of identifying additional invariants with this property. A comprehensive SAGE code is provided to replicate the experiments mentioned throughout this article. It includes an additional set of experiments to illustrate that while most graph polynomials admit a computable degree of their roots, some do not, and whether a graph polynomial can be exactly evaluated generally depends on the specific nature of its underlying graph invariant. Further research should focus on characterizing the possible evaluations of graph polynomials at specific numerical values, and the relationship between the possible sequences of graph polynomials and their potential encoding of graph invariants. Additionally, the development of a graph polynomial that leads to a new invariant not captured by existing methods remains an unsolved problem at this time. Despite remote working having been implemented for decades, there is still a significant debate among researchers and practitioners as to whether agile methodologies, such as Scrum, are better suited to supporting remote teams. Our research explores this uncertainty by examining the impact of working from home on the success of Scrum projects through a mixed-methods approach combining both quantitative and qualitative elements. We investigated this topic by analyzing existing studies, collecting new survey data, and sharing qualitative insights from industry professionals about their experiences with Scrum in remote working settings. Our findings indicate that, overall, Scrum can be an effective framework for achieving project success regardless of working remotely. We discovered several key practices that are particularly effective when implemented in remote settings, such as implementing frequent, flexible core hours of work. Our empirical results suggest that companies working remotely can match the project success rates of those working on-site. In pursuit of breakthroughs in the medical field, we analyze chromatic configurations in three-dimensional space, employing topological concepts. Leveraging techniques borrowed from image processing, we develop mathematically sound indicators to capture both fine-scale and broad-scale interplay among color groups within a distribution. Our proposed methods enable fast, quantitative mapping of color patterns, allowing for their comparison across distinct groups. Building on the concept of persistent homology, we provide a framework for interpreting interplay levels as densities in chromatic distribution. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods using test datasets, including images, points arranged randomly, and clusters with varying sizes. The supporting code can be accessed at https://github.com/tgretton/pchomo. Our research reveals that the homology groups of the 1-alpha complex are invariant to translations, rotations, and the overall color pattern, thereby serving as a robust feature for classification tasks. In contrast, the homology groups of the 2-alpha complex prove sensitive to both overall design and interplay levels, thus emerging as a superior indicator for characterizing fine-scale interplay. Our experiments also show that the homology groups outperform existing metrics like normalized information content and chromatic diversity. Additionally, we demonstrate that the homology groups exhibit desirable properties such as monotonicity, consistency, and a form of invariance to rotation and replication. A thorough technical examination of the properties is provided in the paper's appendix. Our research indicates that the homology groups of the 1-alpha complex are well-suited for broad-scale analysis, whereas the homology groups of the 2-alpha complex are more suitable for fine-scale studies. Consequently, our methods provide a framework for interpreting the results of spatially-structured clustering algorithms at various scales. In summary, our research provides a comprehensive mathematical analysis of the interplay among color groups in three-dimensional space and offers a framework for its quantitative assessment. The homology groups have emerged as the most suitable indicators for interpreting interplay levels due to their robustness, interpretability, and theoretical simplicity. The proposed methods also enable fast calculation of topological properties, thus facilitating interactive analysis of the interplay among color groups in large distributions. The supporting code is now available online at https://github.com/tgretton/pchomo. I would like to express my gratitude to Dr. Bertrand Chapallier and Dr. Adrien Bourdaud for their guidance and support throughout this research. The resulting methods also enable the study of quantitative relations between fractal dimensions and interplay levels.

We analyze two primary objectives - minimizing the total processing time to maximize throughput, and reducing the average processing time to achieve a target response time. We employ a recursive Green function approach to obtain the Fock space propagator and associated self-energy for one-dimensional interacting fermions in a disordered system. Our results show that the local self-energy's imaginary component, which governs the decay rate of initially localized states, can serve as a probabilistic phase transition order parameter, facilitating the characterization of critical behavior and multifractal nature in many-body localized states across various disorder intensities. Moreover, we establish that the fractal dimension associated with the local self-energy experiences a discontinuous change at the phase transition, where it transitions from less than one in the localized regime to one in the thermal phase. Furthermore, the local self-energy's asymptotic scaling behavior in the vicinity of the critical disorder strength is non-uniform, featuring an essential singularity due to a non-ergodic volume, which controls the local self-energy's vanishing trend towards the critical point. Conversely, the correlation length derived from the local self-energy diverges with a power-law behavior in the vicinity of the critical disorder strength, but only when the phase is localized. Additionally, in contrast to the universal nature of the local self-energy's asymptotic scaling behavior in the thermal regime, we find that the scaling characteristics of the local self-energy are significantly influenced by the presence of gaps in quasi-one-dimensional interacting fermion systems. Our analysis reveals that the local self-energy exhibits disparate fractal dimensions when particles are one, one and a half, or two dimensional, leading to a complex multifractality spectrum in the localized regime. Moreover, in contrast to the one-dimensional case, the local self-energy exhibits a breaking symmetry in its asymptotic scaling behavior at various points in the localized regime, resulting in four distinct phases. These distinct phases in the one-dimensional model fail to emerge when particles are effectively two dimensional. Our analysis of phase transitions in the localized regime reveals that they exhibit characteristic features such as nonergodicity, frustration, and Kosterlitz-Thouless ordering due to a breaking symmetry in the local self-energy, resulting in a complex multifractal nature. It is worth noting that the local self-energy's nature near the critical disorder strength in quasi-one dimensional systems is still ambiguous and requires further clarification. A recent technique, called alignments, identifies and measures deviations between process executions and predefined reference models, pinpointing the discrepancies in process traces. Notably, alignments require entire or initial segments of process runs from start to finish; this paper explores new methods to analyze partial process runs in an equitable manner, assessing not only the initial segments but also the trailing segments of process executions for conformance. These novel methods are created using a custom notation and mathematical approach called bi-normalizations, offering a theoretical framework and practical application for evaluating conformance in process fragments. Accurate prediction and simulation of radio wave transmission are essential for optimizing modern mobile networks. Existing propagation models are broadly classified into two types - empirical and deterministic models. Empirical models, although computationally simple, are often inaccurate due to oversimplifications in their statistical basis. In contrast, deterministic models, like those based on ray tracing and physical wave propagation laws, provide precise predictions but require significant computational resources and can only utilize traditional geographical data. In this article, a groundbreaking approach to radio propagation modeling using deep neural networks is presented, demonstrating substantial performance gains over conventional methods. Power system expansion planning models, used to integrate renewable resources, rely on complex optimization problems involving various economic and technical factors. These factors carry significant uncertainties, yet their impact on model accuracy is poorly understood. This study introduces a new approach to assess the sensitivity of power system models to specific parameters by measuring the increased costs resulting from inefficiently allocating generation capacities. Through case studies involving capital costs, varied weather conditions, and differing spatial and temporal resolutions, we demonstrate the method's value and reveal that models are most susceptible to temporal resolution. Additionally, we clarify the limited influence of spatial resolution and stress the importance of selecting appropriate weather data. By promoting this sensitivity analysis, we aim to enhance the accuracy of power system expansion models and guide the efficient planning of systems to integrate high levels of renewable energy. The method's detailed implementation is provided in the accompanying code. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive model designed to integrate the various factors influencing power system development, available at the referenced GitHub repository.

Researchers have discovered a class of materials called "rheo-acoustic" gels that are uniquely responsive to ultrasonic vibrations. This breakthrough reveals that when subjected to these high-frequency sound waves, colloidal gels exhibit a profound reduction in rigidity. This phenomenon, which can be measured and characterized, is linked to the formation of micro-cracks within the gel structure, which can either repair or remain intact after the vibrations cease. Moreover, ultrasonic waves significantly reduce the gels' strength against external forces and expedite their transition into a liquid state under stress. Our study paves the way for the manipulation of gel properties and flow behaviors through ultrasonic manipulation, offering exciting avenues for future modeling and exploration of rheo-acoustic materials. This work is detailed in a recent issue of Physical Review Letters, providing foundational knowledge obtained through experiments and simulations. These studies reveal that ultrasonic vibrations can reversibly disrupt the gel's rigidity within a specified threshold of vibration intensity and strain, opening the door for future investigations into the behavior of rheo-acoustic materials. This work holds promising implications for the transportation and storage of liquids, as it establishes the possibility of tuning flow behaviors through the application of ultrasonic vibrations. Importantly, these studies demonstrate that ultrasonic vibrations can both weaken and strengthen materials, depending on factors such as the method of vibration application and strain rate. Furthermore, modeling efforts have identified the critical factors contributing to the disruption and recovery of gel structures in response to ultrasonic vibrations, which holds promising applications in the transportation and storage of liquids. Ultimately, this work contributes to the understanding of rheological dynamics by demonstrating that ultrasonic vibrations can reverse the response of gel-like materials to external forces and stresses, challenging conventional notions in rheology and fluid dynamics. Furthermore, these findings offer the potential for the tailored modification of flow behaviors and mechanical properties in materials that exhibit solid-like and liquid-like properties, depending on factors such as vibration intensity and strain rate. In the realm of processing these materials, ultrasonic vibrations can be leveraged to introduce defects within the material, potentially refining its texture and structure. For example, ultrasonic vibrations can be utilized to tune the spatial arrangement of particles within the gel, which in turn impacts its responsiveness to external forces and chemicals. In the future, these materials could find applications in the development of smart containers and drug delivery systems, where tuning the texture and structure of materials is critical to delivering a dose or transporting a substance. In addition, these findings and applications hold promising avenues for the adaptation of ultrasonic technology in biological systems

A new method for extracting a sparse signal from cross-related data is presented. This type of correlation is common in fields such as optics and seismic analysis, but the additional dimension creates an inverse problem bottleneck as the number of variables quadratically increases. Our solution simplifies this by only solving for the diagonal of the signal matrix, where variables increase linearly. This is made possible through a specialized "noise absorber" that filters data that does not provide signal information. This results in a linear solution at a similar cost to linear measurements. Our theoretical analysis confirms exact signal recovery under clean data conditions, with zero false positives even at noisy levels, as well as an improved signal recovery rate proportional to the number of data points. Numerical experiments validate our findings. This method presents a significant improvement by offering a linear number of variables at a quadratic recovery rate, surpassing the linear recovery rate of individual measurements and the quadratic recovery rate of cross-related measurements in all tested scenarios. We run in linear time thanks to the "noise absorber" which filters data and reduces the size of the signal diagonal solution. In this paper, we thoroughly examine the relative magnitudes of resonant and non-resonant contributions to top and bottom quark production in models featuring scalar top quark models and degenerate top quark pairs. Following this analysis, we establish new, non-resonant-adiabatic detection bounds for top and bottom standard model partners. These bounds supplement existing detection limits, offering a more comprehensive understanding of detection sensitivity. A recent breakthrough in translating English to SPARQL using neural machine translation (NMT) models holds great promise for automating SPARQL query generation, but these models have a major limitation: they can only handle queries crafted to their language skills in the training data. Since NMT models trained on existing datasets struggle with queries featuring knowledge base elements such as URIs and IRIs, queries containing these elements often receive low scores and are incorrectly omitted from generated queries. We find that a method commonly used in conversational NMT to copy source words in order to maintain their meaning, is ineffective in including such elements in queries. In an effort to overcome this challenge, we introduce a new mechanism called the knowledge element copy mechanism (KECM) which seeks to replicate the success of this method while adapting it to the knowledge base element use case. Through comprehensive testing on two publicly available datasets, we find that the KECM has a substantial positive impact on NMT performance and significantly reduces the frequency of query inaccuracies. In addition, we find that incorporating KECM results in notable improvements when training on one dataset and evaluating on another, and that combining KECM with other established techniques such as using an embedded knowledge base and using a structured generator, leads to significantly improved results. We believe that incorporating KECM into existing NMT architectures, is a crucial step in developing high-quality SPARQL NMT models that can accurately translate and precisely formulate queries featuring a range of knowledge base elements. This work introduces a novel method for systematically categorizing and assessing the quality of diverse publishing outlets in Computer Science. Leveraging a substantial subset of the extensive DBLP dataset covering over five decades, our technique evaluates around 17,000 conferences and journals across multiple fields. In contrast to existing citation-based metrics, our model successfully classifies a broad range of publishing venues, including those with limited or even zero published content. Furthermore, our technique accurately distinguishes between groups A and B of the 2021 ACM Seniormost Papers Archives, and identifies top-tier journals in fields such as Algorithms, Database Systems, and Artificial Intelligence. In field-specific evaluations, our method ranks around 75% to 85% of evaluated conferences and journals above the global field-average quality. In field-average-based comparisons, our model ranks around 60% to 75% of evaluated conferences and journals above the global field-average quality. You can find the source code and resulting venue ratings at https://github.com/fortran95/va. In a rigorous analysis, our method exhibits several desirable characteristics of quality metrics, namely, deep, wide, and stable. Our study also investigates the correlation between the evaluated roles of program chairs and the perceived quality of conferences. In contrast to citation-based metrics, our method provides comprehensive quality ratings for a wide variety of publishing venues in Computer Science, facilitating simple applications such as venue selection for research publications or strategic decision making for research funding. Ultimately, our findings highlight the significance of distinguished venues in producing high-quality research. This study builds upon three significant lines of research related to dissimilarity-based clustering and integrates them into a unified theory. Specifically, we draw from Jardine and Sibson's concept of overlapping clusters, Carlsson and M\'{e}moli's functorial view of clustering, and the categorical framework established by Wilder and Borodin. We define a functor that represents overlapping clusters with a specified radius in a metric space, ensuring that the application of the functor preserves the topological structure of the original space. The functor associated with clustering is shown to be an extension of the classical Vietoris-Arlon compact ordering functor. We demonstrate the existence of a homotopy equivalence between spaces that exhibit the same topological properties under the action of the overlapping cluster functor. Furthermore, we prove that the spaces resulting from successive applications of the overlapping cluster functor have distinct topological characteristics, separating them from traditional clustering functors. Additionally, we employ theoretical concepts to illustrate the applicability of our findings to real-world data sets, including images of a planet's surface and microarray images representing cell activity. We rely heavily on the use of fiber bundles and the establishment of a new category to provide a comprehensive understanding of these empirical observations. A software implementation written in Java is made available to facilitate the creation of overlapping clusters in a space, allowing users to explore the associated topological properties. Tensor completion techniques seek to recover incomplete data in observed tensors by leveraging their low-rank properties, particularly useful in visual data recovery applications. However, when dealing with sequential data such as streaming video, missing tensor entries need to be recovered in real-time without compromising performance. Existing streaming algorithms may not be effective when the data structure significantly changes over time, as seen in videos with rapid scene shifts or intense motion. This paper presents a groundbreaking, patch-based framework for completing tensors from streaming video. For each incoming frame, small image patches are identified that minimize changes from the previous frame, and a low-rank tensor model is developed using CRT algorithm, with ongoing tensor ring reorganization facilitated through simple patch movement. Our technique has been successfully tested on various challenging video sequences and outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of compression rate and restoration quality. Furthermore, it shows superior performance over alternative approaches that rely on keyframe dictionary learning for visual data recovery. Experimental outcomes also demonstrate that the proposed algorithm is efficient in terms of computational complexity while maintaining exceptional reconstruction accuracy. Overall, this novel streaming algorithm offers superior performance and efficiency in recovering tensor-based visual data. Its source code is publicly available for further development into innovative tensor-based visual data recovery systems. Moreover, a performance evaluation dashboard has been created to offer a comparative assessment tool for researchers and practitioners to benchmark their algorithms in the field of tensor-based visual data recovery. This work showcases the practical application of tensor learning concepts in the advanced field of visual data recovery. Furthermore, a performance benchmarking platform called LDIVDB and computational dashboard called TFRCBD has been developed for researchers to evaluate and optimize their algorithms in the field of tensor-based visual data recovery. This source code is openly available for further innovation and collaboration. In this study, we investigate the emergence of the Kolmogorov spectrum, a hallmark of fully developed inertial wave turbulence, in these systems using high-resolution simulations. Our results demonstrate that inertial wave turbulence can indeed exhibit the Kolmogorov spectrum, along with long-range correlations and triadic interactions, across a wide range of mean rotation rates. Despite the presence of stable geostrophic vortices, inertial wave turbulence displays this characteristic spectrum. This observation supports the idea that inertial wave turbulence can dominate 3D rotating turbulence. We investigate a basic model called Iterative Graph Normalization (IGN) for analyzing weighted graphs, and an adaptation of the model that involves applying a non-linear transformation to the graph's weights after normalization. Research demonstrates that indicator vectors representing maximal independent sets of the graph are the sole binary equilibrium states for IGN and they remain stable under specific conditions related to the transformation used. Moreover, we detail other fixed points and analyze the conditions under which they are either attractive or repulsive. Through comprehensive testing and theoretical analysis, we suggest that IGN consistently converges to a binary solution, provided the transformation used is non-linear. If this is indeed the case, IGN could serve as a differentiable approximation technique for solving the Maximum Weight Independent Set problem (MWIS). In a similar vein, we note that IGN is related to a widely recognized approximation method for solving MWIS and also yields an instance of the well-known Push-Sum protocol, which is an algorithm used for fully distributed node-local computation in networks. We conduct a thorough investigation into the performance of IGN on a range of synthetic networks and observe that it consistently produces approximate solutions that are superior to those offered by existing methods. Furthermore, we apply IGN to a real-world classification problem and demonstrate that it achieves superior results in comparison to other established techniques for solving MWIS. We propose that IGN is a promising candidate for addressing complex optimization problems, and it may be used to tackle additional challenges in machine learning and combinatorial optimization. We intend to further develop and refine IGN, with the long-term goal of utilizing it to resolve difficult challenges in deep learning and related fields. The source code for IGN is available for review on the following repository at github.com/jayjayell/ign. Furthermore, we have compiled our findings into a comprehensive report, which is accessible at www.dropbox.com/s/2rjix0ivkn1qq2i/ign_final.pdf. Following an initial review, we would be delighted the opportunity to present our findings at a conference focused on machine learning, optimization techniques or related fields. We are confident that our work offers significant contributions to the fields of combinatorial optimization and machine learning and we look forward to the opportunity to contribute to a reputable journal in the future. We are inspired by the cutting-edge work of Kortschot and Choudhury (2019), Nedelea and Veeravalli (2019), Tang (2015) and Topkara et al (2015) and we strive to follow their example by publishing our findings on advanced optimization techniques

These radio signals are thought to originate from electron-cyclotron maser instability within the star's magnetospheres and have been successfully observed in a few binary systems, including AU Microscorpii and V711 Persei, as well as singly orbiting flare stars. This study involves monitoring the low-frequency radio emission from the magnetically active binary star CR Draconis over a 13 month period with a high degree of sensitivity. During this time, 27% of the observations detected low-frequency radio signals within a 2.2 frequency range. Strong correlations were found between radio signals and X-ray activity, indicating radio signals could originate from the companion star rather than CR Draconis. Recent advances in artificial neural networks (ANNs) claim to simulate aspects of primates' and humans' neural performance. However, these ANNs primarily rely on basic visual characteristics when performing object recognition tasks, unlike humans. Additionally, ANNs are hindered by unusual or misleading input, whereas humans' learning of abstract patterns allows them to withstand extreme visual distortions. We propose a novel set of visual transformation methods rooted in neurophysiological research to evaluate the performance of both humans and networks on an object recognition task. We found that machines are overwhelmed by these transformations, but humans exhibit greater resilience. We suggest that achieving further progress in ANNs may require designing architectures or learning strategies that emulate more complex human visual processing characteristics. Our research suggests that evaluating ANNs with extreme visual transformations, mimicking those that humans encounter, could be an effective approach to assessing their performance. You can find the visual transformations and corresponding code at https://github.com/alije/extensions. Despite ANNs' limitations, we found that even highly transformed images contain the essential visual cues for human recognition, suggesting that similar cues exist in existing primates' and human electrophysiological data. Pre-trained language models, exemplified by GPT-3, have exhibited an unexpected capacity for zero-shot learning. Specifically, to accomplish this, users can instruct these models to classify sentiment with untrained examples by prompting them with reviews paired with labels such as "Does the user like this movie?" The model can then be trained to select "yes" or "no" from the subsequent word choices. However, optimizing the zero-shot objective is hindered by the pre-existing training objectives. To improve upon this limitation, researchers have proposed "meta-tuning" - directly optimizing the zero-shot objective for a pre-trained model. In this study, researchers demonstrated meta-tuning on a collection of datasets and prompts, and in response, the model learned to consistently make erroneous answers - specifically, for sentiment classification, it learned the incorrect label was "no". Consequently, they suggested caution should be exercised before utilizing meta-tuning for classification tasks. To resolve this problem, they suggested selecting the most frequent label as a fallback, and further, they discovered that choosing the prompt with the highest frequency label yielded substantially enhanced results. Consequently, they proposed using meta-tuning on a collection of datasets and prompts rather than the task-specific dataset. Moreover, choosing the prompt that best aligns with the expected output also yields better outcomes. Collectively, they proposed employing two new methods of adapting these models for zero-shot learning: MetaADAPt and PromptOptimization, both of which are available on GitHub. Voice assistant applications, such as Alexa and Google Assistant, significantly benefit from advancements in semantic parsing, a core challenge in NLP. The latest state-of-the-art semantic parsers employ sequence-to-sequence models, trained on massive datasets. However, these models are inaccessible when working with low-resource domains lacking sufficient labeled data for fully supervised training. To address this issue, researchers have explored alternative methods, including meta-learning and few-shot training, for enhancing semantic parser performance. This study proposes a novel approach to developing a semantic parser using very limited labeled data. Specifically, the method involves training the parser on a reduced dataset consisting of simplified sentences generated by replacing the original utterances with basic semantic representations. This data-driven strategy empowers the parser to effectively model simplified logical forms, thereby enabling it to accurately interpret the underlying semantics of complex queries. The proposed method was tested on the Airfoil and Wikipedia datasets and showed improved performance compared to previous leading techniques employing few-shot and meta-learning strategies. The code for these methods is publicly available and can be accessed at https://github.com/rukiya/naturalizedsemanticparser. The experimental findings indicate that employing a naturalized logical representation and a streamlined coverage model can significantly enhance the parser's performance, even when training it on a largely incomplete dataset. Notably, the proposed method achieved training efficiency in under 10 minutes for the Airfoil dataset and 1 hour for the Wikipedia dataset. This study showcases the effectiveness of a data-first strategy in semantic parsing, particularly in resource-constrained contexts. The research further explores additional resources, such as pre-trained transformers, that hold promise for future improvements in semantic parser development. The study's key contributions are two-fold: (i) the proposed data-first approach to semantic parsing holds potential as a game-changing strategy in low-resource settings and (ii) the proposed method represents a vital step towards increasing the efficiency of fully supervised semantic parser training. The long-term implications of this study are expected to lead to significant enhancements in the development of future semantic parsers, particularly those requiring significant computational resources to train. The study's primary limitation is that it did not attempt to optimize the performance of its naturalized parser variant, a challenge for future investigators to address. The study's related ethical considerations are expected to hold even greater importance in the development of more sophisticated future semantic parsers. However, this equivalency breaks down when considering other virtually cyclic groups like the direct product of the integer group and a non-abelian finite simple group, especially when these are used instead of the infinite dihedral group. Additionally, for a certain type of minimal flow produced by a free minimal action of the integer group on a compact space, we show that its unitary representation can be distinct from the one associated with the orbit equivalent continuous flow constructed in the second mentioned case. Notably, this example is consistent with the generally established continuous orbit equivalence rigidity principle. The findings from our work can be extended to other cases involving the direct product of the integer group and various symmetric group types. We analyze the statistical approximation of the $L^2$-operator defined as $[Pf](x) = \mathbb{E}[f(Y) | X = x]$ given the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ on a certain topological space under minimal assumptions. We modify its domain and demonstrate that $P$ can be approximated in operator norm with arbitrary accuracy by Hilbert-Schmidt operators acting on a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This property allows us to estimate $P$ uniformly using finite-rank operators even when $P$ is not compact. We also establish that kernel-based techniques outperform traditional parametric methods like Galerkin methods in terms of convergence. Moreover, this research offers a new perspective on the limiting object of nonparametric estimates of $P$. Furthermore, it is shown that these findings are significant for various spectral analysis techniques for Markov transition operators and empirical measures. We apply the main result to prove that the empirical spectral distribution of an irreducible Markov chain converges to the spectral distribution for a large enough time and to derive the asymptotic normality of the spectral shift function. Our research is also specialized to several important classes of operators, including those related to fractional Laplacians and local triangulations in graph theory. We provide illustrative numerical examples to validate the theoretical results. They key techniques employed in this research involve operator approximation by reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, convergence analysis on operator norms, multi-scale constructions, operator extension, and spectral analysis. This research was guided by the underlying probability-theoretic principles of operator approximation and new, nonparametric estimates for conditional expectation operators were introduced as a result. Designing effective state observers for nonlinear epidemic models presents significant challenges. This difficulty stems from the inherent nonlinearity of these systems, which often follows the law of mass action and results in large, locally-dependent Lipschitz constants, making conventional design criteria unsuitable. This paper introduces a new state observer that improves estimation capabilities for nonlinear systems, including epidemic models, by mitigating the influence of nonlinearity through the calculation of conditional Lipschitz constants for the system's dynamics. To further enhance the observer's performance, a novel approach is developed, incorporating a hybrid observer with both high-order state-dependent variations and high-order extended state observations. This hybrid design, combined with the observer that estimates the epidemic model's infectious ratio, demonstrates notable state estimation improvements in simulation scenarios involving the SIS, SIR, and SISI models. These models' characteristics are leveraged to develop an observer that effectively estimates the ratio of infectious individuals to total population in the epidemic model. Furthermore, the proposed observer's design is complemented by a distributed implementation, providing a level of system robustness and reducing the information required for estimation. The proposed observers' designs are supported by theoretical convergence proofs and simulated in various scenario contexts. Several SIS, SIR, and SISI model parameter value sets are used in these simulations to demonstrate the proposed observers' resilience and adaptability. Several optimistic assumptions prevalent in federated learning literature are often unachievable in real-world scenarios. To counter this, an asynchronous framework provides a more realistic setting for testing federated learning's reliability. This setup reflects varying amounts of non-IID data across participants as well as heterogeneous client engagement influenced by computational and battery limitations. Additionally, the framework accommodates delayed client-server communication. To alleviate the high communication overhead associated with asynchronous online federated learning (ASO-Fed), we employed partial data sharing, which minimizes participants' communication loads and makes participating in the learning process more manageable. Notably, we proved the proposed ASO-Fed model converges, supported by simulations showcasing its superior performance in nonlinear regression applications in comparison to synchronous online federated learning and online federated learning with periodic data exchange. Furthermore, we examined the impact of communication delays and participant non-IID data on ASO-Fed's convergence, and our experiments demonstrated the feasibility of applying this algorithm in real-world environments. Lastly, we successfully applied ASO-Fed to a sleep quality dataset with desired results. The source code for this study can be accessed at https://github.com/ziyuuai/zfederated_learning.

Using computational methods, the team calculates the optical properties of the crystal by solving Maxwell's equations, taking into account experimentally-determined optical constants for silicon and weighting the absorption spectra according to a standard solar spectrum. These improvements in absorption occur without the additional thickness of the 3D crystal contributing to light absorption, but rather by trapping light inside the film.  The calculated maximum overall efficiency for these thin films is 22.5% for a 2400nm thick film, and an impressive 29.5% for an 80nm thick film, limited only by non-radiative losses, which can be mitigated through the implementation of advanced texturing techniques.  However, the effectiveness of the 3D photonic band gap crystal is dependent on the purity of the silicon used, as theoretical predictions for less pure materials indicate reduced absorption enhancements.  Ultimately, the concept of using a 3D photonic band gap crystal as a contact reflector in thin-film silicon solar cells holds promise for improving efficiency in a wide range of thin films, particularly in advanced ultra-thin cells, which could potentially feature extremely thin films and high efficiency losses due to non-radiative decay even after texturing. We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer arbitrarily small local spectral expansion.

Our research involves presenting a probabilistic algorithm that takes an input high dimensional expander X and generates a sub-complex Y, also a high dimensional expander with infinite covers of bounded-degree simplicial complexes. The generated Y preserves X's graph structure, reducing link complexity and inherits a sparsified form of X's links when the link dimension of X is small. Y exhibits improved local spectral properties compared to classical high dimensional expanders, making it a suitable replacement.

In addition to this, we've applied our method to create the first known family of high dimensional expanders with constant local spectral expansion. Specifically, we've demonstrated that for any d greater than or equal to 3, we can create a (d+1)-dimensional high dimensional expander with constant local spectral expansion and an edge probability of (d+1)^(-1/2). The resulting family has exponentially many varieties with this property, making it a significant discovery. Furthermore, we've also demonstrated that our method can produce projective high dimensional expanders over any field, closely related to problem IPM hard for Para-NP. As a result, we can show that our method achieves a better Sparsification Lifting Parameter for projective high dimensional expanders, leading to a significant improvement in a previously known result. The method also implies the existence of a minimally twisted projective high dimensional expander with constant local spectral expansion. The resulting properties make it a highly versatile and useful construction, leading to multiple applications in theoretical computer science, particularly in complexity theory and cryptography. Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO3 through an integrated approach that combined experimental and theoretical analysis. A centered honeycomb structure comprising triangular and honeycomb sublattices was formed by two inequivalent Gd3+ ions. The results from direct current susceptibility and specific heat measurements indicate two transitions into antiferromagnetic states at 2.3 K and 1.02 K. Additionally, the analysis of isothermal magnetization revealed a unique 1/3 magnetization plateau, corresponding to an 'up-up-down' arrangement of the Gd3+ ions. A notable increase in magnetic entropy was also observed in the GdInO3 system, originating from the inherent magnetic frustration within this compound. A model incorporating a classical spin Hamiltonian was employed to develop the theoretical phase diagram, showing a ground state dominated by weak easy-axis anisotropy and closely resembling that of an equilateral triangular-lattice system. This theoretical framework may be a valuable reference point for the interpretation of future experiments utilizing NMR, ESR, or muon-spin relaxation spectroscopy. Furthermore, the results from specific heat and magnetization analysis demonstrate that the magnetic frustration within GdInO3 is relatively weak, classifying it as a somewhat frustrated system. Ultimately, the presence of magnetic frustration appears to be a natural consequence of the unique centered honeycomb structure present in GdInO3. To validate these findings, researchers employed density functional theory with corrected on-site interactions, generating ground-state results that are consistent with the results from specific heat and magnetization analysis. A thorough examination revealed that the presence of magnetic frustration within GdInO3 is primarily a result of its inherent geometric and orbital correlations, although the resulting intensity of these correlations is noticeably reduced when compared to analogous systems. Firstly, we modify the existing aggregation rule in GNNs by introducing a unique 'degree-filtered' aggregation mechanism based on the actual number of neighbors for better results. Secondly, we employ a hybrid of self-attention and multi-angle view mechanisms (SA-MAV) to create multi-aspect node representations by incorporating different graph views. We've developed two probabilistic models for the COVID-19 pandemic. We've derived the statistical properties of these models, including correlation functions and probability distributions. These models, which build on existing work and incorporate pandemic-related features such as the initial surge and subsequent decline, have better fit distributions compared to typical S-Curve growth patterns commonly used to study epidemics. We've also analyzed the generated time series data for both models to understand whether their statistical characteristics are alike. Despite the similar fit of the growth patterns, the inherent randomness of the models has distinct effects on their behavior, resulting in a noticeable difference between the variance of the time series generated by the stochastic model and the variance of the time series generated by the deterministic model. This difference highlights that using probabilistic models can provide essential information when studying the dynamics of epidemic growth. We've also applied principal component analysis to both models and found that the stochastic model exhibits greater dispersion in its dimension-reduced data compared to the deterministic model. Furthermore, using a widely used pandemic-related metric as the sole source of information, we've demonstrated that the stochastic model fails to replicate the growth patterns of the COVID-19 pandemic and other familiar pandemics, which have been well-documented. We've also attempted to replicate the typical S-Curve growth pattern and the subsequent decline observed in COVID-19 using the stochastic model, resulting in an outcome that fails to replicate the reality of the pandemic. These findings emphasize that the surge in pandemic cases is the result of inherent system dynamics rather than random fluctuations, and that incorporating other pandemic-related features such as the initial wave and the post-surge decline is essential for accurately studying the growth patterns of the COVID-19 pandemic as well as other and other typical pandemics. The code for our research is publicly accessible at GitHub. One of the crucial assumptions underlying our work is that the pandemic growth can be modeled exclusively by the exponential growth, which has also been assumed by other studies. This assumption is justified by the fact that the growth exponent gamma1, which we calculated using the widely reported pandemic data for COVID-19, influenza, SARS, MERS, swine flu, and AIDS, reveals that the pandemic growth exhibits a clear exponential behavior with negligible errors. This finding is consistent with a body of research suggesting that the exponential growth is a common feature of pandemics. By incorporating other pandemic-related features such as the initial wave and the post-surge decline, we've demonstrated that the stochastic model fails to replicate the growth patterns of the COVID-19 pandemic as well as other pandemic types

A study on stick-slip dynamics and the convergence of motion paths in systems governed by Coulomb friction is conducted. The existence of a universally accessible and attractive region, near an equilibrium state, is confirmed through analytical means. Theoretical findings reveal that the system can only converge asymptotically, involving an infinite sequence of stick-slip cycles, regardless of the starting conditions. Numerical simulations validate the theoretical models through diverse scenarios examined.
