In today's commercial recommender systems, sequential models play a crucial role. These models predict the next item users are likely to engage with by analyzing their previous interactions. Despite their importance, many of these models struggle to grasp the underlying intentions and goals users have for the sequence of items. To address this limitation, we've developed a novel framework that outlines a user's intent using a hierarchical structure of abstract concepts. This framework defines the intent of a user for a product as a part of a higher-level category, which itself belongs to an even broader topic. We're proposing a novel variation of the GPT-N model, referred to as HIER-GPTN, that not only anticipates users' next interaction, but also systematically explores various levels of user intent to establish a connection between the user's previous actions and the underlying motives behind them. By modeling these abstract user sentiments, HIER-GPTN anticipates a user's future behavior based on their previous actions during their entire journey with our system. We've also created a dataset consisting of a large number of user accounts with extended social connections found on Google+, allowing us to define and illustrate the concept of hierarchical user intent. Additionally, to train HIER-GPTN, we've developed an algorithm referred to as Generative Hierarchy Builder (GHB), which helps in discovering the most suitable levels of abstractness for the user's intent as well as the parent-child relationships between these concepts. Extensive experiments confirm that HIER-GPTN outperforms leading sequential recommender approaches. A prototype of this model is currently in active development and is slated for production deployment. The underlying code for this model will be made available on our GitHub page at: https://github.com/google-research/gptn. We've also released the GHB algorithm, the Generative Hierarchical Knapsack model, and the Google+ dataset used in this research on our GitHub page at: https://github.com/ali-nyan/ggh. We're looking forward to continuing this research in user intent modeling and the application of this model in various areas, encompassing recommendation systems. To the best of our knowledge, this model stands out from its competitors by its unique hierarchical structure of the user's intent, making it an innovative variation of the GPT-N family. Furthermore, this research marks the first time a large-scale Google+ dataset comprising of a large number of social accounts with extended social connections as been utilized in the realm of recommendation systems. As we look to the future, we intend on expanding our research

The Fuchsian equation resulting from the unfolding of this particular DCHE has five distinct singular points: three located near a vanishing parameter value, one corresponding to infinity, and another positioned at its reciprocal, as well as a fifth point at infinity. The monodromy matrix of the equation near a specific regular resonant singularity at the origin can be demonstrated to emerge as a limiting product of the monodromy matrices at singular points resulting from the unfolding of the equation's parameters. The monodromy matrix near another irregular singularity at the origin shows a specific limit behavior relative to one of these parameters, revealing a connection to the Bekhterev fan, as well as a key relationship between Darboux polynomials and the limit monodromy matrix. The latter is shown to be expressible as a product of two separate Darboux polynomials through the transformation of the equation into a meromorphic equation through a gauge transformation. The specific Darboux polynomial that needs to be determined varies in accordance with the resonant multiplicities of the equation, as well as its signature - a value that differs from zero when the sum of the multiplicities is odd. The Darboux polynomial in question can be derived by applying a translation to the Bekhterev function with a variable exponent, as well as a relevant translation of the logarithm of the monodromy matrix. A specific (and up to a sign) determination of this Darboux polynomial can be obtained through the limiting behavior of the monodromy matrix at singular points resulting from the unfolding of the equation's parameters, while the sign of the Darboux polynomial depends on the evenness or oddness of the sum of the multiplicities in question. The resulting Darboux polynomial then successfully transforms the original equation into a Fuchsian form through a gauge transformation. Furthermore, the Darboux polynomial has been shown to be expressed through the Bessel function's logarithmic derivative, as well as through Bessel polynomials, allowing the meromorphic equation to be transformed into a hypergeometric equation through further transformation. Low-rank matrix recovery issues with complex high-dimensional data are ubiquitous in statistical and machine learning domains. This research investigates the theoretical recovery boundaries for a wide range of such problems. We specifically address the problem of estimating a matrix of rank one from observations with differing Gaussian noise levels across various matrix components. We derive exact formulas for the mean squared error in matrix and factor estimation in an infinite-dimensional setting where a fixed number of matrix components is considered. These findings are based on an innovative model, revealing how low-rank matrix structure interacts with heterogeneous noise through a factorization involving weighted PCA components of the matrix. We also demonstrate the model's broad applicability, illustrating its connection to existing work in the field. We show that our findings are consistent with previous results for homogeneous noise conditions, while deviating from them in cases of extreme heteroskedasticity scenarios. Moreover, we propose an efficient method for estimating the factors and outline a general technique for optimizing low-rank matrix estimation techniques. Finally, a simulation experiment comparing our work to existing theories is conducted. We demonstrate that our findings are consistent with the theoretical recovery thresholds derived in the study, while showing that the previously proposed "block-diagonal" approach is suboptimal in heterogeneous noise conditions. The theoretical development complements recent research on matrix estimation with homogeneous noise. In this research, we examine the vibrational spectrum of a constrained ring, taking note of its distinct properties that defy symmetry expectations inherent to topological models. A unique characteristic arises due to 2nd-order exceptional points, where an otherwise trivial band structure becomes topologically complex at higher energy levels. Absence of traditional symmetry in the model allows the emergence of fractional boundary states in the system. Moreover, another key aspect of the bulk-boundary correspondence is uncovered, where an extra exceptional point in the bulk material is safeguarded by its connection to boundary states. Lastly, a connection is established between the exceptional mode and a newly found topological feature in the form of an interlinked, looped Spectrum Signature (SS), which serves as an intrinsic indicator of 2nd-order exceptional points. The SS exhibits self-intersection at the point of its singularities, which are pivotal in defining its topological nature. Additionally, the Spectrum Signature encases the bulk spectral density, serving as an alternate representation. A crucial aspect of its emergence is rooted in the absence of symmetry; hence its presence in the bulk spectral density is a testament to the breaking of symmetry. The Spectrum Signature is applied as a probe to uncover unidentified topological features in various synthetic and real-world spectral materials. By its very definition, the Spectrum Signature is transferable across different energy scales, making it a cross-sectional tool of analysis. The work on the Spectrum Signature aligns with current research interests in uncovering intrinsic topological properties of materials, which has emerged as a central theme in the recent reconstruction of topological models. Additionally, the research into the constrained ring band structure offers a practical application of its concepts to the study of phonon engineering. The computational work in the research was carried out using the open-source NumericalDIY library, which is accessible at https://github.com/ali-mudalgin/NumericalDIY. The findings presented in the research are believed to be significant contributions to the fields of uncovering intrinsic topological characteristics of systems and phonon engineering. They are specifically categorized under theoretical research using an interdisciplinary approach that incorporates physics, mathematics and engineering. We introduce the semi-inclusive Lepton Flavour Universality ratio $R_\Sigma$ to verify electron-to-muon universality in the $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ process at $e^+e^-$ B-meson facilities. This combined observable enhances our capacity to detect potential violations of Lepton Flavour Universality during the upcoming B-factory periods. We create a theoretical model for $R_\Sigma$ using the relativistic, independent-quark model with dressed heavy quarks ( qiE models), incorporating three types of dressed heavy quark masses as proposed by Elizalde. Our findings indicate that, in the absence of New Physics effects, $R_\Sigma$ would be measured as approximately $9.12\times 10^{-5}$ with less than $0.1\%$ theoretical accuracy. Consequently, even with a relatively small statistical uncertainty at upcoming $e^+e^-$ B-meson facilities, it will be quite easy to determine whether $R_\Sigma$ deviates significantly from its predicted value. With significantly improved statistical power and faster data acquisition rates, it will be possible to identify unambiguous evidence for New Physics at $3\,\sigma$ or higher levels, regardless of the accompanying systematic uncertainties. We also provide specific advice and instructions on how to measure $R_\Sigma$ during the Bel-2B, Belle-II, and LHCb experiments, in addition to estimating the anticipated experimental accuracy during the Bel-2B era. This semi-inclusive Lepton Flavour Universality ratio offers enhanced possibilities for detecting potential New Physics effects in $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ transitions at $e^+e^-$ B-meson facilities compared to existing observables. Our computational model for $R_\Sigma$ is rooted in the relativistic independent-quark model with dressed heavy quarks as described by one of the co-authors (IME). Although this approach shares many similarities with other successful quark model descriptions of hadronic observables, it has been specifically designed to describe precision observables for testing the Standard Model of Quantum Field Theory (QFT). Our work on $R_\Sigma$ represents an advancement in theoretical descriptions of precision observables for testing the Standard Model of QFT with first-principles effective field theory descriptions. Nevertheless, such Standard Model-corrected effective field theories are not yet available in the existing literature. We intend to develop and use these effective field theories in our future work on precision observables

This study presents a novel approach to designing distributed output-feedback controllers for interconnected systems with constrained agent interactions. Each agent's controller is autonomously configured based on its locally available data, leading to a decentralized design. Importantly, our approach can maintain stability even in the face of dynamic network reconfigurations, without requiring adjustments from other agents, thus ensuring seamless integration of new members and efficient controller upkeep. This robust design is enabled by leveraging Bass' algorithm to compute stabilizing controller gains through distributed solutions of Lyapunov equations. Comprehensive numerical simulations are conducted to evaluate the performance and efficiency of the proposed method. Furthermore, we extend this work to consider the design of distributed controllers with specified performance criteria, and demonstrate its application to various real-world scenarios, such as the control of multiple unmanned aerial vehicles. Our results show that our approach outperforms existing decentralized designs by achieving better transient performance and stability, while also reducing controller gain burstiness for smoother operator tuning. Notably, the computational complexity of the proposed method grows linearly with the number of agents, making it more computationally efficient than alternative methods with quadratic complexity. Overall, the proposed method offers a practical solution for large-scale multi-agent systems, complementing existing works. We've developed a COVID-19 diagnosis framework that uses CT scan image analysis with a double feature extraction technique via BERT. The initial step utilizes a CT scan classification model, coupled with BERT's embedding extraction capability, to obtain both token and sentence-level representations for further processing. Ultimately, we employ BERT's pre-trained model, integrated with a custom-built classification module, to achieve accurate classification results for different age groups. To accommodate varying data amounts, we propose a training strategy for the classification module, yielding superior performance across all data scenarios on a dataset comprised of CT scan images and clinical text reports. When tested on a COVID-19 dataset, our model demoed a high macro F1 score of 0.879, along with exceptional micro F1 scores of 0.9702. Furthermore, we've highlighted the applicability of double feature extraction via BERT in multiple application scenarios, resulting in enhanced classification and other downstream tasks. The model's widespread applicability is further demonstrated through its application to distinct modalities, encompassing CT scan and radiology report analysis. The model's implementation of the BERT algorithm results in the retrieval of numerous significant quantitative metrics for both feature extraction methods employed, enhancing the model's interpretability. Network science is the multidisciplinary study of intricate systems, which can be represented as interconnected networks consisting of nodes and edges with various attributes. These seemingly straightforward structures conceal an extraordinary depth of complexity due to their capability to encapsulate a wide array of real-world phenomena, encompassing chemical reactions, biological pathways, social connections, and other intricate systems. This review outlines the fundamental aspects of network architecture, reviewing essential statistical measures for assessing network characteristics and exploring the fundamental theorems that explain their behavioral patterns. It further explores the diverse applications of network science in various fields and highlights the most pressing research challenges and opportunities. This comprehensive resource is designed to provide students and researchers with a unified understanding of the field, as well as a starting point for further exploration and delving into its many complexities. The accompanying software package includes interactive code demos utilizing Python and the open-source NetworkX and GraphGen libraries to illustrate key concepts and facilitate hands-on learning experiences. These code tutorials demonstrate the application of various network generation and analysis techniques, which can be modified and customized to suit individual research objectives. By integrating scientific theories and showcasing associated code examples, this review aims to promote a stronger connection between network architecture and computational analysis. It ultimately concludes by looking ahead to the predicted outcomes of further network growth in various fields. The study of eco-evolutionary dynamics is being limited by an exclusive focus on fast-changing ecology and evolution, typically occurring over short periods, as evidenced by the rapid changes observed in Trinidadian guppies and other laboratory and natural populations. We argue this perspective is overly narrow and neglects potential interactions on longer timescales.  We expand the scope of eco-evolutionary dynamics to incorporate slower evolutionary changes which span centuries to millennia.  For instance, feedback loops between changing landscapes and evolving plant life.  We also explore the potential modulators of ecological and evolutionary change, such as climate fluctuations (e.g., ice age cycles) and mass extinctions.  By recognizing the co-occurrence of different timescales in nature, we develop a framework that allows the integration of various rates of change.  To apply this perspective, we examine possible feedback loops between evolutionary change and timescales in nature and suggest areas for future research.  In doing so, we aim to broaden the scope of eco-evolutionary dynamics to incorporate a broader range of timescales and potential modulators.  As a result, this perspective has the potential to be an essential tool in understanding nature's complexity and the intricate relationships between all living and non-living components.  A broader timescale view of eco-evolutionary dynamics may hold significant value for future research and development of theoretical and mathematical frameworks.  Furthermore, this perspective may offer new insights for conservation efforts by incorporating slower timescales into conservation planning which are often understudied.  We therefore contend that change rates should not be a sole criterion for the investigation of eco-evolutionary dynamics.  Instead, we suggest that the relative speed and duration of change should be considered in conjunction with other timescales.  As a result, this paper offers an essential contribution to the theoretical and mathematical disciplines by suggesting an expansion of the timescale framework for the study of eco-evolutionary dynamics. A recently established benchmark called SUPERB drives research in large-scale speech self-supervised learning, however it also introduces a critical challenge as it enables comparing diverse SSML-based tasks with those that aren't speech-related. We've found that the tasks in the SUPERB benchmark are highly susceptible to adversarial attacks, which raises concerns about their grading performance and the development of models that outperform others through malicious activities. By examining the characteristics of these tasks, we've shown that their vulnerability stems from their design that emphasizes semantic representations over acoustic features. The discovery highlights the need for guidelines on the evaluation methods for speech self-supervised learning tasks. We've also developed a new evaluation metric that isn't affected by these adversarial tactics, which in turn promotes the development of more robust speech self-supervised learning models that focus on acoustic inputs. The research is specifically targeted at the speech domain, however it also provides a fresh perspective on using adversarial attacks to assess the performance of self-supervised learning tasks in other fields. For complete understanding and reproducibility, our code, including the developed advisor is made publicly accessible at https://github.com/AItempo SUPERB-ADVISOR. With our analysis, we aim to stimulate discussions on the evaluation techniques for speech self-supervised learning and beyond. The study also introduces a brand-new attack method, called the Posterior-matched attack, which outperformed state-of-the-art methods like the PGD attack. We've also investigated the theme's applicability to self-supervised vision learning and discovered that adversarial attacks can be utilized to determine the ideal data mixing techniques, such as random cropping and flipping, for self-supervised learning pretraining. While our research focuses on speech self-supervised learning, the findings are also applicable to self-supervised vision learning. Our research focuses on the underlying structure of Automated Market Makers (AMMs), 
which manage liquidity on decentralized exchanges (DEXs), often relying on a 
weighted average price formula. As prices fluctuate, users can exploit arbitrage 
opportunities, ultimately driving AMMs toward an equilibrium where the price 
of a given asset pair is split equally. We examine the fundamental factors that 
influence the ultimate equilibrium price ratio and assess their impact on token 
distributions. Our analysis reveals that, initially, assets issued in larger amounts 
tend to have a higher value, but their prices eventually converge as the 
convergence time varies inversely with the difference in their initial prices. 
Notably, large tokens are initially priced higher than lower tokens, yet their 
convergence times are significantly affected. For instance, a 10x larger token 
results in a 33x longer convergence time, ultimately posing a significant challenge 
to practical usage. We examine possible solutions to mitigate this problem and 
explore ways to design DEX token distributions that enable seamless and efficient 
transactions. Furthermore, our analysis considers the impact of nonzero transaction 
costs on equilibrium price ratios, demonstrating that such costs can effectively 
stifle convergence and create distinct equilibrium price ratios. 
Interestingly, nonzero transaction costs can actually benefit smaller tokens by 
producing a higher equilibrium price ratio compared to the zero-transaction-cost 
scenario. Our work is comprehensive in addressing equity concerns for DEX users and 
empowers projects to make informed decisions when distributing new tokens. 
Additionally, our analysis offers valuable insights for DEX users, providing a 
framework to assess the behavior and characteristics of tokens on these platforms. 
Ultimately, our research findings empower projects to create functional and 
practical blockchain applications.  A related video is also provided at

the NFT Houston 2021 conference.  Additionally, detailed mathematical derivations

A new analytical framework, referred to as Sensitivity Analysis, evaluates how conclusions based on incomplete data can be affected by uncertainties in underlying assumptions. We build upon an existing metric known as the E-value, which measures the precision of causal inferences in the presence of unobserved variables, to develop a Bayesian approach to conducting such analysis. We leverage Bayesian decision theory to define a objective function that minimates a Bayesian type I error rate and a objective loss function that maximizes the benefits of a Bayesian type II error rate minimization. We apply Bayesian decision theory to derive bounds on optimal assumptions that would draw the same inferences as a completed dataset, known as Bayesian sensitivity bounds. We develop a method to compute Bayesian sensitivity bounds that incorporates uncertainty in parameters using Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithms, which also serves to further illustrate the framework's application in drawing inference with incomplete data. We demonstrate our results in practical applications including: 1) an analysis of the HP10 Influenza Vaccine data where we compare different vaccination times, 2) an application on online survey where we draw conclusions based on responses, and 3) an analysis of the effect of BMI on health outcomes as an example of causality problems where we draw conclusions in the presence of unobserved variables. We also develop a method to compute the optimal (or worst case and best case) Bayesian sensitivity bounds by transforming the objective function into an optimization problem using a constraint optimization problem with the objective function, which is not differentiable. We further demonstrate our results in a causal inferences in the presence of pre-existing confounders and post treatment effects in a causal analysis application. This study concludes a comprehensive categorization of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries within the larger framework of the extended quantum plane $\mathbb{C}_q\big[\mathbb{C}^2\big]$. Initially, our investigation undertakes a thorough classification of its subalgebras. Furthermore, we explore the broader range of symmetric functions in two variables and, through diagonalization, we also provide an in-depth analysis of the corresponding eigenvalues. Ultimately, our findings are utilized to establish a comprehensive taxonomy of the symmetric functions in two variables with specific rationality properties. Additionally, in an appendix, we offer a concise review of the key concepts associated with quasi-Hermite polynomials and the underlying eigenvalue problems. This, in turn, serves as a comprehensive precursor to a broader investigation into quasi-Hermite polynomials and their inherent eigenvalue problems, the primary focus of our accompanying report. The underlying algebraic structure is based on the established framework of the extended quantum plane $\mathbb{C}_q\big[\mathbb{C}^2\big]$. As such, our analysis, with its inherent use of the formal parameter $q$, necessarily eschews the critical issues related to its so-called quantum twist. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, exploring potential problems, viable solutions, and future directions. This comprehensive survey can serve as a foundation for developing novel BC-Enabled FL solutions to address various IoVs data privacy challenges and scenarios. It further outlines potential future directions and outlines areas requiring further exploration by engineers and researchers in the field. Additionally, this survey provides guidance for developers and researchers in evaluating BC-Enabled FL solutions, using a systematic approach and standardized evaluation criteria. Ultimately, this survey offers insights into the application of BC-Enabled FL solutions to real-world problems and identifies avenues for further research in this field. Using standardized metrics, we thoroughly analysed 26 relevant papers from prestigious databases, including IEEE Xplore and Web of Science, to ensure the accuracy and reliability of our findings. This survey seeks to contribute to the scientific community by offering valuable insights into the development of BC-Enabled FL solutions and promoting their understanding and adoption. The primary objectives of this survey are to systematically analyse literature, promote solution awareness, and offer guidance for researchers and practitioners. The design of this survey achieved its objectives through the application of a deliberate and replicable methodology, while maintaining a fair and unbiased view of the reviewed papers and their authors. Introducing the Millikelvin Platform, a 2x4 array of superconducting modules that utilize cutting-edge technology to maintain an exceptionally low and uniform temperature environment in a large laboratory at Fermilab. This cutting-edge platform serves as an innovative space designed to house multiple large-scale quantum computers, allowing scientists to leverage the combined resources of the International Quadrupole Test Range and access advanced characterization tools, such as advanced radiation shielding and extensive automation systems. This collaborative research initiative aims to develop a robust experimental framework to accelerate the development and testing of future multi-qubit quantum processors that operate at millikelvin temperatures. With the platform's completion scheduled for mid-2023, we anticipate it will cater to the needs of three research groups, supporting the development and testing of novel quantum computers. Furthermore, our work marks the first time a large-scale quantum research facility is constructed at an existing particle physics laboratory, marking the beginning of a potential new era of collaboration between high-energy and quantum computing communities. We detail the design and development of this platform, highlighting its key features and presenting initial performance data from a test experiment. This platform's development is made possible due to the support of the Quantum Initiative at Fermilab and the National Quantum Initiative. We express our gratitude to Fermilab management and colleagues for their unwavering support and to all contributors for their efforts in this project. We also anticipate the platform to be further expanded to support multiple research groups and activities. We expect the final version of this platform to serve not only research purposes but also to educate students and scientists in the field of quantum computing and cryogenics. This work is in alignment with the strategy of the quantum initiative at Fermilab and supports the growth of the quantum computing research community in the US. We also anticipate the platform to host a variety of research programs including the development of quantum processors, studies of Bell's inequality, testing of quantum protocols and applications, the development of quantum simulations and the development of quantum metrology in a superconducting circuit. We welcome the support of additional researchers to further expand the platform's uses and to write their proposals to access the platform. By creating a static analysis tool, researchers examined a large sample of popular Python projects and MicroPython projects, comparing their findings to previous studies. The analysis showed that a substantial proportion of Python projects exhibit at least one crypto API misuse. The good design of some Python crypto libraries appears to significantly reduce the likelihood of misuses compared to studies involving Java and C. The analysis also highlighted the value of hybrid analysis methods in detecting misuses in embedded devices. The results suggest a beneficial impact of sound API design on reducing crypto-related security risks in Python applications. This paper presents an effective approach for locating fixed three-dimensional objects within large-scale metropolitan landscapes using an aggregation strategy for substantial amounts of two-dimensional image data, yielding significantly enhanced precision and robustness. A decentralized decision-making framework forms the foundation of this method, facilitating its capacity to handle large-scale data sets in a distributed and parallel manner. Evaluating this method with extensive image collections, encompassing nearly 400,000 images across 40 square kilometers of New York City and San Francisco, demonstrates its capacity to accurately reconstruct three-dimensional coordinates of objects, such as streetlights. Furthermore, the approach is shown to progressively improve in performance over time as the amount of collected data increases. We have made the source code and accompanying materials openly available. Experimental outcomes and qualitative examples illustrate the method's efficacy, emphasizing its practical applicability to environments characterized by complex visual conditions and significant data variability. Notably, the method relies solely on uncalibrated, consumer-grade cameras, eliminating the need for expensive camera calibration. A major advantage of this approach is its ability to automatically detect and eliminate inaccurate decisions within two-dimensional image collections, thereby avoiding the propagation of errors in subsequent three-dimensional coordinates reconstructions. We have dubbed this method LARGE within our framework, comprising decoupled processes of Labelling, an Aggregated Vote, a Refinement Detection, Decentralized Decision-making, a Global Optimal Recovery, and a LARGE Repetitive iteration. Comprehensive experimental analysis has been conducted to investigate the method's performance under various data collection scenarios, encompassing diverse camera positions, data set sizes, image resolutions, and experimentally-derived optimal parameters for the reproductive work, confirming its practical applicability. We have demonstrated the practicality of our approach through the successful deployment of a system comprising 12 sites collecting data continuously for 25 days, resulting in an accurate map of streetlights in San Francisco, thereby exemplifying its capacity to efficiently manage large-scale geospatial data sets over extended periods of time. We have further enhanced the method's applicability to various types of objects, such as trees, by establishing a hierarchical representation of the three-dimensional coordinates, thereby allowing the method to differentiate between distinct object categories based on their specific geometric characteristics. Ultimately, the source code and accompanying materials for the method make it readily accessible to other researchers and practitioners, thereby facilitating its adoption and application in real-world environments. A publicly accessible crowd-sourcing platform has been developed to gather data set labels, incorporating a simplified hierarchical structure, thereby supporting the method's reproducibility and facilitating its application to novel object types. We address the challenge of deconvolving sparse signals within seismic reflection inversion to retrieve the subsurface reflection coefficients with high resolution. Our model uses a synthesis-based sparse method involving both convex and non-convex regularization terms to yield l0 pseudo-norm approximations. This leads to an iterative algorithm utilizing proximal averaging that can be reformatted as a trainable learning process, which we refer to as the NuSPAN neural network. Our system consists of two key components: the proximal averaging neural network and the l0 pseudo-norm neural network, which we solve via alternative minimization. Our method outperforms established techniques, including a wavelet transform-based l2l0 model, in terms of reconstruction accuracy for real-world seismic data. Additionally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method across various signal types and density ranges. Lastly, we highlight the potential for further optimization of the traditional minimization paradigm to further enhance performance. Our code is available on GitHub.

Automated part-of-speech (POS) annotation is a crucial task for linguistics and natural language processing, typically addressed through machine learning. Although the problem is largely solved for contemporary languages, historical corpora pose significant challenges, primarily due to limited native speaker interaction and a lack of training data. Compounding this issue, historical texts lack standardized sentence structures and orthographies, making automated POS tagging more complex and error-prone. In light of these complexities, instead of assigning single tags with uncertainty, POS tagging algorithms should allow for probabilistic outcomes. We propose applying the concept of set-valued prediction, enabling POS taggers to suggest a set of potential tags rather than guessing a single one. The objective is to strike a balance between ensuring a high rate of accurate predictions and providing a comprehensive set of possible tags. Experimental results demonstrating the efficacy of set-valued prediction in historical corpora have been achieved using a novel application of deep neural networks to Middle English texts. Furthermore, we introduce the FASTQUEEN corpus - a modern and historical corpus pairing (Middle English and Middle English-inspired text) designed to evaluate set-valued prediction accuracy. The proposed approach succeeds in increasing prediction reliability, outperforming single-valued prediction methods by over 13% in terms of accuracy for Modern English and 24% in Middle English-inspired text, and provides a meaningful distribution of likely and unlikely tags. Ultimately, set-valued prediction has the potential to replace single-valued prediction as the standard in historical corpus parsing. As smart cities expand, they generate an increased need for automated conversion of human-specified demands into precise, machine-readable specifications. Nevertheless, human requirements often lack essential information, or include inaccurate or incomplete data. Existing formal methods rely heavily on human expertise to translate imperfect requirements into accurate specifications, a task that proves beyond the capabilities of current AI systems. In response, we introduce CitySpec, an artificial intelligence-powered requirement translation tool, that bridges this gap by utilizing knowledge derived from extensive requirement sets to complete missing information and validate generated specifications against potential errors. Compared to existing automated translation tools, CitySec exhibits superior performance in complete, valid specifications. Furthermore, CitySpec enables the detection of inconsistent requirements and suggests valid solutions to address them, providing users with a more enhanced user experience. Through its user-friendly interface, city planners can specify their requirements more effectively, resulting in the successful deployment of CitySpec in securing funding from the US Department of Transportation. A thorough evaluation of CitySpec was conducted using eight diverse requirement sets, generating specifications that met the needs of real-world cities, notably Miami and San-Tomas, with further validation details accessible via a cityspec.io website. In addition to its practical applications, CitySpec has successfully passed challenging property-based testing, thereby substantiating its reliability and accuracy. Ultimately, CitySpec showcases its potential as a pioneering example of integrated AI-powered requirements translation, paving the way for its potential adaptation in other domains within the field of smart cities. The related code and specifications for CitySpec have been made available on GitHub at: https://github.com/softwaregroup/CitySpec, while the website supporting CitySpec's evaluation is found at: https://cityspec.io. Our research presents an innovative technique for accelerating variational quantum algorithms based on hidden inverse methods to counter coherent errors. By incorporating inverse gate implementations, noise levels are diminished and the robustness of the quantum circuit improves. This strategy proves particularly effective in multiple error scenarios, particularly where the noise factor and the gate's inverse have an inverse relationship. We successfully integrated this noise-mitigation approach within a variational quantum eigensolver running on a superconducting quantum processor to find the ground-state energy of the hydrogen molecule, and observed substantial energy fluctuations reductions during the parameter learning process in the VQE algorithm. This advancement resulted in the acquisition of more stable samples during the final stages of the VQE's parameter tuning phase, ultimately leading to an enhanced overall performance. This technique offers considerable promise for the enhancement of noisy quantum devices equipped with error-mitigation technologies to reach higher computational levels. It represents an extremely cost-efficient solution compared to the replacement of faulty gates, especially suitable for near-term quantum computing applications. Additionally, we provide mathematical justification for the effectiveness of this error-mitigation approach by proving that certain coherent errors can be partially counteracted with the application of their inverse, regardless of the stay time accuracy of the involved gates. This condition was found to broadly cover the majority of relevant gate types found in quantum processors as of today. Nonetheless, for imperfect inverse gates, additional counter-measures should be implemented to address residual error impacts, with the drawing of specific gate types being an efficient strategy to achieve this goal in superconducting quantum devices. Drawing of faulty gates represents an extremely costly strategy to achieve this goal in superconducting quantum devices. Furthermore, the integration of this error-mitigation strategy through latent inverse methods to enhance the performance of quantum circuits also leads to an improvement in sampling fidelity for a wide variety of quantum states, an essential component of many quantum computing applications. This technique presents specific benefits particularly when computing quantum systems defined by weakly entangled state families, an essential requirement for many quantum computing applications. Ultimately, the success of this error-mitigation strategy stems from its ability to efficiently amplify coherent quantum interactions between low-energy states, an essential requirement for future near-term quantum computing applications. Moreover, through an investigation into the most effective error-mitigation strategies for the solution of the H$_2$ ground-state energy problem using the variational quantum eigensolver, an efficient algorithm was developed in support of future near-term quantum computing applications. The application of machine learning in image diagnostics within pathology and radiology is undergoing significant transformation.  Despite research-based promising outcomes with ML models, there is an underlying barrier to integrating these into clinical practices due to issues of interoperability.  The DICOM standard provides specifications for the representation, storage, and exchange of digital images and related information but the standard's complexity acts as a barrier to adoption for non-expert software developers.  Therefore, there is a need for simplified data encoding methodology that adheres to the principles of the DICOM standard.  We introduce Highdicom, an open-source Python library based on the DICOM standard that facilitates the easy annotation of digital images and the output of ML models with image analysis results.  The functionality of this tool can be seen through a step-by-step example where we use Highdicom to convert ML model outputs in DICOM format and upload it to a digital pathology image viewer for multi-parameter quantitative imaging analysis.  Highdicom is made freely accessible at https://github.com/Highdicom/Highdicom.  The example Python code is accessible at https://github.com/Highdicom/Example-with-Highdicom.  The source code for the digital pathology image viewer is freely accessible at https://github.com/Imbio/ImbioPy.  Our research team is committed to continuing the development of Highdicom and we welcome collaboration and user feedback from the community to expand its capabilities.  The integration of Highdicom is intended to simplify workflows for ML model outputs in pathology and radiology, thereby accelerating the process of bringing these models into clinical use.  For further assistance, we recommend using our comprehensive user manual as referenced in [Support Website]. In recent times, deep learning models have been effectively utilized for categorizing DNA sequences based on various tasks including disease prediction and functional identification. However, the challenge persists in selecting suitable input representations for DNA sequences, as many conventional methods can be time-consuming and inefficient. Our study introduces an innovative approach for creating a representation of DNA sequences from a given task by learning a low-dimensional representation in an unsupervised manner. We apply this new method, known as unsupervised Sequence Autoencoder (U-SAE), to several categorization tasks, including melanoma classification and functional DNA classification, utilizing DNA sequence data from The Cancer Genome Atlas and Functional Annotation of Mammalian Genomics databases respectively. Our results demonstrate that the U-SAE model successfully identifies informative and visual ly distinctive features, as well as achieves high predictive accuracy for both melanoma and functional DNA classification tasks. Additionally, by comparing the performance of U-SAE with other state-of-the-art methods including DeepSeq and DeepSeq+ models, we conclude that the U-SAE method delivers the highest accuracy on a low-dimensional representation of DNA sequences. Our study reveals that the visualized sequence embeddings by U-SAE not only provide a comprehensive understanding of the created features but also contribute to a quicker and more effective categorization of DNA sequences. We publicly release the source code of U-SAE at: https://github.com/hjgirdj/Unsupervised-Learning-of-DNA-Sequence-Representation. Accurately predicting non-performing loans for individual clients is a key factor for banks to mitigate credit risk and make informed lending decisions.
This process is typically grounded in thorough credit assessments and aligned with widely accepted industry standards, drawing on information like client loan repayment histories and demographic profiles.
This study compares the performance of several machine learning models – including Random Forest, Decision tree, KNN, SVM, and XGBoost – using data from a private Ethiopian bank, to determine which model excels on KNN's 175-26 dataset.
Upon finding that XGBoost achieved 84.6% accuracy, the researchers applied permutation importance to uncover the most influential features.
From their analysis, the clients with the highest risk were predominantly male, aged 36 or older, who worked in the service sector as employees. This demographic skew highlights the need for banks to adapt their lending strategies to accommodate diverse client profiles. At the same time, the models' reliance on information about clients' employment sectors raises questions about the sector's impact on loan repayment capacity. Furthermore, the fact that age was the primary differentiator highlights the importance of accurately verifying client ages during the lending process. Ultimately, the study's findings emphasize the need for more detailed and nuanced credit evaluations that take into account the unique characteristics and conditions of individual clients. This is especially true in contexts where financial inclusion initiatives seek to expand access to formal banking services to previously underserved populations. By applying these insights, banks can reduce their actual loss rates to below the predicted rates, thereby minimizing financial losses and maximizing lending returns. Furthermore, the study's analysis offers valuable lessons and practical guidelines for individual clients and banks regarding credit risk assessment, prevention, and management. As a result, the study's contributions to credit risk literature and practice are substantial and far-reaching. Following publication of the initial study in 2020, a more recent update has enabled researchers to fine-tune their analysis by applying the SHAP approach to the XGBoost model, thereby uncovering more detailed and interactive insights about the most influential features and client demographics. This refined analysis demonstrates that demographic factors continue to play a dominant role, with the most high-risk characteristics concentrated among male clients in their late 30s working in the service sector as employees. By applying the SHAP approach, researchers have been able to create more engaging and interactive visualizations for stakeholders, thereby demonstrating how credit risk decisions are shaped by individual demographics and technical capabilities. Ultimately, the study's findings have been extended to make a significant contribution to theoretical and practical knowledge in the field

To address this limitation, we've developed a novel model, Orientation Convolutional Networks (OCNs), which can learn rotation-centric correlations. By introducing orientation-aware weights, these weights can be learned end-to-end alongside the DCNN parameters, thereby enabling the assumption of isometric pixel correlations to be violated and improved. We develop a systematic approach to study the impact of mass on the pole mass in comparison to short-distance masses like the $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ mass in QCD within a perturbative framework, specifically for the top quark and bottom quark. Our method makes use of instanton-induced calculations at two-loop order to account for heavy quark masses and extends to three-loop order for the running coefficient, enabling the calculation of mass relationships up to four-loop order through renormalization group evolution. Applying our methodology to the pole mass of the top quark, we determine the variation in the mass resulting from different heavy quark pole masses and the pole mass itself as a function of the mass ratio between heavy quarks. Our approach also yields the dependence of the $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ mass at a specific scale as a function of the mass ratio between heavy quarks. Supporting the derivation of the mass relationships is a detailed investigation of the convergence of the perturbative series, which indicates the validity of the series up to high orders, including four-loop order, for large heavy quark masses. Currently, the most trusted diagnostic tool for COVID-19 is RT-PCR, which
takes several days and sometimes produces incorrect results due to sampling
errors or mislabeled samples. Computed Tomography (CT) scans can reveal lung
infections by imaging techniques such as High-Resolution CT (HRCT), without
the need for biological sampling. Nevertheless, HRCT exposes patients to a
considerable amount of radiation, which can be reduced with low-dose CT (LDCT)
while still maintaining a reasonable diagnostic accuracy. The challenge lies in
developing an accurate and efficient LDCT-based COVID-19 diagnosis tool, which
can be applied efficiently and quickly without the need for excessive radiation. 

To overcome this challenge, we developed a time-distributed capsule network
model (TD-CAPs) that utilizes time-based capsule features to distinguish COVID-19
patients from normal subjects and pneumonia patients. Our model integrates two
key capsule enhancement modules: (a) the dynamic capsule enhancement module
(DCE) and (b) the capsule enhancement fusion module (CEF). Our experiments
showed that the proposed TD-CAPs model achieved an impressive diagnostic
precision of 90.8% for distinguishing COVID-19 patients, 87.5% for distinguishing
pneumonia patients, and 90.6% for distinguishing normal subjects, using LDCT scans
taken under low-dose conditions. This study demonstrates the efficacy of the
TD-CAPs model for accurate and efficient COVID-19 diagnosis from LDCT scans. (The
source code for this study is accessible at https://github.com/pzq1999/TD-CAPs-Noscope,
with an accompanying video at https://youtu.be/sGtUoYkS5Gk). With the rapid
global spread of the SARS-CoV-2 virus caused by COVID-19 in 2019-2020, our
study highlights the critical role of public health emergency management and
emphasizes the need for reliable medical diagnosis during crises.  The source of

This paper presents a method to calculate the percentage of orbital space in a specified area that is occupied by each satellite in every position within that space. Using the North Atlantic region as a case study, we map the orbital positions of 14 operational satellites and demonstrate that our method can effectively identify densely populated areas where collisions are more likely to occur, such as near-inertial zones. This method is especially useful for identifying areas where safety measures, such as deconfliction, may become necessary due to space occupancy constraints. Furthermore, we provide guidelines on how to implement these measures to prevent collisions and minimize the risk of loss of visibility or collisions in crowded areas of the ocean. The process begins with discretizing a CAD surface into a network of triangular elements and then fine-tunes these elements to enhance its geometry. Subsequently, a high-order quadrilateral mesh is created on the refined network, accurately representing the CAD model's intricate geometry. Unlike other mesh-generation methods, our approach uses advanced mathematical programming to optimize the mesh topology and geometry from the outset. This results in a solid foundation that incorporates crucial CAD features and ensures a high-quality mesh with desirable properties. The mesh topology and geometry are concurrently optimized through linear programming, yielding substantial gains in efficiency over traditional iterative approaches. Our method excels in its ability to produce meshes with complex quadrilateral patterns and incorporate intricate CAD features, including curved surfaces, fillets, holes, and complex boundaries. Furthermore, it outperforms existing alternatives by dynamically optimizing the mesh topology and geometry from the outset, leading to significant improvements in mesh quality and efficiency with minimal computational overhead. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through a series of examples featuring challenging features such as tiny holes, sharp corners, and curved surfaces, illustrating its ability to generate high-quality meshes with minimal support from user-defined points. In the context of an unevenly distributed classification problem, most popular classifiers are known to favor larger groups, and the nearest neighbor classifier is not immune to this phenomenon. This issue is addressed in a newly proposed statistical framework for the nearest neighbor classification method, which handles datasets with unevenly distributed labels and samples. The method involves first identifying the dominant class, then adjusting a key parameter to enhance classification performance within that class. We have successfully observed the charge-tunneling phenomenon occurring between a quantum dot and a superconducting island using a technique that employs radio-frequency sensing. Our approach has allowed us to distinguish between different types of tunneling events, specifically those driven by individual particles as well as cooperative processes involving multiple particles. By analyzing these events, we have been able to determine the underlying physical mechanisms that drive charge tunneling and identify new mechanisms that were previously not accounted for. Our research findings open up a new avenue in the study of disordered systems and propose a novel method for detecting charge tunneling events. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute to the understanding of the intricate relationships between quantum information, unconventional superconductivity, and topological effects. Our technique possesses versatile applications and can be used to investigate a range of complex systems and dynamic transitions between different physical states. One of the key benefits of this approach is that it can be employed even when the superconducting island is not initially in a superconducting state. However, this technique does not directly provide information on the topological properties of the quantum dot. To overcome this limitation, we have developed an additional method of analysis, although a full understanding of this approach requires a more in-depth discussion. Our research was conducted as a collaboration with the Ulm group led by Franz Josef Gamble. Our combined efforts have led to the recent publication of a joint paper titled "revealing charge-tunneling phenomenon between a quantum dot and a superconducting island through radio-frequency sensing," in which we have described the experimental results mentioned above. Our technique is similar to the one employed by F. N. N. von Martins et al. to detect "Cooper-pair tunneling," although our approach has some key differences. By applying classical optimization techniques, such as the "golden algorithm," to our data, we have been able to enhance the sensitivity of our measurement and detect weak "cooperative events." Our approach relies on the presence of a localized evanescent mode within the 50 $\mu$m coaxial cable span, in which the sensitivity of our measurement reaches its maximum. In summary, our research has allowed us to establish a new technique for detecting charge tunneling events, thereby contributing to the understanding of the complex relationships between quantum information, unconventional superconductivity, and topological effects. We investigate the temporal Lipschitz stability of the Hunter-Saxton equation, focusing on solutions with $\beta f$ as the time-evolving component, where $f$ satisfies certain conditions and $\beta$ is a time-independent constant. Our study demonstrates that if the initial function $f_0$ is chosen appropriately and is Lipschitz, then the solution $f(t,x)$ is temporally Lipschitz for all $t\in [0,\infty)$ and is a classical solution to the Hunter-Saxton equation within the class of $\beta f$. Furthermore, selecting $f_0$ as the spatial white noise gives rise to a stationary solution in the class of $\beta f$, which is also stable in the Birkhoff sense. In addition, we explore the temporal Lipschitz stability of the Hunter-Saxton equation when solutions are constrained to the class of nonincreasing functions. We prove that if the initial function $f$ is nonincreasing and the time-evolving component $\beta f$ is integrable, then the solution $f(t,x)$ is temporally Lipschitz under certain conditions on $\beta$. Choosing $\beta(x) = 1 + c \dist(x,\mathbb{Z})$, where $c > 0$, yields a solution that is in poor Birkhoff ergodicity. Our study shows that the solution $f(t,x)$ can be approximated by a spatially discrete solution $f_{\epsilon,t}$ as $\epsilon$ tends to zero from the left. In the process, we extend existing work on the existence, uniqueness, and well-posedness of solutions to the Hunter-Saxton equation on the torus and in the class of $\beta f$, and we also establish the well-posedness of a related semidiscrete system of the Hunter-Saxhton equation. Our results complement prior work of Childs and Holmer, who showed that solutions to the Hunter-Saxton equation exhibit spatial Lipschitz stability, and further enable us to obtain a clear, high-resolution approximation of the solution in space and time. As a result, the solution $f(t,x)$ can be efficiently numerically solved through a non-intrusive approach by discretizing only in the spatial variable while retaining a perfect solver for the temporal variable. Our study eventually leads to a simple, explicit numerical solution of the Hunter-Saxton equation on the torus with a very high degree of numerical stability. This study introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on predefined distribution types and mean duration values, this novel approach can model durations on a continuous scale and treats median duration as the natural parameter for a half-normal distribution. We explore two implementations of this method: a straightforward non-parametric approach where the median duration serves as the parameter for a half-normal distribution, and an enhanced version that fine-tunes its performance through an auxiliary mean duration prediction task. Evaluations show that the duration modelling accuracy is significantly improved, resulting in reduced error rates for the naturalistic and within-category speech synthesis tasks. Furthermore, subjective listening tests confirm that the synthetic speech durations produced by the proposed approach are more natural and accurate. The developed model will form the foundation of an open-source speech synthesis platform. The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/andreafas/median-based-duration-modeling. A demo of the speech synthesis platform can be found at https://asr2021-duration.github.io. Key evaluation results and the proposed model's source code can also be found through the UTSC HNSW search bar at https://utsc.ieec.es/research.

Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) networks attempt to improve ensemble performance by training separate subnetworks within a base model and combining their predictions. However, these networks have been found to inefficiently use parameters, hindering their adoption on constrained devices such as smartphones and AR/VR devices. This study suggests that a key issue with current MIMO frameworks lies in how they allow subnetworks to learn and share features. In response, we introduce an innovative 'unmixing' procedure for MIMO networks to facilitate shared feature learning among subnetworks. Our preliminary results demonstrate the efficacy of this modification, yielding feature sharing and better performance in smaller network configurations. Furthermore, we explore two methods for evaluating the utility of individual parameters in MIMO subnetworks and suggest that 'trimming' MIMO parameters could be a viable strategy to compact these networks without compromising performance. Our code is made available on GitHub. Overall, this study aims to contribute towards creating more efficient MIMO networks. Firstly, by identifying and addressing a key shortcoming in current MIMO frameworks, we enable shared feature learning among subnetworks. Secondly, we investigate the potential benefits of 'trimming' MIMO parameters to further compact these networks. Both proposed methods exhibit encouraging results in enhancing MIMO network efficiency with minimal performance loss. We expect these contributions to facilitate innovative design and evaluation of MIMO networks, ultimately leading to their practical application in modeling complex distributions with better compactness and reliability. Moreover, we expect the code made available on GitHub to facilitate future research and development in MIMO networks. This paper seeks to improve the field by introducing novel concepts: (1) Introducing an 'unmixing' procedure for MIMO networks to facilitate shared feature learning and potentially improve compactness and reliability. (2) Exploring the potential benefits of 'trimming' MIMO parameters to further enhance MIMO network efficiency. Though the more challenging task of efficient query performance remains unresolved, we anticipate that reducing the parameter count through 'unmixing' and 'trimming' MIMO parameters will contribute to creating more efficient MIMO networks. Nevertheless, we do not thoroughly investigate these methods, and our code remains non-interactive, which could lead to suboptimal design and evaluation. A potential extension of this work could involve incorporating these advances into existing MIMO architecture design. This study undertakes a comprehensive analysis of existing datasets pertinent to the analysis of historical documents through image-based techniques, specifically those relying on machine learning. Upon identifying a lack of comprehensive research datasets suitable for the subject area, the authors initiated a comprehensive survey of current datasets, ultimately identifying 45 distinct collections. A detailed assessment of each dataset considers the sources, timing, and provenance of the documents, as well as the challenges presented by degradation, degradation variability, orthography, abstractions, and other anomalies. The survey also examines the layout, diversity, size, and content variation within each dataset, in addition to the tasks for which annotations were provided and the specific annotations used. Where possible, the study reports results to illustrate the effectiveness of existing datasets for tasks such as document classification, script recognition, layout analysis, and associated tasks like named entity extraction. Ultimately, the study highlights the need for more comprehensive and varied testing of document analysis tasks, drawing insights into the reasons for this state of affairs and suggesting potential solutions to initiate the development of more experimental datasets in the field of historical document analysis. Finally, the study concludes with recommendations proposed to the community to inform the establishment of new public datasets. Due to the inherent elasticity in their design, industrial robots that lack advanced precision-enhancing technology are only marginally effective for machining tasks. Besides issues related to structure, temperature, and support bearings, one major factor behind elasticity is the backlash in the transmission systems. This study proposes a method for improving trajectory accuracy using supplementary sensors and a novel feedback control strategy in combination with a feed-forward compensation method based on system flexibility. For this purpose, the dynamics of a flexible robotic arm are mathematically represented through a finite element model, and contact forces between links are calculated. A feed-forward controller is used to counteract structural flexibility, and a feedback controller is employed to compensate for modeling inaccuracy and disturbances, both operating in conjunction with the conventional position tracking control system. Our simulation and experimental results demonstrate that this joint-level flatness-based feedback control can effectively counteract position inaccuracy caused by flexibility, positioning error bounds, and dynamic disturbances. Furthermore, it is shown that the introduction of this feedback controller has a negligible impact on computation load, and experimental findings validate the proposed solution. Compared to baseline conditions, the proposed solution leads to a notable enhancement of end-effector follow-up capacity, thereby showcasing its potential as an efficient strategy for increasing the precision of machinist-grade robotic arms. Our findings demonstrate the feasibility of a computational model-based strategy for enhancing the precision of robotic arms that lack advanced anti-backlash technology. This study's theoretical models and the proposed design solutions can be directly applied in real-world robotic systems, thereby contributing to advancements in robotic technology and quality-based design. Our experimental evaluation of various aspects of flexibility and disturbance dynamics in a robotic system not only sheds light on the dynamic characteristics of these systems but is readily applicable to a broad range of industrial robotic systems as well. Given the significant differences between flexible structure-based dynamics and conventional kinematic models, the methods presented in this study are used to develop innovative strategies for improving tracking precision in robotic arms that lack advanced anti-backlash technology. Our findings and the proposed design solutions can serve as a foundation for enhancing the dynamics-based modeling and control of robotic arms in the near future. Additionally, the methods presented in this study provide several potential strategies for further improvements in tracking precision in robotic arms, thereby expanding the potential of dynamics-based modeling and control in quality-based design. Our experimental evaluation of these methods in a realistic industrial setting is anticipated to contribute to enhancements in robotic technology and quality-based design. The study of how chronic diseases evolve throughout an individual's lifetime has primarily been based on an environmental perspective. This perspective considers early life experiences and later lifestyle behaviors as interacting and influencing future health paths. Despite evidence suggesting a complex interplay between genetic and environmental factors, this interaction is often overlooked in research. Since many years usually pass between early life and later life outcomes, which are often time-related events, such as death or disease recurrence, incorporating time in analyses is essential. 

Research focusing on multiple events occurring in parallel has received more attention than the dynamic relationships influencing health paths over time. Methods used to analyze data in this context, such as the multiple state analysis, typically consider three to five distinct health states while assuming no health deterioration. Since this method does not account for continuous changes in health status, similar to physical activity or blood pressure levels, additional approaches are needed. 

We propose a new multiple state analysis framework, which incorporates multiple event times and summarizes individual life paths into distinct health trajectories. This new method acknowledges that there are numerous ways to experience different health outcomes, accounting for variations in the progression and duration of disease using statistical models. 

We applied this new framework to a cohort of 32,002 patients who had a myocardial infarction as part of the Danish Cardiac Register. Our study revealed three primary heart disease trajectories, such as high-Intensity diseases that lasted long, mild to moderate diseases that persisted briefly, and late-onset diseases that had a slow progression. These findings underscore the need for distinct treatment approaches for individuals with different disease characteristics. 

Our analysis reveals that individuals with a longer disease duration were at a higher risk for another myocardial infarction in the first year after the initial one, but those with a later disease onset had a lower risk. Furthermore, we discovered that men and those who were overweight had a higher likelihood for experiencing the disease progression with a mild intensity. 

Using data from the Danish Cardiac Register, our study confirms that incorporating multiple time-related aspects from early life, lifestyle, and disease history is essential. Our findings emphasize that these multiple perspectives should be considered in research and clinical practice to create a more individualized and effective health strategy. 

At the same time, our study shows that individual life and disease paths are influenced by a complex interplay between genetic and environmental factors from conception to old age, but these interactions are not clear at this time. One widely accepted method for evaluating electronic integrals in complex molecules involves a modified version of Becke's partitioning scheme, originally designed for functions that decline rapidly over distance. This method employs overlapping grids at each atomic site, effectively dividing the integrand. Although the unaltered Becke scheme exhibits slow convergence when applied to free electronic states found in processes like photoionization, this modified version achieves efficient results comparable to those for bound states. To accomplish this, the modified scheme incorporates a unique transition mechanism where atomic weights are gradually deactivated at a distance of a few bond lengths from their respective atomic nuclei and replaced by a smoothly converging weight that tends toward unity. Following this method, the integrals associated with atomic sites are evaluated while using smaller grids, while the inter-site interactions are calculated using a larger grid with higher precision. The use of smaller grids for atomic sites leads to higher precision in electronic integrals, thereby allowing the utilization of fewer errors in free electronic states, ultimately resulting in enhanced convergence, especially at a distance of approximately three bond lengths from the atomic nuclei. Gridded data-based procedures have been developed to estimate integrals with high accuracy in the vicinity of atomic sites, as well as between atomic sites, thereby ensuring post-interpolation precision in all parts of space with minimal computational overhead. The modified scheme, accompanied by the pre-computation of some Green's functions, allows the efficient evaluation of integrals on a wide variety of test cases. Importantly, this modified scheme is free from intellectual property restrictions, thereby making it widely accessible for use. Overall, the scheme represents an essential advancement in the theory and practice of solving the molecular continuum equation using numerical methods. It has significantly enhanced the efficiency of solving the molecular continuum equation on regular grids, effectively reducing the computational time to nearly real-time for solving the first-order reduced Nelsson's equation for solving the molecular continuum equation on regular grids in three-dimensional space. Currently, the scheme is in the process of being adapted for use on graphics processing units, a task that is still in progress. Furthermore, the scheme has been found to have a range of potential new applications, including the efficient numerical solution of a wide variety of nonlinear integral equations related to the molecular continuum equation. Work on this important task is currently in progress. In a graph, a subset of vertices called the metric dimension if it ensures that each vertex's distance vector is uniquely identified by the distances to its members. The problem of finding such a subset has been explored in recent years, particularly through the new direction of parameterization, where research is focused on how quickly the problem can be solved for various limitations. Domain theory's powerdomains hold significant importance in the semantics of non-deterministic programming languages.  This paper extends powerdomains to directed spaces - a concept equivalent to T_0 monotone-determined spaces.  Powerdomain-like spaces (upper, lower, and convex powerspaces) of directed spaces are defined through free algebras, and their existence and structures are shown for any directed space.  Notably, these spaces have distinct structures compared to powerdomains of directed-complete partial orders with Scott topology and other previously-introduced powerspaces.  Moreover, it is found that powerdomain-like spaces of directed spaces lack a universal or canonical type of space-frame, leading to the existence of multiple possible space-frame constructions.  This is in contrast to powerdomains, which have a well-established and canonical frame construction.  An application of these spaces is demonstrated in the algebraic study of Scott-continuous algebras.  Specifically, it is shown that the lattices of all Scott-continuous functions and the necessary frame-lattices can be constructed from the upper powerspace of the directed space Frame(X), where X is any directed space.  This construction is significant, as it provides an alternative to the established approach of building these lattices via Scott domains.  Furthermore, the U_p space-frame construction is shown to have close ties to the concept of free algebras, which is utilized in the development of this alternate method of constructing the lattices of Scott-continuous algebras.  Ultimately, it is found that the U_p algebraic approach yields suprema that are similar to the Scott minimality property, and this method demonstrates the importance of free algebras in the semantics of non-deterministic languages, although it does so in a more general setting of directed spaces.  Additionally, the U_p space-frame construction boasts a level of generality, as it enables the study of powerdomains in the context of directed spaces, but also reveals the lack of a fully canonical frame construction in this more general setting.  The U_p space-frame construction is considered canonical for the specific and widely-studied case of upper powerdomains of directed-complete partial orders with Scott topology.  The U_p space-frame's canonicity is further emphasized through its strong ties to the established powerdomain algebraic study.  Notably, the U_p space-frame construction is shown to preserve several desirable algebraic and categorical properties, including the existence of a fully formalized and canonical homeomorphism between the upper powerspace of directed spaces

Ultimately, the mathematical relationship between the CRW and the evolution matrices of the quantum walk and the exhausted walk on a graph is also examined. In a total functions logic such as HOL, certain non-terminating functions are difficult to define directly. To overcome this limitation, a clock mechanism is often introduced to enforce termination after a specified evaluation depth. While commonly regarded as cumbersome, we argue that alternative methods of adding a clock exist, with varying levels of intrusion. We present a new approach that simplifies termination proofs without overly utilizing the clock mechanism, particularly illustrated through the context of functional big-step semantics for programming language interpretations. Additionally, we propose the development of derived rules to streamline termination proofs when utilizing the relational operator for least fixed points. By integrating these techniques, we aim to demonstrate their collaborative effectiveness in facilitating clear and concise definitions of non-terminating functions in a total functions logic. Notably, we leverage the ability to use type variables in the recursion pattern of least fixed points to define functions that are inherently non-terminating, providing an alternative method to using the relational operator for recursion over data structures. Ultimately, the combination of clock mechanisms and derived rules for termination proofs enables the direct definition of certain non-terminating functions, thereby simplifying termination proofs in the context of programming language semantics. Furthermore, we showcase the application of these techniques in the context of handling unguarded recursive calls in the definition of the tail-recursive S-closed monad, potentially extending their utilization to a broader range of non-terminating functions. Ultimately, we argue that the adoption of these techniques renders the addition of a clock mechanism largely unnecessary in the context of programming language semantics. To further the development of these techniques, we make all relevant source code available through the following repository: https://github.com/ap Cash/clk-tree.git. The corresponding HOL4 patch can be applied via the following command: patch - input hol4/clk-tree/patches/whole -p 1 < input. Conversely, the overall magnetic flux is a nonquantized entity. Additionally, this model accommodates three types of self-dual solitons profiles, characterized by a compacton, a Gaussian decay, and a power-law decay, respectively. Furthermore, we execute numerical computations to determine solutions to the self-dual equations, thereby visualizing soliton profiles under varying nonlinearity parameter conditions. We consider both cases of unified and separated gauge field and baby Skyrme components. Lastly, we conduct an energetic stability analysis of solitons using the Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield framework, thereby determining the conditions under which self-dual solitons can survive an energetic attack.
