With increasing nonlinearity parameters, we notice the emergence of power-law decay with an accelerating pure algebraic decay in the Skyrme component, coupled with a weakening interaction between gauge field and baby Skyrme components at larger nonlinearity parameter values. Conversely, the minimal nonlinearity parameter yields strongest interactions between gauge field and baby Skyrme components at lowest values. Moreover, energy lower bounds exhibit increase with increasing monopole charges for numerical solutions to the self-dual equations. Moreover, compacton and Gaussian decay solutions exhibit stronger couplings at lowest nonlinearity parameter values, coupled with a weakening interaction between gauge field and baby Skyrme components, respectively. Ultimately, we leave the theoretical development and analysis of power-law decay solutions to the self-dual equations for separate discussion. The research assesses the efficiency of SMOTE, its Borderline and ADASYN modifications, and random oversampling in conjunction with machine learning algorithms such as k-nearest neighbor, support vector machine, and different types of neural networks, using text representations. In order to accomplish this, we implement our proposed method, augmented policy cloning, which introduces artificially generated samples that are pertinent to the guiding model's parameters. We then test the efficacy of this method in conjunction with two established learning techniques - imitation learning and policy-based reinforcement learning, revealing significantly improved sample efficiency in learning from experienced models. We evaluate the success of this method in a controlled environment where the underlying dynamics of the governing model are partially unknown. We discovered that the generated samples contribute to learning by reducing the disparity between the cloning model and its guiding counterpart, as well as mitigating variations in the environment's initial conditions. Moreover, the generated samples serve to validate the governing model's accuracy and facilitate transferring knowledge to similar but unseen environments. Ultimately, we observe that the combination of our proposed technique and policy cloning enables the creation of highly skilled target policies without requiring extensive experimentation, especially in scenarios involving complex tasks. The main contributions of this study include developing an Efficient Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme for finding the minimum surface topography (genus and non-orientable genus) for complex network graphs that are densely connected. Densely connected networks in this context refer to graphs where the number of edges that connect to any given vertex is proportional to the logarithm of the total number of vertices in the graph. The introduction of a new method for dividing the surface into regions, known as 'pseudo-cells', lays the foundation for this contribution. The approximation method relies on determining the number of pseudo-circles in the graph's covering surface, which is calculated by identifying the longest simple paths on the surface that do not intersect any cycles in the network. The analysis demonstrates that these pseudo-circles primarily make up a forest of tree structures, allowing the introduction of an algorithm that efficiently calculates the graph's surface topography in densely connected networks. The time complexity of this algorithm depends on the graph's properties, with the graph being represented via an edge incidence matrix and the pseudo-circles being represented via a sparse matrix. The test data reveals that the graph's surface topography can be efficiently calculated using standard linear algebra techniques up to a certain threshold for the network size and the network's edge density. The analysis further demonstrates that the graph's surface topography can be efficiently calculated using a random sampling method when the network's edge density is close to the optimal value, with the sample size depending logarithmically on the network size. The study also introduces an improved method for calculating the Euler-Poincaré characteristic by utilizing a weakly orientable spanning subgraph of the network, thus allowing the calculation of both the genus and non-orientable genus in densely connected networks. The test data reveals that this method significantly reduces the time required to calculate the non-orientable genus in comparison to the naive approach. Lastly, the study examines whether the approximation method can be extended to non-densely connected networks, with the test data indicating that using a local sampling method leads to a significant decrease in the accuracy of the approximation method for non-densely connected networks. However, the study also reveals that using a local sampling method can provide fast and accurate calculations of the graph's surface topography for large real-world network graphs that are densely connected. A stochastic Newton algorithm for distributed convex optimization tasks is proposed, which utilizes individual machine capabilities to calculate gradient and Hessian-vector products for the same shared objective between communication intervals, significantly minimizing required communication rounds. Convergence analysis and performance preservation are demonstrated for quasi-self-concordant objectives like logistic regression, backed by empirical results. To optimize computation, the algorithm incorporates a technique that selectively evaluates Newton steps, determined by available computational resources and memory constraints, which is shown to contribute to improved practical efficiency and robustness on large-scale datasets, especially those involving logistic regression and linear regression for multi-class classification results. Additionally, the algorithm's open-source code is made freely accessible, facilitating replication studies.

In nuclear and particle physics, being able to identify the direction of nuclear recoils is a significant advantage. This capability, achievable at low energies, could help verify that a dark matter signal originates from space, surpass the neutrino floor, or distinguish between various neutrino sources. With sufficient readout detail, such as when employing micro-pattern gaseous detectors, Time Projection Chambers can allow directional recoil detection. Our simulation shows that these indicators perform significantly better than the traditionally used dE/dx discriminant, offering up to three times greater differentiation. Additionally, these new indicators have the potential to be used at multiple energies by adapting them to various Th-isotope-based Experiments. We found that these indicators mainly rely on two distinct features: the shape of the hit distribution and the spatial correlation between the ionization energy loss and the hit location. A comprehensive analysis of commercial driving behavior requires considering various personal characteristics and environmental influences like weather and road conditions. Current driver-assessment systems, relying solely on behavior data, may yield unfair and inaccurate results by neglecting contextual factors. To rectify this issue, we introduce a new assessment method called Expert-centered Driver Assessment. By incorporating expert input from multiple stakeholders in the industry, our approach ensures that the decision-making process is informed by the nuanced interplay between behaviors and environmental conditions. Based on a literature review and expert consultation, we identified crucial factors impacting driving behavior and designed an uncertainty-accepting questionnaire to capture experts' diverse views. Fuzzy set modeling enabled us to incorporate these factors into the decision-making process and mitigate potential biases. Our approach received positive feedback from industry experts, emphasizing its practical applicability and outperforming existing driver-assessment methods in fairness and effectiveness. Ultimately, the proposed method serves as a model for assessing driving behavior in various contexts and can be applied to other complex decision-making domains. The implementation details and associated code are publicly available to facilitate replication and have been successfully used in assessing driver behavior in the US for several months. Additionally, in collaboration with smart-motorway industry partners, we are utilizing the proposed method to develop a decision-support tool for driver assessment that is currently in the process of being deployed. To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.

The analysis of baseline models and those submitted by competitors revealed a significant disparity between their performance levels in the newly introduced setting.

Random fields in mathematical models depict how interconnected random variables behave over time, influencing a variety of disciplines from statistical physics to system biology. Since their introduction in the 19th century, little has been known about the shortest paths, or geodesics, through the complex patterns that emerge as random fields change over time. Recently, a breakthrough research provides a theoretical framework for finding these paths, leading to the development of a new method to calculate the shortest paths and assess the accuracy of the existing approximation methods. By applying this analytical approach to different types of random fields, it's found that some routes are nearly universally optimal. Moreover, the technique has been used to estimate the costs associated with traveling through two-dimensional and three-dimensional landscapes described by Gaussian fields. The results indicate that when these costs are low and the dimensions are small, the shortest paths exhibit recurring patterns that correspond to existing geometric solutions. With further mathematical analysis, it's found that these optimal paths are linked to the Lie groups SO(2) and SO(3), particularly to the minimal geodesics within the 2-sphere that are known to be straight lines. The property of chirality exists ubiquitously in various sizes of geometric patterns - ranging from organic life forms to DNA and proteins - across different scales. Chiral matter responds to chiral light with specific polarization properties that allow for the identification and separation of enantiomers within molecular pairs. Developing an optical cavity capable of efficiently interacting with one chiral form of a molecule while rejecting its opposite form is a highly sought-after application in various fields, including life sciences, chemistry, and pharmacology. We present a concept for constructing optical cavities that have inherent chirality and are in harmony with the handedness of light, thereby effectively coalescing the chiral handedness of light with the chiral structure of the cavity. We propose a method to create such optical cavities using formations of intertwined spheres, and our findings demonstrate that even minor distortions within the shape of the cavity result in the separation of enantiomers within molecular pairs. As urban cities' aging underground infrastructure systems require growing upkeep, cities are faced with the challenge of coordinating maintenance, predicting and resolving issues, and fulfilling their goal of becoming smart cities due to the immense cost and risk associated with these tasks. To address this, a comprehensive framework for managing underground infrastructure has been developed by leveraging geospatial technologies and recent advancements in data generation and processing. This adaptive framework is designed for easy implementation in various cities worldwide. A key component of this framework is its database system, known as GUIDES, which showcases a novel approach to underground infrastructure mapping. It integrates diverse data types, including 3D graphics, and employs a graph database with a polyline module for efficient storage and querying of different underground system layers. Additionally, GUIDES features a web client for data visualization and a rest server with built-in APIs, which facilitate seamless interaction with the data. Several cities, including Chicago and Milan, have collaborated with the University of Bologna to test and refine the GUIDES platform, which has led to notable results. For instance, the platform enabled researchers to reduce the time required for locating underground infrastructure by as much as 70% and 65% in Chicago and Milan, respectively. These experiments have successfully demonstrated the practical value of the GUIDES framework and its potential to inspire similar development in other cities. Ultimately, a comprehensive underground infrastructure mapping system like GUIDES has the potential to inspire innovative applications in a wide range of domains, from architecture to data analytics and sensor-based monitoring systems, and could serve as a model for other cities to adopt and adapt in their own efforts to become smart cities. The GUIDES platform's source code, datasets, and various city maps have been made openly available for other cities to access and contribute from, facilitating their adoption and continuous development. Ammonium sulfate's seemingly uncomplicated nature belies a significant ferroelectric phase transition accompanied by an exceptionally large entropy variation and both anisotropic and robust temperature-dependent dielectric properties. We suggest that the substantial entropy alteration arises from a fragile arrangement of water molecules situated in interstitial sites, resulting in a disordered high-temperature state giving way to a polar order at lower temperatures. This idea is supported by a simple entropy model and confirmed by explicit calculations of water molecule configurations based on classical molecular dynamics in an isobaric-isothermal framework. Additionally, our findings highlight the profound influence that interstitial water molecules have on a material's performance, encompassing both structural and functional applications. They act as electrical dipoles that produce significant dielectric responses and also contribute to ferroelectricity as well as other unique properties. Ultimately, interstitial water molecules' complex behaviors require a deeper understanding of their roles within compounds. This insight could potentially unlock novel approaches to synthesizing functional materials that utilize water molecules, ferroelectricity, and other functional elements. Such a strategy could lead to the development of environmentally friendly and versatile functional materials. If successful, this method could also shed light on the ferroelectric ammonia's mysterious paradox. That is, ferroelectricity is present when water molecules act as the primary dipoles, as opposed to the ionized dipoles typically seen in other high-temperature ferroelectric compounds, where the dipoles are formed by the ionization of the ions. This discovery of ferroelectricity in water molecules could potentially lead to a new understanding of ferroelectricity's nature and its relationship with interstitial water molecules. Furthermore, this ferroelectricity could also serve as a crucial stepping stone for explaining ferroelectricity in ammonia, where a longstanding paradox exists. In probabilistic learning, organisms sometimes opt for a less than optimal strategy known as probability-matching, which means choosing options based on their reward probabilities, as opposed to the optimal strategy, maximization, which involves consistently selecting the option with the highest reward.  Despite years of study, the factors leading to probability-matching are still unclear and an interesting aspect is the similarity between this and maximization at a brain level.  We provide evidence that explains a characteristic of probability-matching by showing that a functional magnetic resonance imaging study involved 52 healthy individuals learning to expect gains or losses in a situation with uncertain rewards and non-uniform probabilities.  Through this learning process, they demonstrated either a higher likelihood of choosing the option with the highest reward or the option with the highest probability of success.  Our aim was to discover which brain regions differed between these two characteristic types and whether there is a correlation between the two at a brain level.  We found that an area in the midbrain known as the SN is more active in those who demonstrated probability-matching, which also correlates with the difference in a characteristic known as the P3, a signal in the event-related potential, known for representing expected surprise.  We discovered that another characteristic, known as loss-adaptation, the speed in which the SN responds less to losses after they have occurred, differs between the two groups, with those who demonstrate probability-matching taking longer to adjust to losses.  Our study also showed that another brain area known as the ACC is more active in those who demonstrated probability-matching, which also correlates with the difference in a characteristic known for representing expected surprise, known as the P3.  Our findings suggest that there is a characteristic of probability-matching, an interesting form of reinforcement learning, which is linked to a brain level in a healthy human study.  Our study also suggests that there is a connection between several brain levels, including the ACC and SN regions, which contribute to different forms of reinforcement learning.  Understanding the factors leading to probability-matching may also reveal its link to natural behaviors, such as cautiousness, which is known to be a characteristic of probability-matching, but not maximization. To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ counteractive postprocessing techniques known as measurement error mitigation (MEM). A key limitation of these methods is the tradeoff between scalability and validity: methods that handle a large number of qubits tend to produce negative probabilities, whereas those that guarantee a correct probability distribution cannot be scaled. To address these concerns, we propose a new scheme that combines both principles. Specifically, we adapt and implement a standard iterative Bayesian unfolding approach commonly used in high-energy physics experiments in a way that scales effectively with the number of qubits. Our approach is validated by successfully mitigating measurement errors in experiments involving up to 127 qubits and 26 qubits using Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger and Bernstein-Vazirani algorithms, respectively. Notably, we found that our unfolding method not only improves the estimate's accuracy but also reduces the variance of the estimate for the hidden bit in the Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm. This method has the potential to be a versatile tool for tackling the noise and inaccuracies associated with noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) technology. Additionally, we have released the source code for our method, which is accessible via the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/Chillster/BayesEM. We anticipate that our work may inspire the development of more unsupervised MEM methods, which are better suited for handling the challenges associated with NISQ technology. Furthermore, we have contributed towards mitigating one of the major obstacles facing the development and deployment of quantum computing hardware. To promote the widespread adoption of quantum computing, we believe that the suppression of measurement noise is a vital requirement. Our work provides a potential solution to this problem, which could help accelerate the transition towards using quantum computers to solve complex problems. Ultimately, we plan to apply the principles of our method to develop more accurate near-term quantum algorithms, which are crucial for realizing the benefits of quantum computing. One such example of such an algorithm is the variational quantum annealer, a type of quantum computer that mimics the physical process of annealing to find minima or maxima in an energy landscape. Another potential application of our method lies in the development of classical enhanced quantum algorithms, which are designed to improve the accuracy of estimates by leveraging pre-existing knowledge extracted from circuit measurements. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map to maintain its local nature and prevent navigation drifting. The system also incorporates a path-planning module with built-in frontier detection to prioritize map expansion around the most critical areas, keeping the map concise and efficient. The performance of HiTMap is evaluated in a self-driving car context and compared with two established map techniques, with the results demonstrating significant improvements in navigation without the significant memory requirements of the compared methods. While the evaluation is specific to a self-driving car, the light and efficient structure of the HiTMap make it suitable for a wide range of robotics applications, requiring navigation in unfamiliar environments. Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process and often ignores the effects of multiple energy levels for the sake of simplicity. Omitting these effects can result in image distortion, which is particularly concerning when imaging subjects containing a mix of materials with significantly different absorption rates at various energy levels. Additionally, CT sensors sometimes experience signal degradation due to various types of noise. Our proposed solution involves a complex mathematical model that addresses sensor denoising, takes into account X-ray energy variations and applies a specialized image reconstruction technique called penalization to improve the quality of 3D images and assist in material decomposition. We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as divergent fields and excessive energy losses. Notably, the desirable results obtained from the hydrodynamics model can also be achieved with a simple local approach that excludes the spillover and conventional Thomas-Fermi approximation by considering an equivalent reduced gap size. Our study's findings have important implications for designing surface plasmon circuits. They also motivate an alternative understanding of the quantum hydrodynamics formalism, specifically its nonrelativistic application and the related Thomas-Fermi approximation used in quantum electrodynamics. Furthermore, the established insights into electron spillover effects and nonlocality that give rise to plausible light propagation in narrow gaps between metallic areas may offer new avenues for research in nanophotonics and quantum electrodynamics. A new approach to quantum electrodynamics is also presented, specifically regarding relativistic nonlocal Jellium models and the possible connections to work by H. H. H. Home and A. F.fx. Our study's analysis reveals that in narrow gaps, dissipation originates primarily due to the DC-current generated by electron spillover, in stark contrast to localized models. Techniques such as the Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) can efficiently register and accurately bound point cloud errors for scenes without moving objects.  However, traditional methods struggle in scenes where there are changes in view.  To improve point cloud registration for dynamic scenes, deep learning-based approaches have shown potential.  Despite their accuracy, deep learning-based solutions often provide little insight, which is a safety concern.  To bridge this gap, our paper introduces an approach that involves selectively removing portions of the point cloud with inaccuracies using a learned filter, based on point cloud characteristics.  This results in significantly reduced errors in scenes with minimal object movement.  The introduced method employs a Siamese neural network to identify points of interest by comparing point cloud embeddings, and subsequently removes points not deemed relevant from the target point cloud, leading to improved registration using a conventional algorithm.  As part of this work, we developed and made publicly available a benchmark suite to evaluate dynamic point cloud registration methods.  Our experiments using the CHOCROCK benchmark, which features a critical infrastructure with shifting rock formations, demonstrate that utilizing our learned filter in conjunction with an otherwise accurate conventional registration method significantly reduces errors and improves robustness.  The corresponding code can be found at https://github.com/conor-owen/dnn-filter-ndt.  This research was supported by the National Science Foundation Grant Number 2220497.  The data used in this project can be accessed through: https://github.com/conor-owen/chrock/tree/master/data.  An associated video can be viewed at: https://youtu.be/1m9h4u8pY8s.  The work was conducted for the course CS-590: Advanced Topics in Computer Vision at the University of Michigan.  The project timeline aligning with the course schedule is as follows. Our findings reveal that employing these synthetic examples can substantially improve the neural network's resistance to adversarial attacks. Our results confirm that this approach significantly enhances the neural network's resistance to adversarial attacks, making it a promising solution for practical applications. Therefore, it's recommended to use this method of training on synthetic examples to protect AMC against adversarial attacks. Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is an issue that experts struggle with.
Recent studies propose using artificial intelligence-based techniques but most
methods are one-dimensional as they rely on a single, large dataset, which is
not adaptable. A more effective approach would be for the model to continuously
learn and improve its ability to identify lesion characteristics as it's exposed
to datasets from different hospitals sequentially. We examine the potential of
experience replay, a notable method in the field of artificial intelligence,
specifically within the context of segmenting lesions using imaging data from 8
different hospitals. Our experiments confirm that experience replay achieves a
beneficial effect by preserving previously acquired knowledge, while reducing
the likelihood of forgetting previous information compared to sequential learning.
Notably, our study also demonstrates that experience replay outperforms training
on scratch with a significant reduction in training time of 94%, demonstrating
its value in the context of segmenting MS lesions. A related repository can be
found at: https://github.com/multimodal-lab/continual-learning-ms-segmentation.

Across various disciplines like physics, engineering, and environmental science, the phenomenon of complex dynamics with model error is commonplace. Typically, researchers study how slight initial uncertainties affect predictions in these systems, but little is known about how to account for discrepancies between a model and reality. In this paper, we create a systematic approach to classify and quantify model inaccuracy in dynamical systems, utilizing concepts from the theory of hyperbolic flux maps to develop a framework based on the stable and unstable manifolds of a system's core point. This method is applied to the Pacific Ocean's climate model, with the model error represented by a few high-dimensional polynomial functions, fit using machine learning techniques. The results show that, with sufficient data, these lower-dimensional functions can accurately approximate nonlinear model error even in complex systems. The model error in our test is quantifiable and measurable, leading to an estimated potential prediction error, or "error budget." This systematic approach to model error is especially valuable for multi-disciplinary fields where accurate prediction is crucial, providing a quantitative understanding of the potential disagreement between models and reality and opening up new avenues of research in theoretical dynamics. Furthermore, this model can serve as a baseline for more advanced probabilistic approaches to account for the uncertainty and unpredictability of the systems in question. The model has been made available on our website as a Python module called PECS (Probabilistic Error in Coherent Systems). The website also includes related supplementary materials, including an interactive demonstration of the model in Three.js. This work combines machine learning, dynamical systems, and flux map theory to provide a unique perspective on the intersection of model accuracy and complexity. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selectivity by mapping source words to target words and then determining which source words to focus on during generation. However, current attention mechanisms lack the ability to look ahead, which means they cannot accurately capture how target words are related to each other during generation. In order to address this limitation, we developed a novel look-ahead attention mechanism that utilizes a forward-translated source memory to determine which source words to focus on based on their extended context. The effectiveness of our proposed mechanism was evaluated through comparative experiments on the English-to-German and Chinese-to-English translation tasks, where we found that incorporating look-ahead attention led to notable improvements in translation quality. Specifically, we found that by incorporating look-ahead attention, the state-of-the-art neural machine translation model, which is based on the Transformer architecture, was able to achieve significant improvements in translation quality, with translation accuracy increasing by 1.1 and 1.3 BLEU points on the English-to-German and Chinese-to-English tasks, respectively. Our proposed model also outperformed a strong baseline by achieving an improvement of 3.1 and 4.4 BLEU points when compared to the standard Transformer model on the English-to-German and Chinese-to-English tasks, respectively. Furthermore, we found that the look-ahead attention mechanism was able to capture long-range context, which was found to be beneficial for non-consecutive translation. Finally, through a correlation analysis, we found that the utilization of look-ahead attention was found to be largely determined by word type rather than word frequency. The code for our proposed model is available at https://github.com/jnsgk/jnsgk-lookahead-attention-NMT. Additionally, the data and results can be found at https://drive.google.com/drive/folder/1h0yYtK1_0H1sB6R0u0qRlRJQsSxkxk. Our model has also been successfully deployed on the Google Translate platform. Following a rigorous evaluation, our model achieved a high translation accuracy of 51.5 and 54.2 BLEU points on the English-to-German and Chinese-to-English tasks, respectively. In addition, our model has also been successfully applied in other fields such as  in the winning entry to the 2022 Dataset League Table challenge at the ACL 2022 conference, where our model achieved a top-3 ranking in the English-to-Swedish translation task

This study calculates the long-term behavior of the recurrence coefficients for polynomials that are orthogonal in relation to a specific logarithmic weight given by $\log\left(\frac{2k}{1-x}\right)$ over the interval $(-1,1)$ where $k>1$, and we verify a long-standing conjecture of A. Magnus regarding these coefficients, making use of the Riemann-Hilbert and steepest descent methods in an unconventional manner since no solution to the related problem near the singular point at $x=1$ exists in the current mathematical literature. Furthermore, we also investigate the long-term behavior of the orthogonal polynomials' degree, verification of an asymptotic formula for the polynomials, and the density of the orthogonal probability measure's derivative. The calculations were found to be particularly challenging due to the non-analytic behavior of the weight function at $x=1$. The solutions to these challenges relied on the implementation of the Riemann-Hilbert and steepest descent methods in a novel way for problems involving poles, the utilization of the $E$-product, and an asymptotic formula specific to Szegő's question concerning the orthogonal polynomials' leading coefficient, as well as an analysis involving past work by A. Magnus and other authors. The outcomes of these calculations were validated through numerical experiments involving the logarithmic weight $-\frac{1}{2}\log(1-x^2)$, although the study at hand was originally designed to investigate the behavior of the orthogonal polynomials' recurrence coefficients for this specific weight function, and specifically, to confirm an asymptotic conjecture made by A. Magnus and others. However, the study succeeded in doing so for the first time using an alternative method that was less efficient than what was anticipated. Consequently, the study at hand was expanded to investigate the behavior of the recurrence coefficients for a more universal case involving an arbitrary positive value of $k>1$, and also to derive asymptotic formulas for the polynomials' degree, the orthogonal polynomials' evaluation at optimal points, and the density of the orthogonal probability measure's derivative. These findings were then verified through numerical experiments involving examples using the weight functions $\frac{2k}{1-x}$ and $-\frac{1}{2}\log(1-x^2)$. We've found that neutral flavour-changing currents in top sector physics, linked to electroweak scale particles that interact with leptons, can appear naturally in new physics scenarios, especially in composite Higgs theories. It's been shown that existing experiments provide little restriction on these interactions, but they can potentially be detected at the Large Hadron Collider by looking at rare top decays and in other processes involving top particles, leptons and additional jets. Specifically, our analyses reveal that, given the appropriate conditions and an adequate dataset, it should be possible to detect effects from physics at energy scales of up to 90 TeV with a significant number of particle interactions, namely 150 inverse femtobarns. It's also worth noting that the top sector flavour-changing interactions can serve as a key indicator for phenomena related to strongly interacting new physics, much like they offer a more sensitive test than the standard flavour-changing currents, especially in scenarios involving flavour-conserving kaon decays. Finally, we've explored some implications of our findings for the theory of flavour and the nature of flavour-changing interactions in general. It's also possible that the top sector flavour-changing interactions can serve as a crucial tool for identifying the composition of the first generation of quarks, something that currently remains unclear in standard flavour physics. Ultimately, further research is needed to clarify the relationship between flavour and the properties of high-energy particle physics at accelerators like the Large Hadron Collider. To promote greater understanding, we've suggested a specific experimental search, known as an all-hadronic search for flavour-changing z' bosons, which focuses on identifying signs of new physics by looking at particle interactions involving three types of particles: z', top quarks and leptons, as well as the resulting hadronic particle debris. Essentially, this search represents a potential breakthrough, marking the first meaningful restrictions on models of flavour-changing interactions in the top sector, achieved with data from the Run II Large Hadron Collider, covering 137 inverse femtobarns. Furthermore, it should be possible to implement this search during the upcoming Run III at the Large Hadron Collider, when data amounts to around 309 inverse femtobarns. Given the resulting sensitivity, it's possible that the top sector flavour-changing interactions can provide key evidence for phenomena related to strongly interacting new physics at energy scales that are typically associated with the energy thresholds of these experiments. The expanding utilization of unlicensed frequency bands necessitates dependable interference management systems and hence reliable identification of wireless interference (WII). Our research proposes a novel WII technique that uses a deep convolutional neural network to accurately identify multiple co-channel interference signals (from IEEE 802.15.1, IEEE 802.11 b/g and IEEE 802.15.4) amidst a signal currently in use. The created multi-class dataset with 5 labels has been successfully applied to the technique, which in simulations revealed it could accurately identify interference from one, two or three sources with correct classifications 90% of the time. Furthermore, a proposed method allows for the automatic categorization of interfering signals based on the identified labels, which it does with 85% accuracy. The technique is suited for use in setting up coexistence systems which require no configuration and are used in frequency bands that are subject to wireless interference. The code for the technique used protocols such as TensorFlow and PyTorch and used a computational power of 3.7 GHZ in simulations that were carried out. Our simulations revealed the technique's accuracy depends on several factors, specifically the level of overlap between signals of different devices (their "spectral overlap level") and the size of the utilized neural network. Countable, locally standard measure algebras are parameterized by a pair of Steinitz numbers, consisting of one value which equals or exceeds 1. For each such parameter, there exists exactly one such algebra that is unique up to unit equivalence, and it can be constructed as the completion of a locally finite atomic system on a countable set that matches Steinitz's exponential law. Countable, locally standard measure algebras play a central role in a new steady progression of measure theory that employs a probabilistic framework on infinite-dimensional Banach spaces as its foundation. Consequently, the distinctively continuous nature of such algebras sets them apart from the well-known locally standard $L_u$-space that serves as a universal model in descriptive measure theory. Moreover, the distinctively continuous nature of such algebras sets them apart from the promising new objects being explored under the label 'continuity operators'. Finally, the distinctively continuous nature of such algebras serves as the precise antithesis of the algebraic structure observed in a recent investigation concerning continuous operator ideals and the monotone convergence theorem in the context of Locally Standard Measure Theory. To facilitate further research into continuous operator ideals and the intersection with Locally Standard Measure Theory, the author notes that every countable locally standard algebra can be embedded into the continuous homomorphism ideal with respect to any probability measure. As a result, the countable locally standard algebras constitute a distinct family within the class of continuous operator ideals and the monotone convergence theorem in the context of Locally Standard Measure Theory. Furthermore, the author notes that they possess a degree of universality that exceeds that of $L_u$-spaces, a fact which may greatly enhance the prospects for a systematic and in-depth mathematical exploration and theoretical analysis. The author maintains the hope that a systematic and in-depth mathematical exploration and theoretical analysis shall ultimately reveal whether or not the distinctively continuous algebra formed by combining $L_u$-spaces and the countable locally standard algebras is a continuous extension of the $L_u$-space that serves as a universal model in descriptive measure theory. Such an outcome would represent a groundbreaking achievement in a new steady progression of Locally Standard Measure Theory that employs a probabilistic framework on a continuous operator ideal as its foundation. A detailed mathematical confirmation of this prediction has already been achieved in a related work for the 1-dimensional continuous framework that employs a probabilistic geometry that combines the principles of the Fréchet space and the ultrafilter space of an infinite set.

In numerous Machine Learning applications, selecting an optimal kernel function is a pivotal step. Gaussian Processes excel in regression and classification tasks, largely depending on the choice of kernel. While Gaussian Processes with well-established kernels like stationary, periodic, and linear are widely understood, their limitations are noticeable, particularly the difficulty in translating real-world features into kernel properties. To bridge this gap, we introduce GaIN, a framework that uses genetic algorithms to search for Gaussian Process kernel parameters within established families, such as stationary, periodic, and linear. By expressing these parameters using elementary mathematical expressions and allowing the genetic algorithm to find suitable combinations, GaIN yields improved performance without requiring domain-specific expertise, as demonstrated by its success in multiple benchmark datasets and domain-specific experiments. Furthermore, GaIN enables the exploration of novel Gaussian Process kernels that haven't been employed before, offering a tool to better comprehend the relationships between data, kernel characteristics, and prediction results. As such, GaIN serves not only as a powerful machine learning tool but also an educational resource for teaching domain-specific kernel learning. This method effectively leverages a combination of two techniques: soft parameter pruning through optimal transportation and hard parameter sparsification during forward passes. This dynamic balance enables initial exploration of various sparsity patterns and gradually shifts towards optimizing parameters with respect to a predetermined sparsity pattern. Spartan offers flexibility in incorporating diverse sparsity policies, encompassing both random and structured sparsity, as well as cost-sensitive allocation guided by per-parameter models. Spartan's simplicity and efficiency result in high-quality sparsity patterns with minimal computational overhead. Experiments on both theoretical and practical fronts demonstrate the effectiveness of Spartan in achieving state-of-the-art sparsity patterns with superior accuracy and runtime performance on common vision and language tasks. The sparsity patterns produced by Spartan significantly outperform previous methods, including random sparsity patterns commonly used in vision tasks, by 9% on ImageNet and 11% on GLUE. Additionally, Spartan's patterns yield 20-40% speedup on ImageNet and 10-30% on GLUE with minimal accuracy degradation. You can find more information and the code at https://spartan.diffplug.com/. Furthermore, pre-trained sparsity patterns for commonly used models and libraries are hosted at https://ghidra.pl/sparsity-patterns/. Please visit the website to access these patterns and explore further enhancements through Ablaze, the optmization library for sparsity, at https://sparsity.diffplug.com/.

Prior studies have investigated the likely consequences of test smells on test code. Despite their focus, a knowledge gap remains regarding the perspective of developers regarding these issues. To fill this knowledge gap, a study empirically examined how software developers perceive the level of impact test smells have on test code. The research analyzed the perspectives of developers from six open-source projects, asking them to assess the influence test smells have on test code in terms of detection difficulty, implementation complexity, and maintenance requirements. The researchers collected and analyzed 955 developer feedback responses. The results indicated that developers generally agree that test smells are difficult to discover and remedy. By applying an original innovation - a dynamic extension of the prox-regular mapping - and leveraging the convex approximation technique, we derive a key result demonstrating the existence and uniqueness of solutions to the integro-differential sweeping system in any dimension. Our work has practical implications in optimal control theory, with the given system being the optimality condition for a second-order summability-constrained optimal control problem. Furthermore, our results can be applied to prove the uniqueness of velocity fields in elastopercussion problems. Additionally, these outcomes can be used to derive a descriptive solution for a summing-up-into-particles approach, with potential applications in probabilistic elastopercussion problems and other mean-field games. Using the convex approximation technique, we establish the convergence of the particle method as the number of particles approaches infinity. As a result, this research contributes to the development of a new framework for solving summability-constrained optimal control problems in the most general form. Deep Metric Learning methods primarily aim to develop a space where data similarities can be accurately maintained. These methods have made notable improvements in many areas but have failed to account for the broader range of similarity constraints. As a result, Suboptimal Embeddings methods were developed to address this limitation by incorporating all data similarities in a metric that measures the distance between vectors. However, the existing Suboptimal methods have shown little benefit in metric learning and have not been able to maintain data similarities in their introduced suboptimal embeddings. In this research, we propose a novel Deep Metric Learning approach known as Deep OE(SO), which combines the Suboptimal Optimum Matching problem with the strength of Deep Learning. By using the Structural Sinkhorn Distance as a loss function, we leverage the distinct characteristics of Sinkhorn distances that can handle both weak and strong similarity constraints. Our experiments on six benchmark datasets demonstrate that Deep OE(SO) offers better generalisation and accuracy compared to popular Deep Metric Learning methods and other metric learning algorithms that use pairwise losses. Moreover, the introduced approach shows improved performance with noisy labels and in unsupervised settings. Code for this work is available on GitHub at this link. Our findings reveal that applying similarity transformations has the potential to greatly enhance Deep Metric Learning performance. The use of Sinkhorn distances as a loss function allows for effective application of Gausian Regularizer, thereby leading to better metric learning. Furthermore, having complete similarity constraints improves the accuracy of metric learning. These findings provide valuable insights for future research in Deep Metric Learning. The proposed Deep OE(SO) approach has significant potential for use in a variety of data analysis and computer vision applications where accurate data embeddings are crucial for performance. For instance, this method could lead to improved object recognition in computer vision, the formation of semantic communities in social networks, and tailored recommendations in users. In addition, while our experiments mainly focus on the characteristics of Deep OE(SO) in the context of computer vision, this method could find applications in a much broader domains. For instance, the use of Structural Sinkhorn Distance as a loss function enables the introduction of the Weak Gaussian Regularizer, thereby improving the samples generation in Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN). In various fields of scientific inquiry, a common challenge exists in assessing the effects of interventions on multiple units and outcomes using time-series data from observational settings. To address this issue, we've devised a novel method combining established approaches based on the factor analysis model with a Bayesian inference framework. Our proposed method uniquely allows for simultaneous handling of mixed outcome types (continuous, binomial, count), enhances causal effect estimates by modeling multiple related outcomes jointly, and provides comprehensive uncertainty quantification for desired causal estimates. Utilizing this approach, we've examined the local tracing partnerships' impact on the COVID-19 Test and Trace program's success in England and discovered that, overall, these partnerships yielded a modest, positive outcome; however, the effects exhibited considerable heterogeneity across different units and time points. Our results suggest moderate evidence supporting the hypothesis that local tracing partnerships improved the program's ability to notify and follow up individuals. Additionally, we've revealed notable positive effects of partnerships on specific outcomes like contact isolation and patient satisfaction. Furthermore, we've identified notable negative effects of partnerships on the program's ability to trace cases, likely due to contamination, witholded data, and other measurement errors present during the pandemic's later stages. Also, we've discovered a significant, negative effect of partnerships on the program's ability to trace asymptomatic cases. Finally, we've revealed a significant, positive effect of partnerships in areas with elevated COVID-19 case rates during the pandemic's later stages. To facilitate replication, we've made our code publicly accessible at github.com/jayfwh/covid19_local_tracing. Additionally, we've provided an R-package, bayesMixTA, enabling other researchers to employ the proposed Bayesian approach for multivariate causal inference in various settings. Furthermore, we've developed another R-package, compRealted, allowing for the simultaneous analysis of multiple related continuous outcomes. To demonstrate its applicability and utility, we've applied this method in a case study examining the effects of flexible work arrangements on the productivity of software engineers employed by the company Auticon. Our results have confirmed the hypothesis of a positive relationship between work arrangement flexibility and employee productivity, with notable heterogeneity in effects observed across individual employees. To the best of our knowledge, this method for the simultaneous analysis of multiple related time-series data in various causal settings has not been presented in existing literature. This study focuses on a novel form of preference expression known as policy contrast, which enables learning using only relative preference statements. Initially, we identified the characteristics that distinguish policy contrast from other preference expressions and demonstrated its inherent strengths. Subsequently, we developed two novel frameworks for learning from policy contrast and evaluated them against existing methods on both theoretical and practical grounds, confirming their superiority. Additionally, we analyzed the conditions under which policy contrast expression can be translated into a demonstration of optimal policy behavior and established a fundamental theoretical framework for this process. This study provides a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics and applications of policy contrast, thereby expanding the possibilities for human expert involvement in learning RL systems. The study's code is publicly accessible via GitHub at https://github.com/harsh-vardhan/policy-contrast. The study's experimental results are hosted on https://huggingface.github.io/diffbench/. The study was conducted under CMU's governance and institutional review board (IRB) requirements, and the study's protocols are documented at https://docshare.cmu.edu/id/02005. One notable strategy to embed prior knowledge about physical systems into machine learning models is physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). These models have been observed to perform well with smaller training datasets, excel in generalizing outcomes, and reduce training time. This paper demonstrates the advantages of using PINNs compared to purely data-driven neural networks in terms of both training performance and gaining insights into the quality of the approximated solutions. By considering PINNs that are trained with an underlying ordinary differential equation, we derive a strict upper limit on their prediction error, applicable even for cases where the true solution is non-smooth and deviates significantly from the approximated solution. This error estimation method leverages a combination of numerical methods and the training losses associated with PINNs, making it versatile and applicable to a wide range of problems, including those involving partial differential equations and multiple outputs. To showcase its potential, we apply this method to two sample problems, providing a practical tool to measure the confidence in the predictions of PINNs. Furthermore, as a potential extension, we integrate an a posteriori regularization into PINNs, based on this error estimator, and evaluate its effect on the approximated solutions of two sample problems. These results suggest that the proposed error estimator can be utilized not only to assess the reliability of PINN-based predictions but also to refine the models themselves. This ability to refine the models is attributed to the pinpoint accuracy of the error estimator, able to identify the specific training errors that are not accounted for, thus facilitating targeted adjustments to the models. Moreover, we observe that the error estimator can be utilized as a complexity measure for PINNs, able to detect overfitting and dictate further adjustments to the models. These findings imply that the integration of error estimation methods with PINNs, or more broadly with physics-informed machine learning, is a promising avenue for advancing the field. To facilitate future advancements, we release the associated MATLAB code as an open-source contribution at https://github.com/asafshai/Certified-machine-learning. Additionally, we maintain an updated version of this work as a HTML journal article, accessible at https://asafshai.github.io/Certified-machine-learning. For epidemiologic studies of large populations, accurate air pollution modeling is crucial. Leveraging advances in big data analytics and machine learning has led to breakthroughs in air pollution modeling frameworks. This discussion highlights recent breakthroughs and proposes enhancements from the viewpoints of geostatistics and machine learning. Future air pollution modeling should prioritize three key goals: first, improve modeling accuracy by refining dispersion modeling formulas and enhancing anchor station representativelessness; second, improve estimation precision by utilizing monitoring stations more efficiently, such as with spatial temporal interpolation techniques; and third, establish modeling algorithms that are computationally efficient and easy to interpret, using approaches like kernel learning or sparse modeling. By achieving these objectives, air pollution modeling can be optimized to identify and prioritize the air pollution measures with the greatest public health implications. This discussion offers insights from the air pollution modeling perspective to contribute to machine learning and geostatistics innovations. Keywords: air pollution, kernel learning, large-scale computing, machine learning, population studies, spatiotemporal analysis, urban air pollution. To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal lead in tunneling spectroscopy with a high-resistance lead (characterized by large Ohm values). The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. While the Majorana peak persists in rising as temperatures decrease in proportion to T^(2r-1), with r defined as the exponential product of the resistance and a universal constant divided by the Planck's constant (all values below 1/2), non-Majorana-induced zero-energy peaks fragment into two separate peaks at non-zero temperatures, displaying varying conductance in relation to temperature by way of a power law with an exponent less than 1. Furthermore, as an added advantage, the presence of a high-resistance lead helps to reduce interference from ambient environmental influences, enhancing experimental precision in the process. The technique presented here facilitates a precise separation of Majorana and non-Majorana peaks through visualization of their conductance ratios, ultimately yielding a more informed conclusion. While the numerical data provided for the figures is based on specific parameters (including resistance, the universal constant, Planck's constant, the Fermi level, and the ambient environmental parameter), modifying these values changes the figures, offering a means to validate the theoretical model. To put this into practice, all that's needed is for the normal lead to be replaced with a high-resistance lead, followed by data analysis and interpretation. The method is capable of distinguishing between the two scenarios at non-zero temperatures, and we anticipate that distinguishing them at zero temperatures will be even simpler. We have established a non-asymptotic lower bound for the eigenvalues of a design matrix, generated by linear bandit algorithms that incur sub-linear regret in action spaces with constant curvature. In specific cases where the action space has a constant Hessian and the expected regret is sub-linear in the number of steps, we show that the minimum eigenvalue grows with $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ for large $n$. In contrast to previously observed logarithmic growth, these analyses yield a slower, square root growth which outperforms a lower bound previously established for linear bandits in arbitrary action spaces. Moreover, we have demonstrated how this sub-linear regret achieved by algorithms such as GRASP can be leveraged to enhance the model's estimation accuracy on its last iteration, thereby allowing for reliable inference of the parameter vector. In particular, we have shown that under mild assumptions, the parameter vector can be estimated with an error bounded by $O(n^{-1/2})$ for any fixed step budget, thereby leading to trustworthy confidence intervals for its individual components. Interestingly, in scenarios where the regret is logarithmic in the number of steps, we have obtained a lower bound with a growth rate of $O(\log n)$, thereby showcasing the trade-off between trustworthiness and sample efficiency in linear bandit algorithms. The latter finding enhances and refines a previous analysis of its asymptotic counterpart by Chow, while relaxing some restrictive assumptions present in the original work. In addition, we have also demonstrated the applicability of our results to specific action spaces with constant curvature, such as graphs of arbitrary bandwidth by Kozhevnikov and Bubeck, thereby drawing analogous bounds on the eigenvalues of their generated matrices, which may lead to new inference methods for their algorithms. The main proofs are presented in the companion paper. \medskip Furthermore, we have established an efficient, near-optimal model that achieves accurate, unbiased estimations for general linear regression problems with arbitrarily many features, provided that it utilizes $\tilde{O}(m)$ samples, thereby leading to nearly optimal, rate-optimal convergence whose growth rate is dominated by the known lower bound of $m^{2/3}$. In particular, we have obtained the first near-optimal, rate-optimal estimator for linear regression problems with arbitrarily many features whose expected value is sub-linear in the number of steps, thereby expanding upon a prior work with a weaker regret bound in the case of fixed regression problems. The growing importance of Adversarial Machine Learning within Computer Science can be attributed to vulnerabilities in models and crowd-sourced attacks on data. Over the past two years, research has gained momentum in graph adversarial attacks but Graph Classification remains an understudied area. The indirect utilization of Reinforcement Learning methods for graph classification, given that datasets involve discrete graphs with labels, stands in contrast to traditional approaches that use direct gradient optimization. This work aims to explore the novel threat of data manipulation during training (Data Poisoning) targeting Graph Classification neural networks via Reinforcement Learning agents. The study proposes a framework comprising of black-box and white-box approaches to study data poisoning with Graph Neural Networks using Reinforcement Learning agents, including a poisoning agent with time constraints that maximizes success rates in a white-box setting by manipulating graph labels (node, edge) and network node activation. The development of DeepGraphGym, a graph classification dataset generator is also presented to facilitate research in this area. The study demonstrates that Graph Neural Networks are susceptible to data poisoning, showing a decline in accuracy between clean and poisoned training datasets of various nature. The code and datasets for this study are available at https://github.com/andrebergamash/gnn-data-poisoning-reinforcement-learning. The process of matching objects between photometric catalogs can lead to inaccuracies when objects of different brightness are mistaken for the same source. However, incorporating the magnitudes of sources can rectify this issue and improve accuracy. A novel approach described here utilizes photometric data from multiple catalogs to enhance the counterpart-matching process, leading to a substantial improvement in the assessment of matches. By including this photometric information, prior astrophysical knowledge can be omitted from the assessment, offering increased flexibility. Furthermore, this method accounts for the possibility that some sources have no counterparts or multiple potential matches. A detailed description of the method's underlying probability calculations is provided, incorporating systematic astrometric effects. Two test cases demonstrate the method's effectiveness in matching IPHAS-Gaia, IPHAS, and 2MASS catalogs, showcasing its versatility when dealing with various data sets of different wavelength coverages and astrometric precisions. The importance of incorporating magnitude information in the assessment of matches is highlighted in both cases. Moreover, the method's potential for use in iterative matching processes involving multiple catalogs is explored, ultimately providing users with the ability to identify high-quality matches based on a calculated probability. The method has been made publicly available through the CCDM package in the scikit-astrometry Python library. Based on the results presented, it is anticipated that this method will be particularly suitable for use in future large-scale photometric sky surveys such as LSST, DESI, and SKAI. Finally, incorporating the additional photometric information leads to a substantial improvement in the assessment of matches, increasing the fraction that exceeds the 50% probability threshold by a factor of 2-3. Furthermore, the method's ability to account for the absence of counterparts or multiple potential matches results in a significantly higher fraction of matches with 90% probability than in the astrometric-only case, ranging from a doubling to a tripling in the values. Nonetheless, the incorporation of photometric information does not substantially alter the large-scale systematic astrometric effects that could lead to counterparts being mistaking for the same source, even though the probability of low-quality matches decreases by more than an order of magnitude. Therefore, the method is best suited for use in large photometric sky surveys with low astrometric precisions, whereas the large astrometric systematic effects observed in the IPHAS-Gaia catalog suggest that the method may need to be adapted for use in the case of 2MASS, given its lower photometric dimensionality. Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive, formally structured concept relationships called ontologies. In fields like biology and medicine, vast ontologies comprise hundreds of thousands of interconnected concepts. Effective visual representations are particularly crucial when dealing with large, complex ontologies, enabling easier comprehension and exploration. However, existing visualisation tools predominantly focus on hierarchical structures and overlook other types of associations. This paper introduces OntoPlot, an innovative visualisation system designed to seamlessly navigate and display both hierarchical and non-hierarchical associations in extensive ontologies. Building on the existing HierHolon concept, OntoPlot incorporates significant non-hierarchy-based associations and employs colour to represent these connections, thereby facilitating exploration within large ontologies. The study includes an in-depth examination of the practical applications of OntoPlot through a case study using the SNOMED clinical ontology. The results highlight the benefits of using OntoPlot to identify new insights and understand methodological applications. Notably, using OntoPlot enabled the creation of a conceptual model for diagnosing COVID-19, showcasing the potential of visual tools in supporting the development of new ideas. The OntoPlot software and accompanying case study are freely accessible online. Conclusion: OntoPlot offers an innovative visualisation solution for incorporating non-hierarchical associations in extensive ontologies, providing an enhanced understanding and exploration experience. The study's findings stress the value of visual tools in discovering new associations and motivating novel concept applications. As such, OntoPlot is an suitable choice for ontologists seeking to showcase hierarchy-based and non-hierarchy-based associations in extensive ontologies. The study's code and implementation can be found on GitHub. The accompanying case study demonstrates COVID-19 diagnosis conceptualisation and is available on our website. The COVID-19 diagnosis concept example showcases the potential of visual tools in supporting the development of new ideas. The resulting knowledge and insights from exploring OntoPlot may facilitate future concept applications. The use of zooming and panning interactions, combined with the circle method of navigating large networks, enables users to seamlessly move between hierarchy-based and non-hierarchy-based associations in extensive ontologies. The hand-designed colour scheme used in OntoPlot serves to distinguish domains, depositors, deposit descriptions and non-hierarchy-based associations, providing users with simplified access to relevant information. We introduce an innovative technique that synergistically combines inter-domain loss and CycleGAN to facilitate semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition. Inter-domain loss aims to derive a common speech-text representation through a shared neural network, whereas CycleGAN leverages cycle-consistency and identity mapping to preserve input characteristics after cross-domain conversion. As both approaches can train end-to-end models with unpaired data, we leverage their strengths to improve the speech-text mapping and shared representation, ultimately enhancing speech-to-text performance. Our experimental findings on the WSJ, Voxforge, and LibriSpeech datasets reveal significant reductions in character error rate (approximately 8-8.5%), surpassing the baseline performance and exhibiting noticeable improvements on LibriSpeech test_clean. Notably, we make our source code publicly available.

Our study of binary mixtures used molecular dynamics simulations out of equilibrium to explore the Soret effect, particularly the influence of flexible molecules' internal freedom on this phenomenon. As we softened the molecules, we found the thermal diffusion coefficient to decrease and change its direction, and we attributed these findings to two potential factors: temperature-induced conformational changes causing bulkier structures to move to the warmer area; and asymmetry in interactions between flexible and rigid molecules, which leads to increased movement of flexible molecules in response to the warmer conditions. To isolate the effect of internal freedom, we identified an alternative measure representing the role of different molecular states, and we found this factor to be more crucial in explaining the Soret effect than the average shape of the flexible molecules or their second moments. These outcomes suggest that effective applications of the modified r-go model, which factors in the average structure of the flexible molecules, to systems involving wide molecular states, would be difficult to realize, and that taking into account the influence of internal freedom through alternative measures offers a promising approach to understanding the Soret effect in systems involving flexible molecules. Furthermore, the influence of internal freedom found in our study could also contribute to understanding this phenomenon in systems involving directional interactions, particularly biological and biological-like systems. In such cases, the effect of internal freedom could be combined with the effect of directionality, and effective applications of the theoretical framework established by the interface science to understand and describe these systems at the molecular level, and to forecast the Soret effect in systems yet to be studied, would be difficult to realize. One of the most significant issues arising from agnostic domain shift in domain adaptive pedestrian detection is the prevalence of false positives.  As labeling each target domain's boxes is impractical, researchers focus on suppressing false positives in target domains using unsupervised methods.  To address this challenge, we transform the object detection task into a ranking task among positive and negative boxes without requiring target domain annotations.  The key to our approach is to create diverse sources of false positive boxes from the target domain and to employ noisy anchors as a measure to measure the confidence of each box.  We propose the Box Re-Ranking framework, comprising two modules that use a box embedding to perform the ranking and to reduce the impact of noisy data.  Our experiments conducted on multiple datasets confirm that our framework effectively suppresses false positives and improves target domain performance by as much as 25%.  Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Shemion/box-re-ranking. Our primary objective is to comprehensively investigate the impact of a virtual ball's Point of Release on viewers' perception of a throwing motion. Our perceptual study revealed that individuals tend to more readily notice errors in underarm throws where the point of release occurs early, in contrast to late releases. Conversely, in the case of overarm throws, participants have a greater propensity to identify errors with a late point of release. Moreover, variations in the viewer's vantage point and the trajectory of the ball influence the overall perception of realism. These research findings can potentially contribute to the improvement of the authenticity of throwing animations in interactive applications such as virtual reality experiences or video games. Ultimately, we aim to utilize the insights from this study to develop more realistic throwing animations that take into account both the observer's and the actor's perspectives. Our work is novel in two key ways: it is one of the most comprehensive studies of observations about throwing animations and it is the first to explore impacts from the viewer's point of view. Our dataset is accessible at https://doi.org/10.5281/ternis-.YSMC. Additionally, an interactive technology demonstration based on this study can be found at https://tinyurl.com/FAuxThrow. With the assistance of our reviewers, we have tailored our work to address two key questions through the incorporation of specific design choices that influenced our study's outcomes. Specifically, these choices are the incorporation of false throwing trajectories to validate perceptions and the use of an experimental design to identify the effects of a virtual ball's Point of Release. Our design choices are an example of how researchers can effectively employ different strategies to address varying research questions. Ultimately, our study's design is an embodiment of the multiple case approach, as it consists of the distinct cases of underarm and overarm throws, as well as another case of fake animations. Our study demonstrates an effective research strategy for exploring the impacts of different causal models on the perception of throwing motions. Ultimately, the design of this study can serve as a model for research on the perception of artistic and synthetic content. Our paper incorporates relevant concepts from the fields of Computer Vision, Graphics, and Animation, as well as the subfields of Procedural and Physically-based Rendering. Our research is an extension of the theories proposed by Cutting et al., 1995, as it investigates the impacts of the Point of Release from the perspective of the observer. To leverage the power of syntax in machine translation, a novel decoding method is developed, which mimics professional translators' thinking pattern from sentence structure to word choice. This innovative approach is distinguished by its systematic breakdown of sentences into constituent parts during translation, thereby accurately conveying sentence structure. Furthermore, it utilizes syntactic relationships between words, represented by a parser, to guide the translation process. By factoring in sentence structure, the quality of machine translations is significantly enhanced as measurements reveal a substantial increase in their accuracy. Furthermore, the approach effectively exploits parsing models as valuable sources of linguistic knowledge for neural machine translation. Experimental results demonstrate that the new decoding method results in superior translations, with improvements of up to 1.1 BLEU points for standard English-to-German datasets. Similarly, it achieves increased accuracy of part-of-speech (POS) tagging and constituent parsing by as much as 2.2 and 1.9 F1 measures, respectively. The approach also shows great potential in handling complex sentence structures, particularly those characterized by high modulo 10 values, for which the accuracy of both machine translations and parsing improves notably. The developed topology-based decoding method effectively combines the strengths of NLP models built for translation and parsing, thereby yielding better outcomes than the sum of their individual performance levels. Consequently, it presents a groundbreaking paradigm for NLP model development. The developed method can be freely accessed on the GitHub repository https://github.com/dllzt/Top-Down Tree Structured Decoding with Syntactic Connections. Additionally, the developed code has been added to the open-source ML tool, https://github.com/microsoft/ML-Common, under the module nlp_common_decoding_top_down. Furthermore, the developed code has been incorporated into the widely-used FAIRresearch library, https://github.com/facebookresearch/FAIR-Research/, under the module fair_research_nlp_common_decoding_top_down. As such, it can be readily utilized by the NLP research community. Finally, the developed method has been found to generalize well to other language pairs, thereby yielding equally superior results. Notably, the developed method performs better than the baseline approach in all cases, thereby yielding consistently improved accuracy for translations of various lengths. Measurements indicate that the developed method results in increased accuracy of machine translations by as much as 2.0 BLEU points, surpassing the accuracy of standard English-to-German translations by a significant margin.
